Then $\begin{array} { r } { I ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ( u ) d W ( u ) } \end{array}$ defined by $( 4 . 3 . 3 )$ has the following properties. 

{i} (Continuity) As a function of the upper limit of integmtion t, the paths of I(t) are continuous. 

(ii} (Adaptivity) For each t, I(t) is $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ -measumble. 

{iii} (Linearity) If $\begin{array} { r } { I ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \Delta ( u ) d W ( u ) } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { J ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } { \boldsymbol { \Gamma } } ( u ) d W ( u ) } \end{array}$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { I ( t ) \pm J ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \left( \Delta ( u ) \pm \Gamma ( u ) \right) d W ( u ) } \end{array}$ ; furthermore, for every constant $^ { c , }$ $\begin{array} { r } { c I ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } c \Delta ( u ) d W ( u ) } \end{array}$ 

{iv} (Martingale) J(t) is a martingale. 

(v) (Ito isometry) $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbb { E } I ^ { 2 } ( t ) = \mathbb { E } \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ^ { 2 } ( u ) d u . } \end{array}$ 

{vi} (Quadratic variation) $\begin{array} { r } { [ I , I ] ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ^ { 2 } ( u ) ~ d u . } \end{array}$ 

Example 4 . 3. 2. We compute $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } W ( t ) d W ( t ) } \end{array}$ . To do that, we choose a large integer n and approximate the integrand $\varDelta ( t ) = W ( t )$ by the simple process 

$$
\Delta_ {n} (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} W (0) = 0 & \text {if} 0 \leq t <   \frac {T}{n}, \\ W \left(\frac {T}{n}\right) & \text {if} \frac {T}{n} \leq t <   \frac {2 T}{n}, \\ \vdots \\ W \left(\frac {(n - 1) T}{n}\right) & \text {if} \frac {(n - 1) T}{n} \leq t <   T, \end{array} \right.
$$

as shown in Figure 4.3.2. Then $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty }$ IE $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } | \varDelta _ { n } ( t ) - W ( t ) | ^ { 2 } d t = 0 . } \end{array}$ . By definition, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \int_ {0} ^ {T} W (t) d W (t) & = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \Delta_ {n} (t) d W (t) \\ & = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W \left(\frac {j T}{n}\right) \left[ W \left(\frac {(j + 1) T}{n}\right) - W \left(\frac {j T}{n}\right) \right]. \end{array}\tag{4.3.4}
$$

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/71f6c563-4bd5-49c7-9234-946db79f6010/3b71eee200929f5d98778c10e050ef29ba521247a4b0e05530c703f7e8ea48d7.jpg)



Fig. 4.3.2. Simple process approximating Brownian motion.


To simplify notation, we denote $\begin{array} { r } { W _ { j } = W \left( \frac { j T } { n } \right) } \end{array}$ . As a precursor to evaluating the limit in (4.3.4), we work out equation (4.3.5) below. The second equality in (4.3.5) is obtained by making the change of index $\pmb { k } = j + 1$ in the first sum. The third equality uses the fact that $\begin{array} { r } { W _ { 0 } = W ( 0 ) = 0 . } \end{array}$ . We have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} (W _ {j + 1} - W _ {j}) ^ {2} = \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j + 1} ^ {2} - \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} W _ {j + 1} + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} ^ {2} \\ = \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} W _ {k} ^ {2} - \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} W _ {j + 1} + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} ^ {2} \\ = \frac {1}{2} W _ {n} ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {k} ^ {2} - \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} W _ {j + 1} + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} ^ {2} \\ = \frac {1}{2} W _ {n} ^ {2} + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} ^ {2} - \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} W _ {j + 1} \\ = \frac {1}{2} W _ {n} ^ {2} + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} (W _ {j} - W _ {j + 1}). \end{array}\tag{4.3.5}
$$

From (4.3.5) , we conclude that 

$$
\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W _ {j} \left(W _ {j + 1} - W _ {j}\right) = \frac {1}{2} W _ {n} ^ {2} - \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left(W _ {j + 1} - W _ {j}\right) ^ {2}.
$$

In the original notation, this is 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W \left(\frac {j T}{n}\right) \left[ W \left(\frac {(j + 1) T}{n}\right) - W \left(\frac {j T}{n}\right) \right] \\ = \frac {1}{2} W ^ {2} (T) - \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ W \left(\frac {(j + 1) T}{n}\right) - W \left(\frac {j T}{n}\right) \right] ^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

Letting $n \to \infty$ in (4.3.4) and using this equation, we get 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} W (t) d W (t) = \frac {1}{2} W ^ {2} (T) - \frac {1}{2} [ W, W ] (T) = \frac {1}{2} W ^ {2} (T) - \frac {1}{2} T.\tag{4.3.6}
$$

We contrast 4.3.6) with ordinary calculus. If g is a diferentiable function with $g ( 0 ) = 0$ , then 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} g (t) d g (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {T} g (t) g ^ {\prime} (t) d t = \frac {1}{2} g ^ {2} (t) \Big | _ {0} ^ {T} = \frac {1}{2} g ^ {2} (T).
$$

The extra term $- { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } T$ in 4.3.6) comes from the nonzero quadratic variation of Brownian motion and the way we constructed the Ito integral, always evaluating the integrand at the left-hand endpoint of the subinterval (see the right-hand side of (4.3.4) ) . If we were instead to evaluate at the midpoint , replacing the right-hand side of 4.3.4) by 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W \left(\frac {(j + \frac {1}{2}) T}{n}\right) \left[ W \left(\frac {(j + 1) T}{n}\right) - W \left(\frac {j T}{n}\right) \right],\tag{4.3.7}
$$

then we would not have gotten this term (see Exercise 4.4) . The integral obtained by making this replacement is called the Stratonovich integral, and the ordinary rules of calculus apply to it. However, it is inappropriate for finance. In finance, the integrand represents a position in an asset and the integrator represents the price of that asset. We cannot decide at 1 :00 p.m. which position we took at 9:00 a.m. We must decide the position at the beginning of each time interval, and the Ito integral is the limit of the gain achieved by that kind of trading the time between trades approaches zero. 

For functions $\pmb { g } ( t )$ that have a derivative, integrals such as $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } g ( t ) d g ( t )$ are not sensitive to this distinction (i.e. , the Ito integral and Stratonovich integral approximations have the same limit , which is ${ \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } g ^ { 2 } ( T ) )$ . For functions that have a nonzero quadratic variation, integrals are sensitive to where in the subintervals the approximating integrands are evaluated. 

The upper limit of integration $_ { T }$ in ( 4.3.6) is arbitrary and can be replaced by any $t \geq 0$ . In other words, 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {t} W (u) d W (u) = \frac {1}{2} W ^ {2} (t) - \frac {1}{2} t, \quad t \geq 0.\tag{4.3.8}
$$

Theorem 4.3 . l (iv) guarantees that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } W ( u ) d W ( u ) } \end{array}$ is a martingale and hence has constant expectation. At $\pmb { t = 0 }$ , this martingale is $\mathbf { 0 , }$ and hence its expectation must always be zero. This is indeed the case because $\mathbb { E } W ^ { 2 } ( t ) = t .$ If the term $- { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } t$ were not present, we would not have a martingale. D 

## 4.4 Ito-Doeblin Formula

The addition of Doeblin's name to what has traditionally been called the Ito formula is explained in the Notes, Section 4.9. 

## 4.4.1 Formula for Brownian Motion

We want a rule to "diferentiate" expressions of the form $f ( W ( t ) )$ , where $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } )$ is a diferentiable function and $W ( t )$ is a Brownian motion. If $W ( t )$ were also diferentiable, then the chain rule from ordinary calculus would give 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} f (W (t)) = f ^ {\prime} (W (t)) W ^ {\prime} (t),
$$

which could be written in diferential notation as 

$$
d f (W (t)) = f ^ {\prime} (W (t)) W ^ {\prime} (t) d t = f ^ {\prime} (W (t)) d W (t).
$$

Because $W$ has nonzero quadratic variation, the correct formula has an extra term, namely, 

$$
d f (W (t)) = f ^ {\prime} (W (t)) d W (t) + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} (W (t)) d t.\tag{4.4.1}
$$

This is the lto-Doeblin formula in diferential form. Integrating this, we obtain the lto-Doeblin formula in integral form: 

$$
f (W (t)) - f (W (0)) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime} (W (u)) d W (u) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime \prime} (W (u)) d u.\tag{4.4.2}
$$

The mathematically meaningful form of the lt6-Doeblin formula is the integral form (4.4.2) . This is because we have precise definitions for both terms appearing on the right-hand side. The first, $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } f ^ { \prime } ( W ( u ) ) d W ( u ) } \end{array}$ , is an Ito integral, defined in the previous section. The second, $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } f ^ { \prime \prime } ( W ( u ) )$ du, is an ordinary (Lebesgue) integral with respect to the time variable. 

For pencil and paper computations, the more convenient form of the ltO-Doeblin formula is the diferential form (4.4. 1 ) . There is an intuitive meaning but no precise definition for the terms $d f \left( W ( t ) \right)$ $d W ( t )$ , and dt appearing in this formula. The intuitive meaning is that $d f \big ( W ( t ) \big )$ is the change in $f \bigl ( W ( t ) \bigr )$ when t changes a "little bit" dt, $d W ( t )$ is the change in the Brownian motion when t changes a "little bit" dt, and the whole formula is exact only when the "little bit" is "infinitesimally small." Because there is no precise definition for "little bit" and "infinitesimally small," we rely on (4.4.2) to give precise meaning to (4.4. 1 ) . 

The relationship between (4.4. 1 ) and (4.4.2) is similar t o that developed in ordinary calculus to assist in changing variables in an integral. If asked to compute the indefinite integral $\begin{array} { r } { \int f ( { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { u } } } } ) f ^ { \prime } ( { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { u } } } } ) } \end{array}$ du, we might make the change of variable ${ \pmb v } = { \pmb f } ( { \pmb u } )$ and write dv $\mathbf { \bar { \rho } } = f ^ { \prime } ( u ) d u .$ , so that the indefinite integral becomes J v dv, which is $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } v ^ { 2 } + C = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } { \dot { f } } ^ { 2 } ( u ) + C$ , where $c$ is a constant of integration. The final formula 

$$
\int f (u) f ^ {\prime} (u) d u = \frac {1}{2} f ^ {2} (u) + C
$$

is correct, as can be verified by diferentiating ${ \scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } f ^ { 2 } ( u ) + C$ to get $f ( u ) f ^ { \prime } ( u )$ . We do not attempt to give precise definitions to the terms dv and du appearing in the equation $d v = f ^ { \prime } ( u )$ du used in deriving it. 

We formalize the preceding discussion with a theorem that provides a formula slightly more general than ( 4.4.2) in that it allows f to be a function of both t and x. 

Theorem 4.4.1 (ItO-Doeblin formula for Brownian motion) . Let ${ f } ( t , x )$ be a function for which the partial derivatives $f _ { t } ( t , x ) , f _ { x } ( t , x )$ , and $\scriptstyle f _ { x x } ( t , x )$ are defined and continuous, and let $W ( t )$ be a Brownian motion. Then, for every $T \geq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} f (T, W (T)) & = f (0, W (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {t} (t, W (t)) d t \\ & \quad + \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x} (t, W (t)) d W (t) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x x} (t, W (t)) d t. \end{array}\tag{4.4.3}
$$

SKETCH OF PROOF: We first show why (4.4.3) holds when $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } x ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ . In this case, $\pmb { f } ^ { \prime } ( \pmb { x } ) = \pmb { x }$ and $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) = 1$ . Let $\pmb { x } _ { j + 1 }$ and $\pmb { x } _ { j }$ be numbers. Taylor's formula implies 

$$
f (x _ {j + 1}) - f (x _ {j}) = f ^ {\prime} (x _ {j}) (x _ {j + 1} - x _ {j}) + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} (x _ {j}) (x _ {j + 1} - x _ {j}) ^ {2}.\tag{4.4.4}
$$

In this case, Taylor's formula to second order is exact (there is no remainder term) because $\pmb { f ^ { \prime \prime \prime } }$ and all higher derivatives of $f$ are zero. We return to this matter later. 

Fix $T > 0 ,$ and let $\boldsymbol { \pi } = \{ t _ { 0 } , t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { n } \}$ be a partition of $[ 0 , T ] \ ( \mathrm { i . e . , 0 = }$ $t _ { 0 } < t _ { 1 } < \cdots < t _ { n } = T )$ . We are interested in the diference between ${ \dot { f } } \left( W ( 0 ) \right)$ and $f \bigl ( W ( T ) \bigr )$ . This change in $f \left( W ( t ) \right)$ between times $t = 0$ and $\mathbf { \nabla } \mathbf { t } = T$ can be written as the sum of the changes in $f ( W ( t ) )$ over each of the subintervals $[ t _ { j } , t _ { j + 1 } ]$ . We do this and then use Taylor's formula (4.4.4) with $x _ { j } = W ( t _ { j } )$ and $x _ { j + 1 } = W ( t _ { j + 1 } )$ to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (W (T)) - f (W (0)) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \big [ f \big (W (t _ {j + 1}) \big) - f \big (W (t _ {j}) \big) \big ] \\ = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f ^ {\prime} (W (t _ {j})) \big [ W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) \big ] \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f ^ {\prime \prime} (W (t _ {j})) \big [ W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) \big ] ^ {2}. \end{array}\tag{4.4.5}
$$

For the function $\textstyle f ( x ) = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } x ^ { 2 }$ , the right-hand side of (4.4. 5) is 

$$
\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W (t _ {j}) \left[ W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) \right] + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) \right] ^ {2}.\tag{4.4.6}
$$

If we let $\| \varPi \| \to 0 .$ , the left-hand side of (4.4.5) is unafected and the terms on the right-hand side converge to an Ito integral and one-half of the quadratic variation of Brownian motion, respectively: 

$$
\begin{array}{l}f (W (T)) - f (W (0))\\= \lim _ {\| \Pi \| \rightarrow 0} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} W (t _ {j}) [ W (\iota_ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) ] + \lim _ {\| \Pi \| \rightarrow 0} \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} [ W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) ] ^ {2}\\= \int_ {0} ^ {T} W (t) d W (t) + \frac {1}{2} T\\= \int_ {0} ^ {T} f ^ {\prime} (W (t)) d W (t) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} f ^ {\prime \prime} (W (t)) d t.\end{array}\tag {4.4.7}
$$

This is the ItO-Doeblin formula in integral form for the function $\textstyle f ( x ) = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } x ^ { 2 }$ If instead of the quadratic function $f ( x ) = { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } x ^ { 2 }$ we had a general function $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } )$ , then in (4.4.5) we would have also gotten a sum of terms containing $[ W ( t _ { j + 1 } ) - W ( t _ { j } ) ] ^ { 3 }$ But according to Exercise 3.4 of Chapter 3, $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { n - 1 } \left| W ( t _ { j + 1 } ) - W ( t _ { j } ) \right| ^ { 3 } } \end{array}$ has limit zero as $\| \varPi \|  0$ . Therefore, this term would make no contribution to the final answer. 

If we take a function ${ f } ( t , x )$ of both the time variable t and the variable x, then Taylor's Theorem says that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (t _ {j + 1}, x _ {j + 1}) - f (t _ {j}, x _ {j}) \\ = f _ {t} (t _ {j}, x _ {j}) (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) + f _ {x} (t _ {j}, x _ {j}) (x _ {j + 1} - x _ {j}) \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} (t _ {j}, x _ {j}) (x _ {j + 1} - x _ {j}) ^ {2} + f _ {t x} (t _ {j}, x _ {j}) (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) (x _ {j + 1} - x _ {j}) \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2} f _ {t t} (t _ {j}, x _ {j}) (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) ^ {2} + \text { higher - order   terms. } \end{array} \tag {4}\tag{4.4.8}
$$

We replace $\pmb { x } _ { j }$ by $W ( t _ { j } )$ , replace $\pmb { x } _ { j + 1 }$ by $W ( t _ { j + 1 } )$ , and sum: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (T, W (T)) - f (0, W (0)) \\ = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ f \left(t _ {j + 1}, W \left(t _ {j + 1}\right)\right) - f \left(t _ {j}, W \left(t _ {j}\right)\right) \right] \\ = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {t} \left(t _ {j}, W \left(t _ {j}\right)\right) \left(t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}\right) + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {x} \left(t _ {j}, W \left(t _ {j}\right)\right) \left(W \left(t _ {j + 1}\right) - W \left(t _ {j}\right)\right) \\ + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {x x} \left(t _ {j}, W \left(t _ {j}\right)\right) \left(W \left(t _ {j + 1}\right) - W \left(t _ {j}\right)\right) ^ {2} \\ + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {t x} \left(t _ {j}, W \left(t _ {j}\right)\right) \left(t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}\right) \left(W \left(t _ {j + 1}\right) - W \left(t _ {j}\right)\right) \\ + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {t t} \left(t _ {j}, W \left(t _ {j}\right)\right) \left(t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}\right) ^ {2} + \text { higher   -   order   terms. } \end{array} \tag {4.4}\tag{4.4.9}
$$

When we take the limit as $\| \varPi \|  0$ , the left-hand side o f (4.4.9) is unaffected. The first term on the right-hand side of (4.4.9) contributes the ordinary (Lebesgue) integral 

$$
\lim _ {\| I \| \rightarrow 0} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {t} (t _ {j}, W (t _ {j})) (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) = \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {t} (t, W (t)) d t
$$

to the final answer. As $\| \varPi \|  0 .$ , the second term contributes the Ito integral $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } f _ { x } \big ( t , W ( t ) \big ) \mathop { d W } ( t ) } \end{array}$ . The third term contributes another ordinary (Lebesgue) integral, $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { 2 } \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } f _ { x x } ( t , W ( t ) ) ~ d t } \end{array}$ , similar to the way we obtained this integral in (4.4.7) . In other words , in the third term we can replace $\left( W ( t _ { j + 1 } ) - W ( t _ { j } ) \right) ^ { 2 }$ by $t _ { j + 1 } - t _ { j }$ . This is not an exact substitution, but when we sum the terms this substitution gives the correct limit as $\| \varPi \|  0 .$ Se Remark 3.4.4 for more discussion of this point. With this substitution, the third term on the right-hand side of (4.4.9) contributes $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { 2 } \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } f _ { x x } \big ( t , W ( t ) \big ) } \end{array}$ dt. These limits of the first three terms appear on the right-hand side of (4.4.3) . The fourth and fifth terms contribute zero. Indeed, for the fourth term, we observe that 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\lim _ {\| \Pi \| \rightarrow 0} \left| \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {t x} (t _ {j}, W (t _ {j})) (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) (W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j})) \right|\\\leq \lim _ {\| \Pi \| \rightarrow 0} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left| f _ {t x} (t _ {j}, W (t _ {j})) \right| \cdot (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) \cdot | W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) |\\\leq \lim _ {\| \Pi \| \rightarrow 0} \max _ {0 \leq k \leq n - 1} \left| W (t _ {k + 1}) - W (t _ {k}) \right| \cdot \lim _ {\| \Pi \| \rightarrow 0} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left| f _ {t x} (t _ {j}, W (t _ {j})) \right| (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j})\\= 0 \cdot \int_ {0} ^ {T} | f _ {t x} (t, W (t)) d t = 0.\end{array}\tag {4.4.10}
$$

The fifth term is treated similarly: 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\lim _ {\| I I \| \rightarrow 0} \left| \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {t t} (t _ {j}, W (t _ {j})) (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) ^ {2} \right|\\\leq \lim _ {\| I I \| \rightarrow 0} \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} | f _ {t t} (t _ {j}, W (t _ {j})) | \cdot (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) ^ {2}\\\leq \frac {1}{2} \lim _ {\| I I \| \rightarrow 0} \max _ {0 \leq k \leq n - 1} (t _ {k + 1} - t _ {k}) \cdot \lim _ {\| I I \| \rightarrow 0} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} | f _ {t t} (t _ {j}, W (t _ {j})) | (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j})\\= \frac {1}{2} \cdot 0 \cdot \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {t t} (t, W (t)) d t = 0.\end{array}\tag {4.4.17}
$$

The higher-order terms likewise contribute zero to the final answer. 

Remark $4 . 4 . 2 .$ . The fact that the sum (4.4. 1 0) of terms containing the product $( t _ { j + 1 } - t _ { j } ) \big ( W ( t _ { j + 1 } ) - W ( t _ { j } ) \big )$ has limit zero can be informally recorded by the formula dt $d W ( t ) = 0$ . Similarly, the sum ( 4.4. 1 1 ) of terms containing $( t _ { j + 1 } - t _ { j } ) ^ { 2 }$ also has limit zero, and this can be recorded by the formula dt dt = 0. We can write these terms if we like in the ltO-Doeblin formula, so that in diferential form it becomes 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d f (t, W (t)) \\ = f _ {t} (t, W (t)) d t + f _ {x} (t, W (t)) d W (t) + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} (t, W (t)) d W (t) d W (t) \\ \qquad + f _ {t x} (t, W (t)) d t d W (t) + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} (t, W (t)) d t d t, \end{array}
$$

but 

$$
d W (t) d W (t) = d t, \quad d t d W (t) = d W (t) d t = 0, \quad d t d t = 0,\tag{4.4.12}
$$

and the ItO-Doeblin formula in diferential form simplifies to 

$$
d f (t, W (t)) = f _ {t} (t, W (t)) d t + f _ {x} (t, W (t)) d W (t) + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} (t, W (t)) d t.\tag{4.4.13}
$$

In Figure 4.4. 1 , we illustrate the Taylor series approximation of the diference $f \bigl ( \bar { W } ( t _ { j + 1 } ) \bigr ) - f \bigl ( W ( t _ { j } ) \bigr )$ for a function $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } )$ that does not depend on t. The first-order approximation, which is $f ^ { \prime } \bigl ( W ( t _ { j } ) \bigr ) \bigl ( W ( t _ { j + 1 } ) - W ( t _ { j } ) \bigr )$ , has an error due to the convexity of the function f(x). Most of this error is removed by adding in the second-order term $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { 2 } f ^ { \prime \prime } \big ( W ( t _ { j } ) \big ) \big ( W ( t _ { j + 1 } ) - W ( t _ { j } ) \big ) ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , which captures the curvature of the function f(x) at $x = W ( t _ { j } )$ 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/71f6c563-4bd5-49c7-9234-946db79f6010/aca7592133b6c5d2807e8e8b158e7716ecff15e0bf3841738a6d9747904058bf.jpg)



Fig. 4.4.1. Taylor approximation to $f \bigl ( W ( t _ { j + 1 } ) \bigr ) - f \bigl ( W ( t _ { j } ) \bigr )$


In other words, 

$$
f \big (W (t _ {j + 1}) \big) - f \big (W (t _ {j}) \big) = f ^ {\prime} \big (W (t _ {j}) \big) \big (W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) \big) + \text {   small   error,   }\tag{4.4.14}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} f \big (W (t _ {j + 1}) \big) - f \big (W (t _ {j}) \big) & = f ^ {\prime} \big (W (t _ {j}) \big) \big (W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) \big) \\ & \quad + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (W (t _ {j}) \big) \big (W (t _ {j + 1}) - W (t _ {j}) \big) ^ {2} \\ & \quad + \text { smaller   error. } \end{array} \tag {4}\tag{4.4.15}
$$

In both (4.4. 14) and (4.4. 1 5 ) , as $\| \pmb { \cal { I } } \|  0 ,$ , the errors approach zero. However, before we let $\| \boldsymbol { \Pi } \|  0$ , we must first sum these equations over $j ,$ and the smaller we make lllll , the more terms there are in the sum. When we sum both sides of (4.4. 14) , the errors accumulate, and although the error in each summand approaches zero as $\| \varPi \| \to 0 ,$ the sum of the errors does not. When we use the more accurate approximation (4.4. 15), this does not happen; the limit of the sum of the smaller errors is zero. We need the extra accuracy of (4.4. 15) because the paths of Brownian motion are so volatile (i.e. , they have nonzero quadratic variation) . This extra term makes stochastic calculus diferent from ordinary calculus. 

The ItO-Doeblin formula often simplifies the computation of Ito integrals. For example, with $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } x ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , this formula says that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{2} W ^ {2} (T) = f \big (W (T) \big) - f \big (W (0) \big) \\ \qquad = \int_ {0} ^ {T} f ^ {\prime} \big (W (t) \big) d W (t) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (W (t) \big) d t \\ \qquad = \int_ {0} ^ {T} W (t) d W (t) + \frac {1}{2} T. \end{array}
$$

Rearranging terms, we have formula ( 4.3.6) and have obtained it without going through the approximation of the integrand by simple processes as we did in Example 4.3.2. 

## 4.4. 2 Formula for Ito Processes

We extend the ItO-Doeblin formula to stochastic processes more general than Brownian motion. The processes for which we develop stochastic calculus are the Ito processes defined below. Almost all stochastic processes, except those that have j umps, are ItO processes. 

Definition 4.4.3. Let $W ( t ) , \ t \ \geq \ 0 .$ , be a Brownian motion, and let $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ $\mathbf { \Delta t } \geq \mathbf { 0 } ,$ , be an associated filtration. An Ito process is a stochastic process of the form 

$$
X (t) = X (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varDelta (u) d W (u) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varTheta (u) d u,\tag{4.4.16}
$$

where $X ( 0 )$ is nonrandom and $\pmb { \varDelta } ( \pmb { u } )$ and $\boldsymbol { \Theta } ( { \boldsymbol u } )$ are adapted stochastic ${ \pmb { p r o - } }$ cesses.2 

In order to understand the volatility associated with Ito processes, we must determine the rate at which they accumulate quadratic variation. 

Lemma 4.4.4. The quadratic variation of the ItO process $( 4 . 4 . 1 6 )$ is 

$$
[ X, X ] (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varDelta^ {2} (u) d u.\tag{4.4.17}
$$

PROOF: We introduce the notation $\begin{array} { r } { I ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ( u ) d W ( u ) , R ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \theta ( u ) } \end{array}$ du. Both these processes are continuous in their upper limit of integration t. To determine the quadratic variation of X on $[ 0 , t ]$ , we choose a partition $\pi =$ $\{ t _ { 0 } , t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { n } \}$ of $[ 0 , t ] \ ( { \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } } 0 = t _ { 0 } < t _ { 1 } < \cdots < t _ { n } = t )$ and we write the sampled quadratic variation 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ X (t _ {j + 1}) - X (t _ {j}) \right] ^ {2} = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ I (t _ {j + 1}) - I (t _ {j}) \right] ^ {2} + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ R (t _ {j + 1}) - R (t _ {j}) \right] ^ {2} \\ + 2 \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ I (t _ {j + 1}) - I (t _ {j}) \right] \left[ R (t _ {j + 1}) - R (t _ {j}) \right]. \end{array}
$$

As $\| \varPi \|  0 ,$ , the first term on the right-hand side, $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { n - 1 } \left[ I ( t _ { j + 1 } ) - I ( t _ { j } ) \right] ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ converges to the quadratic variation of I on $[ 0 , t ]$ , which according to Theorem 4 . 3 . 1 (vi) is $\begin{array} { r } { [ I , I ] ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \Delta ^ { 2 } ( u ) } \end{array}$ du. The absolute value of the second term is bounded above by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \max _ {0 \leq k \leq n - 1} \left| R (t _ {k + 1}) - R (t _ {k}) \right| \cdot \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left| R (t _ {j + 1}) - R (t _ {j}) \right| \\ \qquad = \max _ {0 \leq k \leq n - 1} \left| R (t _ {k + 1}) - R (t _ {k}) \right| \cdot \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left| \int_ {t _ {j}} ^ {t _ {j + 1}} \Theta (u) d u \right| \\ \qquad \leq \max _ {0 \leq k \leq n - 1} \left| R (t _ {k + 1}) - R (t _ {k}) \right| \cdot \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \int_ {t _ {j}} ^ {t _ {j + 1}} | \Theta (u) | d u \\ \qquad = \max _ {0 \leq k \leq n - 1} \left| R (t _ {k + 1}) - R (t _ {k}) \right| \cdot \int_ {0} ^ {t} | \Theta (u) | d u, \end{array}
$$

and as $\| \varPi \| \to 0$ , this has limit $\begin{array} { r } { 0 \cdot \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } | \theta ( u ) | d u = 0 } \end{array}$ because $R ( t )$ is continuous. The absolute value of the third term is bounded above by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 2 \max _ {0 \leq k \leq n - 1} \left| I (t _ {k + 1}) - I (t _ {k}) \right| \cdot \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left| R (t _ {j + 1}) - R (t _ {j}) \right| \\ \quad \leq 2 \max _ {0 \leq k \leq n - 1} \left| I (t _ {k + 1}) - I (t _ {k}) \right| \cdot \int_ {0} ^ {t} | \Theta (u) |   d u, \end{array}
$$

and this has limit $\begin{array} { r } { 0 \cdot \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } | \theta ( u ) | ^ { 2 } d u = 0 \mathrm { a s } \| \varPi \| \to 0 } \end{array}$ because $\pmb { I } ( t )$ is continuous. We conclude that $\begin{array} { r } { [ X , X ] ( t ) = [ I , I ] ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ^ { 2 } ( u ) d u . } \end{array}$ 0 

The conclusion of Lemma 4.4.4 is most easily remembered by first writing ( 4.4. 16) in the diferential notation 

$$
d X (t) = \Delta (t) d W (t) + \Theta (t) d t\tag{4.4.18}
$$

and then using the diferential multiplication table (4.4. 12) to compute 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} d X (t) d X (t) & = \Delta^ {2} (t) d W (t) d W (t) + 2 \Delta (t) \Theta (t) d W (t) d t + \Theta^ {2} (t) d t d t \\ & = \Delta^ {2} (t) d t. \end{array} \tag {4.4}\tag{4.4.19}
$$

This says that, at each time t, the process X is accumulating quadratic variation at rate $\varDelta ^ { 2 } ( t )$ per unit time, and hence the total quadratic variation accumulated on the time interval $[ 0 , t ]$ is $\begin{array} { r } { [ X , X ] ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \Delta ^ { 2 } ( u ) } \end{array}$ du. This quadratic variation is solely due to the quadratic variation of the Ito integral $\begin{array} { r } { I ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ( u ) d W ( u ) } \end{array}$ . The ordinary integral $\begin{array} { r } { R ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \ d \theta ( u ) } \end{array}$ du has zero quadratic variation and thus contributes nothing to the quadratic variation of $X$ 

Notice in this connection that having zero quadratic variation does not necessarily mean that $R ( t )$ is nonrandom. Because $\boldsymbol { \Theta } ( \boldsymbol { u } )$ can be random, $R ( t )$ can also be random. However, $R ( t )$ is not as volatile as $I ( t )$ . At each time t, we have a good estimate of the next increment of $R ( t )$ . For small time steps $h > 0 ,$ 

$$
R (t + h) \approx R (t) + \Theta (t) h,
$$

and we know both $R ( t )$ and $\Theta ( t )$ at time t. This is like investing in a money market account at a variable interest rate. At each time, we have a good estimate of the return over the near future because we know today's interest rate. Nonetheless, the return is random because the interest rate ( e in this analogy) can change. In contrast, I is more volatile. At time $\mathbf { } ^ { t , }$ one estimate of $I ( t + h )$ is 

$$
\boldsymbol {I} (t + h) \approx \boldsymbol {I} (t) + \Delta (t) \big (\boldsymbol {W} (t + h) - \boldsymbol {W} (t) \big),
$$

but we do not know $W ( t + h ) - W ( t )$ at time t. In fact , $W ( t + h ) - W ( t )$ is independent of the information available at time t. This is like investing in a stock. 

So far we have discussed integrals with respect to time, such as $R ( t ) =$ $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \theta ( u )$ du appearing in ( 4.4. 16) and Ito integrals (integrals with respect to Brownian motion) such as $\begin{array} { r } { I ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ( u ) d W ( u ) } \end{array}$ , also appearing in (4.4. 16 ) . I n addition, we shall need integrals with respect t o Ito processes (i.e. , integrals of the form $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } T ( u ) d X ( u )$ , where $\boldsymbol { r }$ is some adapted process). We define such an integral by separating dX (t) into a $d W ( t )$ term and a dt term as in (4.4. 18 ) . 

Definition 4.4.5. Let $X ( t ) , t \geq 0$ , be an Ito process as described in Definition $4 . 4 . 3 ,$ , and let $I ( t ) , t \geq 0 ,$ be an adapted process. We define the integral with respect to an Ito process 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {t} \Gamma (u) d X (u) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Gamma (u) \Delta (u) d W (u) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Gamma (u) \Theta (u) d u.\tag{4.4.20}
$$

We again work through the sketch of the proof of Theorem 4.4. 1 , but with the Ito process $X ( t )$ replacing the Brownian motion $W ( t )$ . In place of (4.4.9) , we now have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (T, X (T)) - f (0, X (0)) \\ = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {t} (t _ {j}, X (t _ {j})) (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {x} (t _ {j}, X (t _ {j})) (X (t _ {j + 1}) - X (t _ {j})) \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {x x} (t _ {j}, X (t _ {j})) (X (t _ {j + 1}) - X (t _ {j})) ^ {2} \\ \quad + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {t x} (t _ {j}, X (t _ {j})) (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) (X (t _ {j + 1}) - X (t _ {j})) \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} f _ {t t} (t _ {j}, X (t _ {j})) (t _ {j + 1} - t _ {j}) ^ {2} + \text { higher - order   terms. } \end{array} \tag {4.4}\tag{4.4.21}
$$

The last two sums on the right-hand side have zero limits as $\| \varPi \| \to 0$ for the same reasons the analogous terms have zero limits in the sketch of the proof of Theorem 4.4. 1 (see (4.4. 10) and (4.4. 1 1 ) ) . The higher-order terms likewise have limit zero. The limit of the first term on the right-hand side of (4.4.21) i s $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } f _ { t } { \bigl ( } t , X ( t ) { \bigr ) } d t$ . The limit of the second term is 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x} (t, X (t)) d X (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x} (t, X (t)) \Delta (t) d W (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x} (t, X (t)) \Theta (t) d t.
$$

Finally, the limit of the third term on the right-hand side of (4.4. 19) is 

$$
\frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x x} (t, X (t)) d [ X, X ] (t) = \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x x} (t, X (t)) \Delta^ {2} (t) d t
$$

because the Ito process X (t) accumulates quadratic variation at rate $\varDelta ^ { 2 } ( t )$ per unit time (Lemma 4.4.4) . These considerations lead to the following generalization of Theorem 4.4. 1 . 

Theorem 4.4.6 {ItO-Doeblin formula for Ito process) . Let $X ( t )$ $t \geq 0 ,$ be an Ito process as described in Definition $4 . 4 . 3 ,$ and let ${ f } ( t , x )$ be a function for which the partial derivatives $f _ { t } ( t , x ) , f _ { x } ( t , x )$ , and $f _ { x x } ( t , x )$ are defined and continuous. Then, for every $T \geq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (T, X (T)) \\ = f (0, X (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {t} (t, X (t)) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x} (t, X (t)) d X (t) \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x x} (t, X (t)) d [ X, X ] (t) \\ = f (0, X (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {t} (t, X (t)) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x} (t, X (t)) \Delta (t) d W (t) \\ \quad + \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x} (t, X (t)) \Theta (t) d t + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {T} f _ {x x} (t, X (t)) \Delta^ {2} (t) d t. \end{array}\tag{4.4.22}
$$

Remark 4.4. 7 (Summary of stochastic calculus). Theorem 4.4.6 is stated in mathematically precise language. Every term on the right-hand side has a solid definition, and in the end the right-hand side reduces to a sum of a nonrandom quantity $f \bigl ( 0 , X ( 0 ) \bigr )$ , three ordinary (Lebesgue) integrals with respect to time, and an Ito integral. 

However, it is easier to remember and use the result of this theorem if we recast it in diferential notation. We may rewrite ( 4.4.22) as 

$$
d f (t, X (t)) = f _ {t} (t, X (t)) d t + f _ {x} (t, X (t)) d X (t) + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} (t, X (t)) d X (t) d X (t).\tag{4.4.23}
$$

The guiding principle here is that we write out the Taylor series expansion of $f \bigl ( t , X ( t ) \bigr )$ with respect to all its arguments, which in this case are t and $X ( t )$ We take this Taylor series expansion out to first order for every argument that has zero quadratic variation, which in this case is $\mathbf { } t ,$ and we take the expansion out to second order for every argument that has nonzero quadratic variation, which in this case is $X ( t )$ 

We may reduce (4.4.23) to an expression that involves only dt and $d W ( t )$ by using the diferential form (4.4. 18) of the Ito process $( \mathbf { i . e . , ~ } d X ( t ) ~ =$ $\Delta ( t ) d W ( t ) + \theta ( t ) d t )$ and the formula (4.4. 19) for the rate at which $X ( t )$ accumulates quadratic variation $( { \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } } d X ( t ) d X ( t ) = \Delta ^ { 2 } ( t ) d t )$ . This is obtained by squaring the formula for $d X ( t )$ and using the multiplication table (4.4. 12) . Making these substitutions in (4.4. 23) , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d f (t, X (t)) = f _ {t} (t, X (t)) d t + f _ {x} (t, X (t)) \varDelta (t) d W (t)} \\ & {\qquad + f _ {x} (t, X (t)) \varTheta (t) d t + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} (t, X (t)) \varDelta^ {2} (t) d t.} \end{array}\tag{4.4.24}
$$

Ito calculus is little more than repeated use of this formula in a variety of situations. 0 

## 4.4.3 Examples

We conclude this section with three examples illustrating Remark 4.4. 7. Many more examples are developed in subsequent sections and in the exercises. 

Example $4 { \cdot } 4 { \cdot } 8$ (Generalized geometric Brownian motion). Let $W ( t ) , t \geq 0 .$ be a Brownian motion, let $\mathcal { F } ( t ) , t \geq 0$ , be an associated filtration, and let ${ \pmb { \alpha } } ( t )$ and $\sigma ( t )$ be adapted processes. Define the Ito process 

$$
X (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma (s) d W (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Big (\alpha (s) - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (s) \Big) d s.\tag{4.4.25}
$$

Then 

$$
d X (t) = \sigma (t) d W (t) + \left(\alpha (t) - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (t)\right) d t,
$$

and 

$$
d X (t) d X (t) = \sigma^ {2} (t) d W (t) d W (t) = \sigma^ {2} (t) d t.
$$

Consider an asset price process given by 

$$
S (t) = S (0) e ^ {X (t)} = S (0) \exp \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma (s) d W (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left(\alpha (s) - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (s)\right) d s \right\},\tag{4.4.26}
$$

where $S ( 0 )$ is nonrandom and positive. We may write $S ( t ) = f \bigl ( X ( t ) \bigr )$ , where $f ( x ) = S ( 0 ) e ^ { x } , f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = S ( 0 ) e ^ { x }$ , and $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) = S ( 0 ) e ^ { x }$ . According to the It6- Doeblin formula 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} d S (t) & = d f \big (X (t) \big) \\ & = f ^ {\prime} \big (X (t) \big) d X (t) + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X (t) \big) d X (t) d X (t) \\ & = S (0) e ^ {X (t)} d X (t) + \frac {1}{2} S (0) e ^ {X (t)} d X (t) d X (t) \\ & = S (t) d X (t) + \frac {1}{2} S (t) d X (t) d X (t) \\ & = \alpha (t) S (t) d t + \sigma (t) S (t) d W (t). \end{array}\tag{4.4.27}
$$

The asset price $S ( t )$ has instantaneous mean rate of return ${ \pmb \alpha } ( t )$ and volatility $\sigma ( t )$ . Both the instantaneous mean rate of return and the volatility are allowed to be time-varying and random. 

This example includes all possible models of an asset price process that is always positive, has no jumps, and is driven by a single Brownian motion. Although the model is driven by a Brownian motion, the distribution of $S ( t )$ does not need to be log-normal because ${ \pmb { \alpha } } ( t )$ and $\sigma ( t )$ are allowed to be timevarying and random. If a and $\pmb { \sigma }$ are constant, we have the usual geometric Brownian motion model, and the distribution of $S ( t )$ is log-normal. 

In the case of constant a and $\pmb { \sigma }$ , ( 4.4.26) becomes 

$$
S (t) = S (0) \exp \left\{\sigma W (t) + \left(\alpha - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) t \right\}.\tag{4.4.28}
$$

One can incorrectly argue from this formula that since Brownian motion is a martingale (i.e. , it has no overall tendency to rise or fall) , the mean rate of return for $S ( t )$ must be $\scriptstyle { \alpha - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \sigma ^ { 2 } }$ . The error in this argument is that although $W ( t )$ is a martingale, $S ( 0 ) e ^ { \bar { \sigma } W ( t ) }$ is not. The convexity of the function $e ^ { \sigma x }$ imparts an upward drift to $S ( 0 ) e ^ { \sigma W ( t ) }$ . In order to correct for this, one must subtract ${ \scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \sigma ^ { 2 } t$ in the exponential; the process $S ( 0 )$ exp $\textstyle { \left\{ \sigma W ( t ) - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \sigma ^ { 2 } t \right\} }$ is a martingale (see Theorem 3.6. 1) . If we now add at in the exponential, we get $S ( t )$ , a process with mean rate of return $\pmb { \alpha }$ 

The lt6-Doeblin formula automatically keeps track of these efects, even when a and $\pmb { \sigma }$ are time-varying and random. If $\alpha = 0 ,$ , then ( 4.4.27) yields 

$$
d S (t) = \sigma (t) S (t) d W (t).
$$

Integration of both sides yields 

$$
S (t) = S (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma (s) S (s) d W (s).
$$

The right-hand side i s the nonrandom constant $S ( 0 )$ plus an Ito integral, which is a martingale, and hence (in the case $\alpha = 0 )$ 

$$
S (t) = S (0) \exp \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma (s) d W (s) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma^ {2} (s) d s \right\}\tag{4.4.29}
$$

is a martingale. In other words, the term $\sigma ( t ) S ( t ) d W ( t )$ on the right-hand side of (4.4. 27) contributes no drift , just pure volatility, to the asset price. 

When ${ \pmb { \alpha } } ( t )$ is a nonzero random process, (4.4.27) shows that it plays the role of the mean rate of return. In the case of time-varying and random ${ \pmb { \alpha } } ( t )$ we will call this the instantaneous mean rate of return since it depends on the time (and the sample path) where it is evaluated. 0 

The preceding example supplies the heart of the proof of the following theorem. 

Theorem 4.4.9 (Ito integral of a deterministic integrand) . Let $W ( s )$ $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { \mathscr { s } } \geq 0 , } \end{array}$ be a Brownian motion, and let $\pmb { \varDelta } ( \pmb { s } )$ be a nonrandom function of time. Define $\begin{array} { r } { I ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ( s ) d W ( s ) } \end{array}$ . For each $t \geq 0$ , the random variable $I ( t )$ is normally distributed with expected value zero and variance $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ^ { 2 } ( s ) } \end{array}$ ds . 

PROOF: The mean and variance of $I ( t )$ are easy to determine. Since $I ( t )$ is a martingale and $I ( 0 ) = 0 $ we must have $\mathbb { E } I ( t ) = I ( 0 ) = 0$ . Ito's isometry (Theorem 4.3. 1 (v) ) implies that 

$$
\operatorname{Var} I (t) = \mathbb {E} I ^ {2} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varDelta^ {2} (s) d s.
$$

We do not need to take the expected value of $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ^ { 2 } ( s ) } \end{array}$ ds on the right-hand side of this formula because $\pmb { \varDelta } ( \pmb { s } )$ is not random. 

The challenge is to show that $I ( t )$ is normally distributed. We shall do this by establishing that $I ( t )$ has the moment-generating function of a normal random variable with mean zero and variance $\begin{array} { r l } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ^ { 2 } ( s ) } \end{array}$ ds , which is (see (3 . 2 . 1 3 ) ) 

$$
\mathbb {E} e ^ {u I (t)} = \exp \left\{\frac {1}{2} u ^ {2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varDelta^ {2} (s) d s \right\} \mathrm{forall} u \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{4.4.30}
$$

Because $\pmb { \varDelta } ( \pmb { s } )$ is not random, ( 4.4.30) is equivalent to 

$$
\mathbb {E} \exp \left\{u I (t) - \frac {1}{2} u ^ {2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \varDelta^ {2} (s) d s \right\} = 1,
$$

which may be rewritten as 

$$
\mathbb {E} \exp \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} u \Delta (s) d W (s) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} (u \Delta (s)) ^ {2} d s \right\} = 1.\tag{4.4.31}
$$

But the process 

$$
\exp \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} u \varDelta (s) d W (s) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \bigl (u \varDelta (s) \bigr) ^ {2} d s \right\}
$$

is a martingale. Indeed, it is a generalized geometric Brownian motion with mean rate of return $\alpha = 0 ;$ ; see $\left( 4 . 4 . 2 9 \right)$ with $\sigma ( \mathscr { s } ) = \mathscr { u } \varDelta ( \mathscr { s } )$ . Furthermore, this process takes the value 1 at $\pmb { t = 0 }$ , and hence its expectation is always 1 . This gives us (4.4.31 ) . 0 

Note that (4.4.31) always holds, regardless of whether $\pmb { \varDelta } ( \pmb { s } )$ is random. However, we need to assume that $\pmb { \varDelta } ( \pmb { s } )$ is nonrandom in order to obtain the moment-generating function formula (4.4.30) from (4.4.31). When $\pmb { \varDelta } ( \pmb { s } )$ is random, there is no reason that the distribution of $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varDelta ( s ) d W ( s ) } \end{array}$ should be normal. 

Example $4 . 4 . 1 0$ (Vasicek interest rate model). Let $W ( t ) , t \geq 0 ,$ , be a Brownian motion. The Vasicek model for the interest rate process $R ( t )$ is 

$$
d R (t) = (\alpha - \beta R (t)) d t + \sigma d W (t),\tag{4.4.32}
$$

where $\alpha , \beta ,$ and $\pmb { \sigma }$ are positive constants. Equation (4.4.32) is an example of a stochastic diferential equation. It defines a random process, $R ( t )$ in this case, by giving a formula for its diferential, and the formula involves the random process itself and the diferential of a Brownian motion. 

The solution to the stochastic diferential equation ( 4.4.32) can be determined in closed form and is 

$$
R (t) = e ^ {- \beta t} R (0) + \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \big (1 - e ^ {- \beta t} \big) + \sigma e ^ {- \beta t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {\beta s} d W (s),\tag{4.4.33}
$$

a claim that we now verify. In particular, we compute the diferential of the right-hand side of (4.4.33) . To do this, we use the ItO-Doeblin formula with 

$$
f (t, x) = e ^ {- \beta t} R (0) + \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \bigl (1 - e ^ {- \beta t} \bigr) + \sigma e ^ {- \beta t} x
$$

and $\begin{array} { r } { X ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } e ^ { \beta s } d W ( s ) } \end{array}$ . Then the right-hand side of (4.4.33) is $f \bigl ( t , X ( t ) \bigr )$ The technique we are using is to separate the right-hand side into two parts: an ordinary function of two variables t and $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \mathbf { \pmb { x } } , \mathbf { \delta } }$ which has no randomness in it, and an Ito process $X ( t )$ , which contains all the randomness. For the It6-Doeblin formula, we shall need the following partial derivatives of ${ f } ( t , { \pmb x } )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f _ {t} (t, x) = - \beta e ^ {- \beta t} R (0) + \alpha e ^ {- \beta t} - \sigma \beta e ^ {- \beta t} x = \alpha - \beta f (t, x), \\ f _ {x} (t, x) = \sigma e ^ {- \beta t}, \\ f _ {x x} (t, x) = 0. \end{array}
$$

We shall also need the diferential of $X ( t )$ , which is $d X ( t ) = e ^ { \beta t } d W ( t )$ . We shall not need dX $( t ) d X ( t ) = e ^ { 2 \beta t }$ dt because $f _ { x x } ( t , x ) = 0 .$ The ItO-Doeblin formula states that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d f (t, X (t)) \\ = f _ {t} (t, X (t)) d t + f _ {x} (t, X (t)) d X (t) + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} (t, X (t)) d X (t) d X (t) \\ = (\alpha - \beta f (t, X (t))) d t + \sigma d W (t). \end{array}
$$

This shows that $f \bigl ( t , X ( t ) \bigr )$ satisfies the stochastic diferential equation (4.4.32) that defines $R ( t )$ . Moreover, $f \bigl ( 0 , X ( 0 ) \bigr ) = R ( 0 )$ . Because $f \bigl ( t , X ( t ) \bigr )$ satisfies the equation defining R(t) and has the same initial condition as $R ( t )$ , it must be the case that $f ( t , X ( t ) ) = R ( t )$ for all $t \geq 0$ 

Theorem 4.4.9 implies that the random variable $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } e ^ { \beta s } d W ( s )$ appearing on the right-hand side of (4.4.33) is normally distributed with mean zero and variance 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {2 \beta s} d s = \frac {1}{2 \beta} \big (e ^ {2 \beta t} - 1 \big).
$$

Therefore, $R ( t )$ is normally distributed with mean $\begin{array} { r } { e ^ { - \beta t } R ( 0 ) + \frac { \alpha } { \beta } \left( 1 - e ^ { - \beta t } \right) } \end{array}$ and variance $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { \sigma ^ { 2 } } { 2 \beta } ( 1 - e ^ { - 2 \beta t } ) } \end{array}$ . In particular, no matter how the parameters $\alpha > 0$ $\beta > 0$ , and $\sigma > 0$ are chosen, there is positive probability that $R ( t )$ is negative, an undesirable property for an interest rate model. 

The Vasicek model has the desirable property that the interest rate is mean-reverting. When $\begin{array} { r } { R ( t ) = \frac { \alpha } { \beta } } \end{array}$ , the drift term (the dt term) in (4.4.32) is zero. When $\begin{array} { r } { R ( t ) > \frac { \alpha } { \beta } } \end{array}$ , this term is negative, which pushes $R ( t )$ back toward $\frac { \alpha } { \beta }$ When $\begin{array} { r } { R ( t ) ~ < ~ \frac { \dot { \alpha } } { \beta } } \end{array}$ , this term is positive, which again pushes $R ( t )$ back toward $\frac { \alpha } { \beta }$ - If $\begin{array} { r } { R ( 0 ) = \frac { \alpha } { \beta } } \end{array}$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbb { E } R ( t ) = \frac { \alpha } { \beta } } \end{array}$ for all $t \geq 0 .$ If $R ( 0 ) \neq \frac { \alpha } { \beta }$ ' then $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t  \infty } \mathbb { E } R ( t ) = \frac { \alpha } { \beta } } \end{array}$ 0 

Example 4 . 4 . 1 1 (Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) interest rate model}. Let $W ( t )$ $\mathbf { \delta t } \geq 0 ,$ be a Brownian motion. The Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model for the interest rate process $R ( t )$ is 

$$
d R (t) = \left(\alpha - \beta R (t)\right) d t + \sigma \sqrt {R (t)} d W (t),\tag{4.4.34}
$$

where $\alpha , \beta ,$ and $\pmb { \sigma }$ are positive constants. Unlike the Vasicek equation (4.4.32) , the CIR equation (4.4.34) does not have a closed-form solution. The advantage of (4.4.34) over the Vasicek model is that the interest rate in the CIR model does not become negative. If $R ( t )$ reaches zero, the term multiplying dW (t) 

vanishes and the positive drift term a dt in equation ( 4.4.34) drives the interest rate back into positive territory. Like the Vasicek model, the CIR model is mean-reverting. 

Although one cannot derive a closed-form solution for (4.4.34) , the distribution of $R ( t )$ for each positive t can be determined. That computation would take us too far afield. We instead content ourselves with the derivation of the expected value and variance of $R ( t )$ . To do this, we use the function $f ( t , x ) = e ^ { \beta t } x$ and the ItO-Doeblin formula to compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \left(e ^ {\beta t} R (t)\right) \\ = d f (t, R (t)) \\ = f _ {t} (t, R (t)) d t + f _ {x} (t, R (t)) d R (t) + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} (t, R (t)) d R (t) d R (t) \\ = \beta e ^ {\beta t} R (t) d t + e ^ {\beta t} (\alpha - \beta R (t)) d t + e ^ {\beta t} \sigma \sqrt {R (t)} d W (t) \\ = \alpha e ^ {\beta t} d t + \sigma e ^ {\beta t} \sqrt {R (t)} d W (t). \end{array}\tag{4.4.35}
$$

Integration of both sides of (4.4.35) yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} e ^ {\beta t} R (t) = R (0) + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {\beta u} d u + \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {\beta u} \sqrt {R (u)} d W (u) \\ = R (0) + \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \bigl (e ^ {\beta t} - 1 \bigr) + \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {\beta u} \sqrt {R (u)} d W (u). \end{array}
$$

Recalling that the expectation of an Ito integral is zero, we obtain 

$$
e ^ {\beta t} \mathbb {E} R (t) = R (0) + \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \bigl (e ^ {\beta t} - 1 \bigr)
$$

or, equivalently, 

$$
\mathbb {E} R (t) = e ^ {- \beta t} R (0) + \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \bigl (1 - e ^ {- \beta t} \bigr).\tag{4.4.36}
$$

This is the same expectation as in the Vasicek model. 

To compute the variance of $R ( t )$ , we set $X ( t ) = e ^ { \beta t } R ( t )$ , for which we have already computed 

$$
d X (t) = \alpha e ^ {\beta t} d t + \sigma e ^ {\beta t} \sqrt {R (t)} d W (t) = \alpha e ^ {\beta t} d t + \sigma e ^ {\frac {\beta t}{2}} \sqrt {X (t)} d W (t)
$$

and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbb { E } X ( t ) = R ( 0 ) + \frac { \alpha } { \beta } \big ( e ^ { \beta t } - 1 \big ) } \end{array}$ . According to the ltO-Doeblin formula (with $f ( x ) = x ^ { 2 } , f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = 2 x$ , and $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) = 2 )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & d \big (X ^ {2} (t) \big) = 2 X (t)   d X (t) + d X (t)   d X (t) \\ & \qquad = 2 \alpha e ^ {\beta t} X (t)   d t + 2 \sigma e ^ {\frac {\beta t}{2}} X ^ {\frac {3}{2}} (t)   d W (t) + \sigma^ {2} e ^ {\beta t} X (t)   d t. \end{array}\tag{4.4.37}
$$

Integration of ( 4.4.37) yields 

$$
X ^ {2} (t) = X ^ {2} (0) + \left(2 \alpha + \sigma^ {2}\right) \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {\beta u} X (u) d u + 2 \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {\frac {\beta u}{2}} X ^ {\frac {3}{2}} (u) d W (u).
$$

Taking expectations, using the fact that the expectation of an Ito integral is zero and the formula already derived for $\mathbb { E } X ( t )$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathbb {E} X ^ {2} (t) = X ^ {2} (0) + \left(2 \alpha + \sigma^ {2}\right) \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {\beta u} \mathbb {E} X (u) d u} \\ & {\qquad = R ^ {2} (0) + \left(2 \alpha + \sigma^ {2}\right) \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {\beta u} \Big (R (0) + \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \big (e ^ {\beta u} - 1 \big) \Big) d u} \\ & {\qquad = R ^ {2} (0) + \frac {2 \alpha + \sigma^ {2}}{\beta} \Big (R (0) - \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \Big) \big (e ^ {\beta t} - 1 \big) + \frac {2 \alpha + \sigma^ {2}}{2 \beta} \cdot \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \big (e ^ {2 \beta t} - 1 \big).} \end{array}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathbb {E} R ^ {2} (t) = e ^ {- 2 \beta t} \mathbb {E} X ^ {2} (t)} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {- 2 \beta t} R ^ {2} (0) + \frac {2 \alpha + \sigma^ {2}}{\beta} \Big (R (0) - \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \Big) \big (e ^ {- \beta t} - e ^ {- 2 \beta t} \big)} \\ & {\qquad + \frac {\alpha (2 \alpha + \sigma^ {2})}{2 \beta^ {2}} \big (1 - e ^ {- 2 \beta t} \big).} \end{array}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathrm{Var} \big (R (t) \big) = \mathbb {E} R ^ {2} (t) - \big (\mathbb {E} R (t) \big) ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {- 2 \beta t} R ^ {2} (0) + \frac {2 \alpha + \sigma^ {2}}{\beta} \Big (R (0) - \frac {\alpha}{\beta} \Big) \big (e ^ {- \beta t} - e ^ {- 2 \beta t} \big)} \\ & {\qquad + \frac {\alpha \big (2 \alpha + \sigma^ {2} \big)}{2 \beta^ {2}} \big (1 - e ^ {- 2 \beta t} \big) - e ^ {- 2 \beta t} R ^ {2} (0)} \\ & {\qquad - \frac {2 \alpha}{\beta} R (0) \big (e ^ {- \beta t} - e ^ {- 2 \beta t} \big) - \frac {\alpha^ {2}}{\beta^ {2}} \big (1 - e ^ {- \beta t} \big) ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{\beta} R (0) \Big (e ^ {- \beta t} - e ^ {- 2 \beta t} \Big) + \frac {\alpha \sigma^ {2}}{2 \beta^ {2}} \big (1 - 2 e ^ {- \beta t} + e ^ {- 2 \beta t} \big).} \end{array}\tag{4.4.38}
$$

In particular, 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \operatorname{Var} (R (t)) = \frac {\alpha \sigma^ {2}}{2 \beta^ {2}}.
$$

## 4.5 Black-Scholes-Merton Equation

The addition of Merton's name to what has traditionally been called the Black-Scholes equation is explained in the Notes, Section 4o9o 

In this section, we derive the Black-Scholes-Merton partial diferential equation for the price of an option on an asset modeled as a geometric Brownian motion. The idea behind this derivation is the same as in the binomial model of Chapter 1 of Volume I, which is to determine the initial capital required to perfectly hedge a short position in the option. 

## 4.5.1 Evolution of Portfolio Value

Consider an agent who at each time t has a portfolio valued at $X ( t )$ . This portfolio invests in a money market account paying a constant rate of interest r and in a stock modeled by the geometric Brownian motion 

$$
d S (t) = \alpha S (t) d t + \sigma S (t) d W (t).\tag{4.5.1}
$$

Suppose at each time t, the investor holds $\varDelta ( t )$ shares o f stock. The position $\varDelta ( t )$ can be random but must be adapted to the filtration associated with the Brownian motion $W ( t ) , t \geq 0$ . The remainder of the portfolio value, $X ( t ) - \varDelta ( t ) S ( t )$ , is invested in the money market account. 

The diferential $d X ( t )$ for the investor's portfolio value at each time t is due to two factors, the capital gain $\Delta ( t ) d S ( t )$ on the stock position and the interest earnings $r \big ( X ( t ) - \Delta ( t ) S ( t ) \big )$ dt on the cash position. In other words, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} d X (t) & = \varDelta (t) d S (t) + r \bigl (X (t) - \varDelta (t) S (t) \bigr) d t \\ & = \varDelta (t) \bigl (\alpha S (t) d t + \sigma S (t) d W (t) \bigr) + r \bigl (X (t) - \varDelta (t) S (t) \bigr) d t \\ & = r X (t) d t + \varDelta (t) (\alpha - r) S (t) d t + \varDelta (t) \sigma S (t) d W (t). \end{array}\tag{4.5.2}
$$

The three terms appearing in the last line of (4.5.2) can be understood as follows: 

(i) an average underlying rate of return r on the portfolio, which is reflected by the term $r X ( t ) d t$ 

(ii) a risk premium $\alpha - r$ for investing in the stock, which is reflected by the term $\Delta ( t ) ( \alpha - r ) S ( t ) d t$ , and 

(i) a volatility term proportional to the size of the stock investment, which is the term $\Delta ( t ) \sigma S ( t ) d W ( t )$ 

The discrete-time analogue of equation (4.5.2) appears in Chapter 1 of Volume I as ( 1 .2. 12) : 

$$
X _ {n + 1} = \Delta_ {n} S _ {n + 1} + (1 + r) (X _ {n} - \Delta_ {n} S _ {n}).
$$

We may rearrange terms in this equation to obtain 

$$
X _ {n + 1} - X _ {n} = \Delta_ {n} (S _ {n + 1} - S _ {n}) + r (X _ {n} - \Delta_ {n} S _ {n}),\tag{4.5.3}
$$

which is analogous to the first line of (4.5.2) , except in (4.5.3) time steps forward one unit at a time, whereas in (4.5.2) time moves forward continuously. 

See Exercise 4. 10 for additional discussion of the rationale for equation ( 4.5.2) in option pricing. 

We shall often consider the discounted stock price $e ^ { - r t } S ( t )$ and the discounted portfolio value of an agent, $e ^ { - r t } X ( t )$ . According to the ItO-Doeblin formula with $f ( t , x ) = e ^ { - r t } x$ , the diferential of the discounted stock price is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \big (e ^ {- r t} S (t) \big)} \\ & {= d f \big (t, S (t) \big)} \\ & {= f _ {t} \big (t, S (t) \big) d t + f _ {x} \big (t, S (t) \big) d S (t) + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} \big (t, S (t) \big) d S (t) d S (t)} \\ & {= - r e ^ {- r t} S (t) d t + e ^ {- r t} d S (t)} \\ & {= (\alpha - r) e ^ {- r t} S (t) d t + \sigma e ^ {- r t} S (t) d W (t),} \end{array}\tag{4.5.4}
$$

and the diferential of the discounted portfolio value is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \left(e ^ {- r t} X (t)\right) \\ = d f (t, X (t)) \\ = f _ {t} (t, X (t)) d t + f _ {x} (t, X (t)) d X (t) + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} (t, X (t)) d X (t) d X (t) \\ = - r e ^ {- r t} X (t) d t + e ^ {- r t} d X (t) \\ = \Delta (t) (\alpha - r) e ^ {- r t} S (t) d t + \Delta (t) \sigma e ^ {- r t} S (t) d W (t) \\ = \Delta (t) d \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right). \end{array}\tag{4.5.5}
$$

Discounting the stock price reduces the mean rate of return from $\alpha ,$ the term multiplying $S ( t )$ dt in (4.5. 1 ) , to $\alpha - r ,$ the term multiplying $e ^ { - r t } S ( t )$ dt in (4.5.4) . Discounting the portfolio value removes the underlying rate of return $\mathbf { \vec { r } ; }$ compare the last line of (4.5.2) to the next-to-last line of (4.5.5) . The last line of (4.5.5) shows that change in the discounted portfolio value is solely due to change in the discounted stock price. 

## 4.5.2 Evolution of Option Value

Consider a European call option that pays $\left( S ( T ) - K \right) ^ { + }$ at time ${ \pmb T } .$ . The strike price K is some nonnegative constant. Black, Scholes, and Merton argued that the value of this call at any time should depend on the time (more precisely, on the time to expiration) and on the value of the stock price at that time, and of course it should also depend on the model parameters $\pmb { r }$ and $\pmb { \sigma }$ and the contractual strike price $\pmb { K }$ . Only two of these quantities, time and stock price, are variable. Following this reasoning, we let $c ( t , \pmb { x } )$ denote the value of the call at time t if the stock price at that time is $\boldsymbol { S } ( t ) = \boldsymbol { x }$ . There is nothing random about the function ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ . However, the value of the option is random; it is the stochastic process $c \big ( t , S ( t ) \big )$ obtained by replacing the dummy variable x by the random stock price $S ( t )$ in this function. At the initial time, we do not know the future stock prices $S ( t )$ and hence do not know the future option values $c \big ( t , S ( t ) \big )$ . Our goal is to determine the function ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ so we at least have a formula for the future option values in terms of the future stock prices. 

We begin by computing the diferential of $c \big ( t , S ( t ) \big )$ . According to the ltO-Doeblin formula, it is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d c (t, S (t)) \\ = c _ {t} (t, S (t)) d t + c _ {x} (t, S (t)) d S (t) + \frac {1}{2} c _ {x x} (t, S (t)) d S (t) d S (t) \\ = c _ {t} (t, S (t)) d t + c _ {x} (t, S (t)) (\alpha S (t) d t + \sigma S (t) d W (t)) \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{2} c _ {x x} (t, S (t)) \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) d t \\ = \left[ c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + \alpha S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) c _ {x x} (t, S (t)) \right] d t \\ \qquad + \sigma S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) d W (t). \end{array}\tag{4.5.6}
$$

We next compute the diferential of the discounted option price $e ^ { - r t } c { \big ( } t , S ( t ) { \big ) }$ Let $f ( t , x ) = e ^ { - r t } x$ . According to the ltO-Doeblin formula, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \big (e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \big)} \\ & {\quad = d f \left(t, c (t, S (t))\right)} \\ & {\quad = f _ {t} \big (t, c (t, S (t)) \big) d t + f _ {x} \big (t, c (t, S (t)) \big) d c (t, S (t))} \\ & {\qquad + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} \big (t, c (t, S (t)) \big) d c (t, S (t)) d c (t, S (t))} \\ & {\quad = - r e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) d t + e ^ {- r t} d c (t, S (t))} \\ & {\quad = e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r c (t, S (t)) + c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + \alpha S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) \right.} \\ & {\qquad \left. + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) c _ {x x} (t, S (t)) \right] d t + e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) d W (t)} \end{array}\tag{4.5.7}
$$

## 4.5.3 Equating the Evolutions

A (short option) hedging portfolio starts with some initial capital $X ( 0 )$ and invests in the stock and money market account so that the portfolio value $X ( t )$ at each time $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ agrees with $c ( t , S ( t ) )$ . This happens if and only if $e ^ { - r t } X ( t ) = e ^ { - r t } c ( t , S ( t ) )$ for all t. One way to ensure this equality is to make sure that 

$$
d \left(e ^ {- r t} X (t)\right) = d \left(e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t))\right) \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T)\tag{4.5.8}
$$

and $X ( 0 ) = c ( 0 , S ( 0 ) )$ . Integration of (4.5.8) from 0 to t then yields 

$$
e ^ {- r t} X (t) - X (0) = e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) - c (0, S (0)) \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T).\tag{4.5.9}
$$

If $X ( 0 ) \ = \ c ( 0 , S ( 0 ) )$ , then we can cancel this term in (4.5.9) and get the desired equality. 

Comparing (4. 5. 5) and (4.5.7) , we see that (4.5.8) holds if and only if 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Delta (t) (\alpha - r) S (t) d t + \Delta (t) \sigma S (t) d W (t) \\ = \left[ - r c (t, S (t)) + c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + \alpha S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) c _ {x x} (t, S (t)) \right] d t \\ + \sigma S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) d W (t). \end{array} \tag {4.5.10}
$$

We examine what is required in order for ( 4.5. 10) to hold. 

We first equate the $d W ( t )$ terms in (4.5. 10) , which gives 

$$
\Delta (t) = c _ {x} (t, S (t)) \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T).\tag{4.5.11}
$$

This is called the delta-hedging rule. At each time t prior to expiration, the number of shares held by the hedge of the short option position is the partial derivative with respect to the stock price of the option value at that time. This quantity, $c _ { x } ( t , S ( t ) )$ , is called the delta of the option. 

We next equate the dt terms in (4.5. 10) , using (4. 5. 1 1 ) , to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\alpha - r) S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) \\ = - r c (t, S (t)) + c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + \alpha S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) c _ {x x} (t, S (t)) \\ \text { for   all } t \in [ 0, T). \end{array} \tag {4.5}\tag{4.5.12}
$$

The term $\alpha S ( t ) c _ { x } ( t , S ( t ) )$ appears on both sides of (4.5. 12) , and after canceling $\mathbf { i t } ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} r c (t, S (t)) & = c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + r S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) c _ {x x} (t, S (t)) \\ & \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T). \end{array}\tag{4.5.13}
$$

In conclusion, we should seek a continuous function $c ( t , \boldsymbol { x } )$ that is a solution to the Black-Scholes-Merton partial diferential equation 

$$
c _ {t} (t, x) + r x c _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} x ^ {2} c _ {x x} (t, x) = r c (t, x) \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T), x \geq 0,\tag{4.5.14}
$$

and that satisfies the terminal condition 

$$
c (T, x) = (x - K) ^ {+}.\tag{4.5.15}
$$

Suppose we have found this function. If an investor starts with initial capital $X ( 0 ) = c ( 0 , S ( 0 ) )$ and uses the hedge $\Delta ( t ) = c _ { x } ( t , S ( t ) )$ , then (4 . 5 . 10) will hold for all $t \in [ 0 , T )$ . Indeed, the $d W ( t )$ terms on the left and right sides of (4.5.10) agree because $\Delta ( t ) = c _ { x } ( t , S ( t ) )$ , and the dt terms agree because (4.5. 14) guarantees (4.5.13) . Equality in (4.5. 10) gives us (4.5.9) . Canceling $X ( 0 ) = c ( 0 , S ( 0 ) )$ and $e ^ { - r t }$ in this equation, we see that $X ( t ) = c ( t , S ( t ) )$ for all $t \in [ 0 , T )$ . Taking the limit as $t \uparrow T$ and using the fact that both $X ( t )$ and $c ( t , S ( t ) )$ are continuous, we conclude that $X ( T ) = c ( T , S ( T ) ) = \left( S ( T ) - K \right) ^ { + }$ This means that the short position has been successfully hedged. No matter which of its possible paths the stock price follows, when the option expires, the agent hedging the short position has a portfolio whose value agrees with the option payof. 

## 4.5.4 Solution to the Black-Scholes-Merton Equation

The Black-Scholes-Merton equation (4.5. 14) does not involve probability. It is a partial diferential equation, and the arguments t and x are dummy variables, not random variables. One can solve it by partial diferential equation methods. In this section, however, rather than showing how to solve the equation, we shall simply present the solution and check that it works. In Subsection 5.2.5, we present a derivation of this solution based on probability theory. 

We want the Black-Scholes-Merton equation to hold for all ${ \textbf { \em x } } \geq 0$ and $t \in [ 0 , T )$ so that (4.5. 14) will hold regardless of which of its possible paths the stock price follows. If the initial stock price is positive, then the stock price is always positive, and it can take any positive value. If the initial stock price is zero, then subsequent stock prices are all zero. We cover both of these cases by asking (4.5. 14) to hold for all ${ \pmb x } \geq { \bf 0 } .$ . We do not need (4.5. 14) to hold at $t = T ,$ although we need the function ${ \boldsymbol { c } } ( t , { \boldsymbol { x } } )$ to be continuous at $\mathbf { \nabla } \mathbf { \boldsymbol { t } } = \mathbf { \nabla } T$ . If the hedge works at all times strictly prior to $\mathbf { \nabla } _ { \mathbf { T } }$ , it also works at time T because of continuity. 

Equation (4.5. 14) is a partial diferential equation of the type called backward parabolic. For such an equation, in addition to the terminal condition (4.5. 15) , one needs boundary conditions at $\pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ and $\pmb { x } = \infty$ in order to determine the solution. The boundary condition at ${ \pmb x } = { \bf 0 }$ is obtained by substituting ${ \pmb x } = { \bf 0 }$ into (4.5. 14) , which then becomes 

$$
c _ {t} (t, 0) = r c (t, 0).\tag{4.5.16}
$$

This is an ordinary diferential equation for the function $c ( t , 0 )$ of t, and the solution is 

$$
c (t, 0) = e ^ {r t} c (0, 0).
$$

Substituting $\mathbf { \nabla } t = T$ into this equation and using the fact that $c ( T , 0 ) = ( 0 -$ $K ) ^ { + } = 0 ,$ , we see that $c ( 0 , 0 ) = 0$ and hence 

$$
c (t, 0) = 0 \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{4.5.17}
$$

This is the boundary condition at $\pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ 

As $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { x }  \infty , } \end{array}$ , the function ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ grows without boq.nd. In such a case, we give the boundary condition at ${ \pmb x } = \infty$ by specifying the rate of growth. One way to specify a boundary condition at $\pmb { x } = \infty$ for the European call is 

$$
\lim _ {x \rightarrow \infty} [ c (t, x) - (x - e ^ {- r (T - t)} K) ] = 0 \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{4.5.18}
$$

In particular, $c ( t , x )$ grows at the same rate as x as $\pmb { x }  \infty$ Recall that ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ is the value at time t of a call on a stock whose price at time t is x. For large x, this call is deep in the money and very likely to end in the money. In this case, the price of the call is almost as much as the price of the forward contract discussed in Subsection 4.5.6 below (see (4. 5.26 ) ) . This is the assertion of (4. 5 . 18) . 

The solution to the Black-Scholes-Merton equation (4.5.14) with terminal condition (4.5.15) and boundary conditions (4.5.17) and (4.5. 18) is 

$$
\boldsymbol {c} (t, \boldsymbol {x}) = \boldsymbol {x} N \left(\boldsymbol {d} _ {+} (T - t, \boldsymbol {x})\right) - K e ^ {- r (T - t)} N \left(\boldsymbol {d} _ {-} (T - t, \boldsymbol {x})\right), 0 \leq t <   T, \boldsymbol {x} > 0,\tag{4.5.19}
$$

where 

$$
d _ {\pm} (\tau , x) = \frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {\tau}} \left[ \log \frac {x}{K} + \left(r \pm \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2}\right) \tau \right],\tag{4.5.20}
$$

and N is the cumulative standard normal distribution 

$$
N (y) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi}} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {y} e ^ {- \frac {z ^ {2}}{2}} d z = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi}} \int_ {- y} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- \frac {z ^ {2}}{2}} d z.\tag{4.5.21}
$$

We shall sometimes use the notation 

$$
\operatorname{BSM} (\tau , x; K, r, \sigma) = x N \left(d _ {+} (\tau , x)\right) - K e ^ {- r \tau} N \left(d _ {-} (\tau , x)\right),\tag{4.5.22}
$$

and call $\mathbf { B S M } ( \tau , x ; K , r , \sigma )$ the Black-Scholes-Merton function. In this formula, and x denote the time to expiration and the current stock price, respectively. The parameters $K , r ,$ and a are the strike price, the interest rate, and the stock volatility, respectively. 

Formula (4.5.19) does not define ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ when $\mathbf { \nabla } \mathbf { \mathbf { } } t = T \mathbf { \nabla }$ (because then $\tau = T -$ $\pmb { t = 0 }$ and this appears in the denominator in ( 4.5.20)) , nor does it define ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ when ${ \pmb x } = { \bf 0 }$ (because log x appears in (4.5.20) , and log O is not a real number) . However, (4.5.19) defines $c ( t , \pmb { x } )$ in such a way that lim ${ \bf \Phi } _ { t  T } c ( t , x ) = ( x - K ) ^ { + }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \downarrow 0 } c ( t , x ) = 0 . } \end{array}$ . Verification of all of these claims is given as Exercise 4.9. 

## 4.5.5 The Greeks

The derivatives of the function ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ of (4.5.19) with respect to various variables are called the Greeks. Two of these are derived in Exercise 4.9, namely delta, which is 

$$
c _ {x} (t, x) = N \big (d _ {+} (T - t, x) \big),\tag{4.5.23}
$$

and theta, which is 

$$
c _ {t} (t, x) = - r K e ^ {- r (T - t)} N \left(d _ {-} (T - t, x)\right) - \frac {\sigma x}{2 \sqrt {T - t}} N ^ {\prime} \left(d _ {+} (T - t, x)\right).\tag{4.5.24}
$$

Because both N and $N ^ { \prime }$ are always positive, delta is always positive and theta is always negative. Another of the Greeks is gamma, which is 

$$
c _ {x x} (t, x) = N ^ {\prime} \bigl (d _ {+} (T - t, x) \bigr) \frac {\partial}{\partial x} d _ {+} (T - t, x) = \frac {1}{\sigma x \sqrt {T - t}} N ^ {\prime} \bigl (d _ {+} (T - t, x) \bigr).\tag{4.5.25}
$$

Like delta, gamma is always positive. 

In order to simplify notation in the following discussion, we sometimes suppress the arguments $( t , \pmb { x } )$ of ${ \pmb c } ( { \pmb t } , { \pmb x } )$ and $( T - t , \pmb { x } )$ of $d _ { \pm } ( T - t , x )$ . If at time t the stock price is $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \mathbf { \mathcal { X } } , \mathbf { \delta } }$ then the short option hedge of (4.5. 1 1 ) calls for holding $c _ { x } ( t , x )$ shares of stock, a position whose value is $x c _ { x } = x N ( d _ { + } )$ . The hedging portfolio value is $c = x N ( d _ { + } ) - K e ^ { - r ( T - t ) } N ( d _ { - } )$ , and since ${ \pmb x } c _ { { \pmb x } } ( t , { \pmb x } )$ of this value is invested in stock, the amount invested in the money market must be 

$$
c (t, x) - x c _ {x} (t, x) = - K e ^ {- r (T - t)} N (d _ {-}),
$$

a negative number. To hedge a short position i n a call option, one must borrow money. To hedge a long position in a call option, one does the opposite. In other words, to hedge a long call position one should hold $- \pmb { c _ { x } }$ shares of stock (i.e. , have a short position in stock) and invest $K e ^ { - r ( T - t ) } N ( d _ { - } )$ in the money market account. 

Because delta and gamma are positive, for fixed $\mathbf { } ^ { t , \mathrm { ~ ~ } }$ the function ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ is increasing and convex in the variable $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \pmb { x } , }$ as shown in Figure 4.5. 1. Suppose at time t the stock price is $\pmb { x } _ { 1 }$ and we wish to take a long position in the option and hedge it. We do this by purchasing the option for $c ( t , x _ { 1 } )$ , shorting $c _ { x } ( t , x _ { 1 } )$ shares of stock, which generates income $x _ { 1 } c _ { x } ( t , x _ { 1 } )$ , and investing the diference, 

$$
M = x _ {1} c _ {x} (t, x _ {1}) - c (t, x _ {1}),
$$

in the money market account. We wish to consider the sensitivity to stock price changes of the portfolio that has these three components: long option, short stock, and long money market account. The initial portfolio value 

$$
c (t, x _ {1}) - x _ {1} c _ {x} (t, x _ {1}) + M
$$

is zero at the moment t when we set up these positions. 

If the stock price were to instantaneously fall to $\pmb { x _ { 0 } }$ as shown in Figure 4.5. 1 and we do not change our positions in the stock or money market account, then the value of the option we hold would fall to $c ( t , x _ { 0 } )$ and the liability due to our short position in stock would decrease to ${ \pmb x } _ { 0 } c _ { x } ( t , { \pmb x } _ { 1 } )$ · Our total portfolio value, including M in the money market account, would be 

$$
c (t, x _ {0}) - x _ {0} c _ {x} (t, x _ {1}) + M = c (t, x _ {0}) - c _ {x} (t, x _ {1}) (x _ {0} - x _ {1}) - c (t, x _ {1}).
$$

This is the diference at $\pmb { x _ { 0 } }$ between the curve $\boldsymbol { y } = c ( t , \boldsymbol { x } )$ and the straight line $y = c _ { x } ( t , x _ { 1 } ) ( x - x _ { 1 } ) + c ( t , x _ { 1 } )$ in Figure 4.5. 1. Because this diference is positive, our portfolio benefits from an instantaneous drop in the stock price. 

On the other hand, if the stock price were to instantaneously rise to $\pmb { x _ { 2 } }$ and we do not change our positions in the stock or money market account, then the value of the option would rise to $c ( t , x _ { 2 } )$ and the liability due to our short position in stock would increase to $x _ { 2 } c _ { x } ( t , x _ { 1 } )$ . Our total portfolio value, including M in the money market account, would be 

$$
c (t, x _ {2}) - x _ {2} c _ {x} (t, x _ {1}) + M = c (t, x _ {2}) - c _ {x} (t, x _ {1}) (x _ {2} - x _ {1}) - c (t, x _ {1}).
$$

This is the diference at $\pmb { x _ { 2 } }$ between the curve $\pmb { y } = c ( t , \pmb { x } )$ and the straight line $\pmb { y } = c _ { x } ( t , \pmb { x } _ { 1 } ) ( \pmb { x } - \pmb { x } _ { 1 } ) + c ( t , \pmb { x } _ { 1 } )$ in Figure 4.5. 1 . This diference is positive, so our portfolio benefits from an instantaneous rise in the stock price. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/71f6c563-4bd5-49c7-9234-946db79f6010/078dfe56c824cc5e4bf079c684080bb83d6f467a9ab91e6c6c86384d86015a87.jpg)



Fig. 4 . 5 . 1 . Delta-neutral position.


The portfolio we have set up is said to be delta-neutral and long gamma. The portfolio is long gamma because it benefits from the convexity of ${ \boldsymbol { c } } ( t , { \boldsymbol { x } } )$ as described above. If there is an instantaneous rise or an instantaneous fall in the stock price, the value of the portfolio increases. A long gamma portfolio is profitable in times of high stock volatility. 

"Delta-neutral" refers to the fact that the line in Figure 4.5. 1 is tangent to the curve $\pmb { y } = c ( t , \pmb { x } )$ . Therefore, when the stock price makes a small move, the change of portfolio value due to the corresponding change in option price is nearly ofset by the change in the value of our short position in the stock. The straight line is a good approximation to the option price for small stock price moves. If the straight line were steeper than the option price curve at the starting point $\pmb { x } _ { 1 }$ , then we would be short delta; an upward move in the stock price would hurt the portfolio because the liability from the short position in stock would rise faster than the value of the option. On the other hand, a downward move would increase the portfolio value because the option price would fall more slowly than the rate of decrease in the liability from the short stock position. Unless a trader has a view on the market , he tries to set up portfolios that are delta-neutral. If he expects high volatility, he would at the same time try to choose the portfolio to be long gamma. 

The portfolio described above may at first appear to ofer an arbitrage opportunity. When we let time move forward, not only does the long gamma position ofer an opportunity for profit, but the positive investment in the money market account enhances this opportunity. The drawback is that theta, the derivative of ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ with respect to time, is negative. As we move forward in time, the curve $\pmb { y } = c ( t , \pmb { x } )$ is shifting downward. Figure 4.5. 1 is misleading because it is drawn with t fixed. In principle, the portfolio can lose money because the curve $c ( t , \pmb { x } )$ shifts downward more rapidly than the money market investment and the long gamma position generate income. The essence of the hedging argument in Subsection 4.5.3 is that if the stock really is a geometric Brownian motion and we have determined the right value of the volatility $\sigma ,$ then so long as we continuously rebalance our portfolio, all these efects exactly cancel! 

Of course, assets are not really geometric Brownian motions with constant volatility, but the argument above gives a good first approximation to reality. It also highlights volatility as the key parameter. In fact, the mean rate of return a of the stock does not appear in the Black-Scholes-Merton equation (4.5. 14) . From the point of view of no-arbitrage pricing, it is irrelevant how likely the stock is to go up or down because a delta-neutral position is a hedge against both possibilities. What matters is how much volatility the stock has, for we need to know the amount of profit that can be made from the long gamma position. The more volatile stocks ofer more opportunity for profit from the portfolio that hedges a long call position with a short stock position, and hence the call is more expensive. The derivative of the option price with respect to the volatility $\sigma$ is called vega, and it is positive. As volatility increases, so do option prices in the Black-Scholes-Merton model. 

## 4.5.6 Put-Call Parity
