# Connections with Partial Diferential Equations

## 6. 1 Introduction

There are two ways to compute a derivative security price: ( 1) use Monte Carlo simulation to generate paths of the underlying security or securities under the risk-neutral measure and use these paths to estimate the risk-neutral expected discounted payof; or (2) numerically solve a partial diferential equation. This chapter addresses the second of these methods by showing how to connect the risk-neutral pricing problem to partial diferential equations. Section 6.2 explains the concept of stochastic diferential equations, which is used to model asset prices. Solutions to stochastic diferential equations have the Markov property, as is discussed in Section 6.3. Because of this, related to each stochastic diferential equation there are two partial diferential equations, one that includes discounting and one that does not. These partial differential equations and their derivations are the subject of Section 6.4. Section 6.5 shows how these ideas can be applied to interest rate models to compute bond prices and the prices of derivatives on bonds. The discussion of Sections 6.2-6.5 concerns one-dimensional processes. The multidimensional theory is outlined in Section 6.6, and a representative example that uses this theory, pricing and hedging an Asian option, is presented in that section. 

## 6.2 Stochastic Diferential Equations

A stochastic diferential equation is an equation of the form 

$$
d X (u) = \beta (u, X (u)) d u + \gamma (u, X (u)) d W (u).\tag{6.2.1}
$$

Here $\beta ( u , x )$ and $\gamma ( \boldsymbol { u } , \boldsymbol { x } )$ are given functions, called the drift and difusion, respectively. In addition to this equation, an initial condition of the form $X ( t ) = x$ <sub>,</sub> where $t \geq 0$ and $x \in \mathbb { R } ,$ is specified. The problem is then to find stochastic process $X ( T )$ , defined for $T \geq t ,$ such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X (t) = x, \\ X (T) = X (t) + \int_ {t} ^ {T} \beta (u, X (u)) d u + \int_ {t} ^ {T} \gamma (u, X (u)) d W (u). \end{array}\tag{6.2.2}
$$

(6 . 2 . 3 ) 

Under mild conditions on the functions $\beta ( { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { u } } } } , { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { x } } } } )$ and $\gamma ( \boldsymbol { \boldsymbol { \boldsymbol { u } } } , \boldsymbol { \boldsymbol { x } } )$ , there exists a unique process $X ( T ) , T \geq t ,$ satisfying (6.2.2) and (6.2.3) . However, this process can be dificult to determine explicitly because it appears on both the left- and right-hand sides of equation (6.2.3) . 

The solution $X ( T )$ at time T will be $\mathcal { F } ( T )$ -measurable $( \mathbf { i . e . } , X ( T )$ only depends on the path of the Brownian motion up to time $T . )$ In fact, since the initial condition $X ( t ) = x$ is specified, all that is really needed to determine $X ( T )$ is the path of the Brownian motion between times t and ${ \mathbf { } } T .$ 

Although stochastic diferential equations are, in general, dificult to solve, a one-dimensional linear stochastic diferential equation can be solved explicitly. This is a stochastic diferential equation of the form 

$$
d X (u) = \left(a (u) + b (u) X (u)\right) d u + \left(\gamma (u) + \sigma (u) X (u)\right) d W (u),\tag{6.2.4}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { { \boldsymbol { a } } ( u ) , \ { \boldsymbol { b } } ( u ) , \ { \boldsymbol { \sigma } } ( u ) } \end{array}$ , and $\gamma ( u )$ are nonrandom functions of time. Indeed, this equation can even be solved when $a ( u ) , b ( u ) , \gamma ( u )$ , and $\sigma ( u )$ are adapted random processes (see Exercise 6. 1) , although it is then no longer of the form (6 . 2 . 1) . In order to guarantee that the solution to (6.2. 1) has the Markov property discussed in Section 6.3 below, the only randomness we permit on the right-hand side of (6.2. 1) is the randomness inherent in the solution $X ( u )$ and in the driving Brownian motions $W ( u )$ . There cannot be additional randomness such as would occur if any of the processes $a ( u ) , b ( u ) , \gamma ( u )$ , and $\sigma ( u )$ appearing in (6.2.4) were themselves random. The next two examples are special cases of (6.2.4) in which $a ( u ) , b ( u ) , \gamma ( u )$ , and $\sigma ( u )$ are nonrandom. 

Example 6. 2. 1 (Geometric Brownian motion). The stochastic diferential equation for geometric Brownian motion is 

$$
d S (u) = \alpha S (u) d u + \sigma S (u) d W (u).
$$

In the notation of (6.2. 1 ) , $\beta ( u , x ) = \alpha x$ and $\gamma ( { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { u } } } } , { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { x } } } } ) = \sigma { \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { x } } } }$ . We know the formula for the solution to this stochastic diferential equation when the initial time is zero and the initial position is $S ( 0 )$ , namely 

$$
S (t) = S (0) \exp \left\{\sigma W (t) + \left(\alpha - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) t \right\}.
$$

Similarly, for $T \geq t$ 

$$
S (T) = S (0) \exp \left\{\sigma W (T) + \left(\alpha - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) T \right\}.
$$

Dividing $S ( T )$ by $S ( t )$ , we obtain 

$$
\frac {S (T)}{S (t)} = \exp \left\{\sigma (W (T) - W (t)) + \left(\alpha - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) (T - t) \right\}.
$$

If the initial condition is given at time t rather than at time zero and is $\begin{array} { r } { { \pmb S } ( t ) = { \pmb x } , } \end{array}$ , then this last equation becomes 

$$
S (T) = x \exp \Big \{\sigma \big (W (T) - W (t) \big) + \Big (\alpha - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} \Big) (T - t) \Big \}.
$$

As expected, when we use the initial condition $\begin{array} { r } { S ( t ) = x , } \end{array}$ then $s ( T )$ depends only on the path of the Brownian motion between times t and $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \mathbf { \mathcal { T } } }$ 

Example 6. 2. 2 {Hull- White interest rote model}. Consider the stochastic differential equation 

$$
d R (u) = \left(a (u) - b (u) R (u)\right) d u + \sigma (u) d \widetilde {W} (u),
$$

where $a ( u ) , b ( u )$ , and $\pmb { \sigma } ( \pmb { u } )$ are nonrandom positive functions of the time variable u and $\bar { W } ( u )$ is a Brownian motion under a risk-neutral measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ . In this case, we use the dummy variable r rather than ${ \pmb x } ,$ and $\beta ( u , r ) = a ( u ) -$ $b ( u ) r , \gamma ( u , r ) = \sigma ( u )$ . Let us take the initial condition $\boldsymbol { R } ( t ) = \boldsymbol { r }$ . We can solve the stochastic diferential equation by first using the stochastic diferential equation to compute 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} d \Big (e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {u} b (v) d v} R (u) \Big) & = e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {u} b (v) d v} \big (b (u) R (u)   d u + d R (u) \big) \\ & = e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {u} b (v) d v} \big (\alpha (u)   d u + \sigma (u)   d \widetilde {W} (u) \big). \end{array}
$$

Integrating both sides from t to $_ { \pmb { T } }$ and using the initial condition $\boldsymbol { R } ( t ) = \boldsymbol { r }$ we obtain the formula 

$$
e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {T} b (v) d v} R (T) = r e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {t} b (v) d v} + \int_ {t} ^ {T} e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {u} b (v) d v} \alpha (u) d u + \int_ {t} ^ {T} e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {u} b (v) d v} \sigma (u) d \widetilde {W} (u),
$$

which we can solve for $\scriptstyle { R ( T ) }$ 

$$
R (T) = r e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} b (v) d v} + \int_ {t} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {u} ^ {T} b (v) d v} \alpha (u) d u + \int_ {t} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {u} ^ {T} b (v) d v} \sigma (u) d \widetilde {W} (u).
$$

This is an explicit formula for the solution $R ( T )$ . The right-hand side of the final equation does not involve the interest rate process $\pmb { R } ( \pmb { u } )$ apart from the initial condition $R ( t ) = r ;$ it contains only this initial condition, an integral with respect to time, and an Ito integral of given functions. Note also that the Brownian motion path between times t and $_ { T }$ only enters this formula. 

Recall from Theorem 4.4.9 that the Ito integral $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { t } ^ { T } e ^ { - \int _ { u } ^ { T } b ( v ) d v } \sigma ( u ) d \widetilde W ( u ) } \end{array}$ of the nonrandom integrand $e ^ { - \int _ { u } ^ { T } b ( v ) d v } \sigma ( u )$ is normally distributed with mean zero and variance $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { t } ^ { T } { e ^ { - 2 \int _ { u } ^ { T } { b ( v ) d v } } \sigma ^ { 2 } ( u ) } } \end{array}$ du. The other terms appearing in the formula above for $R ( T )$ are nonrandom. Therefore, under the risk-neutral measure $ { \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } , R ( T )$ is normally distributed with mean 

$$
r e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} b (v) d v} + \int_ {t} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {u} ^ {T} b (v) d v} \alpha (u) d u
$$

and variance 

$$
\int_ {t} ^ {T} e ^ {- 2 \int_ {u} ^ {T} b (v) d v} \sigma^ {2} (u) d u.
$$

In particular, there is a positive probability that $R ( T )$ is negative. This is one of the principal objections to the Hull-White model. D 

Example 6. 2. 3 {Cox-Ingersoll-Ross interest rate model}. In the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) model, the interest rate is given by the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d R (u) = \left(a - b R (u)\right) d u + \sigma \sqrt {R (u)} d \widetilde {W} (u),\tag{6.2.5}
$$

where $a , b ,$ and $\pmb { \sigma }$ are positive constants. Suppose an initial condition $R ( t ) = r$ is given. Although there is no formula for $\scriptstyle { R ( T ) }$ , there is one and only one solution to this diferential equation starting from the given initial condition. This solution can be approximated by Monte Carlo simulation, and many of its properties can be determined, even though we do not have an explicit formula for it. For instance, in Example 4.4. 1 1 , the mean and variance of $R ( T )$ were computed when the initial time is $t = 0$ and the initial interest rate is $R ( 0 )$ 

Unlike the interest rate in the Hull- White model, the interest rate in the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model cannot take negative values. When the interest rate approaches zero, the term $\sigma \sqrt { R ( u ) } d \widetilde { W } ( u )$ also approaches zero. With the volatility disappearing, the behavior of the interest rate near zero depends on the drift term $\pmb { a } - b R ( \pmb { u } )$ , and this is $\pmb { a } > 0$ when $\begin{array} { r } { R ( u ) = 0 } \end{array}$ . The positive drift prevents the interest rate from crossing zero into negative territory. 

More information about the solution to (6.2.5) is provided in Exercise 6.6 and Remark 6.9. 1 following that exercise. D 

## 6.3 The Markov Property

Consider the stochastic diferential equation (6.2. 1 ) . Let $0 \leq t \leq T$ be given, and let $h ( y )$ be a Borel-measurable function. Denote by 

$$
g (t, x) = \mathbb {E} ^ {t, x} h (X (T))\tag{6.3.1}
$$

the expectation of $h ( X ( T ) )$ , where $X ( T )$ is the solution to (6.2. 1 ) with initial condition $X ( t ) = x .$ . (We assume that $\mathbb { E } ^ { t , x } | h ( X ( T ) ) | < \infty . )$ Note that there is nothing random about ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb t } , { \pmb x } )$ ; it is an ordinary (actually, Borel-measurable) function of the two dummy variables t and $\pmb { x } .$ 

If we do not have an explicit formula for the distribution of $X ( T )$ , we could compute ${ \boldsymbol g } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ numerically by beginning at $X ( t ) = x$ and simulating the stochastic diferential equation. One way to do this would be to use the $_ { E u l e r }$ method, a particular type of Monte Carlo method: choose a small positive step size $\delta ,$ and then set 

$$
X (t + \delta) = x + \beta (t, x) \delta + \gamma (t, x) \sqrt {\delta} \epsilon_ {1},
$$

where $\epsilon _ { 1 }$ is a standard normal random variable. Then set 

$$
X (t + 2 \delta) = X (t + \delta) + \beta \big (t + \delta , X (t + \delta) \big) \delta + \gamma \big (t + \delta , X (t + \delta) \big) \sqrt {\delta} \epsilon_ {2},
$$

where $\epsilon _ { 2 }$ is a standard normal random variable independent of $\epsilon _ { 1 }$ By this device, one eventually determines a value for $X ( T )$ (assuming $\delta$ is chosen so that $\textstyle { \frac { { \dot { \mathbf { T } } } - t } { \delta } }$ is an integer) . This gives one realization of $X ( T )$ (corresponding to one $\omega )$ . Now repeat this process many times and compute the average of $h ( X ( T ) )$ over all these simulations to get an approximate value for ${ \boldsymbol g } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ Note that if one were to begin with a diferent time t and initial value $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \pmb { x } , }$ one would get a diferent answer (i.e. , the answer is a function of t and x) . This dependence on t and x is emphasized by the notation $E ^ { t , { \boldsymbol { x } } }$ in (6. 3 . 1 ) . 

Theorem 6.3. 1 . Let ${ \pmb X } ( { \pmb u } ) , { \pmb u } \ge { \pmb 0 }$ , be a solution t o the stochastic diferential equation {6. 2. 1) with initial condition given at time 0. Then, for $0 \leq t \leq T _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ 

$$
\mathbb {E} \big [ h (X (T)) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ] = g \big (t, X (t) \big).\tag{6.3.2}
$$

While the details of the proof of Theorem 6.3. 1 are quite technical and will not be given, the intuitive content is clear. Suppose the process $X ( u )$ begins at time zero, being generated by the stochastic diferential equation (6.2. 1) , and one watches it up to time t. Suppose now that one is asked, based on this information, to compute the conditional expectation of $h ( X ( T ) )$ , where $T \geq t .$ Then one should pretend that the process is starting at time t at its current position, generate the solution to the stochastic diferential equation corresponding to this initial condition, and compute the expected value of $h ( X ( T ) )$ generated in this way. In other words, replace $X ( t )$ by a dummy x in order to hold it constant, compute $g ( t , x ) = \mathbb { E } ^ { t , x } h ( X ( T ) )$ , and after computing this function put the random variable $X ( t )$ back in place of the dummy x. This is the procedure set forth in the Independence Lemma, Lemma 2.3.4, and it is applicable here because the value of $X ( T )$ is determined by the value of $X ( t )$ , which is $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ -measurable, and the increments of the Brownian motion between times t and ${ \pmb T } .$ , which are independent of $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ 

Notice in the discussion above that although one watches the stochastic process $X ( u )$ for $0 \leq u \leq t ,$ the only relevant piece of information when computing $\mathbb { E } { \big [ } h ( X ( T ) ) { \big | } { \mathcal { F } } ( t ) { \big ] }$ is the value of $X ( t )$ . This means that $X ( t )$ is a Markov process (see Definition 2 .3.6) . We highlight this fact as a corollary. 

Corollary 6.3.2. Solutions to stochastzc diferential equations are Markov processes. 

## 6.4 Partial Diferential Equations

The Feynman-Kac Theorem below relates stochastic diferential equations and partial diferential equations. When this partial diferential equation is solved (usually numerically) , it produces the function ${ \pmb g } ( t , { \pmb x } )$ of ( 6.3. 1 ) . The Euler method described in the previous section for determining this function converges slowly and gives the function value for only one pair $( t , \pmb { x } )$ . Numerical algorithms for solving equation (6.4. 1) below converge quickly in the case of one-dimensional x being considered here and give the function ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb t } , { \pmb x } )$ for all values of $( t , \pmb { x } )$ simultaneously. The relationship between geometric Brownian motion and the Black-Scholes-Merton partial diferential equation is a special case of the relationship between stochastic diferential equations and partial diferential equations developed in the following theorems. 

Theorem 6.4. 1 (Feynman-Kac) . Consider the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d X (u) = \beta (u, X (u)) d u + \gamma (u, X (u)) d W (u).\tag{6.2.1}
$$

Let $h ( y )$ be a Borel-measurable function. Fix $\mathbf { \nabla } T > 0$ , and let $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ be given. Define the function 

$$
g (t, \boldsymbol {x}) = \mathbb {E} ^ {t, \boldsymbol {x}} h (X (T)).\tag{6.3.1}
$$

{We assume that $\mathbb { E } ^ { t , x } | h ( X ( T ) ) | < \infty$ for all t and x.} Then ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb t } , { \pmb x } )$ satisfies the partial diferential equation 

$$
g _ {t} (t, x) + \beta (t, x) g _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, x) g _ {x x} (t, x) = 0\tag{6.4.1}
$$

and the terminal condition 

$$
g (T, x) = h (x) \text {   for   all   } x.\tag{6.4.2}
$$

The proof of the Feynman-Kac Theorem depends on the following lemma. 

Lemma 6.4.2. Let $X ( u )$ be a solution to the stochastic diferential equation $( 6 . 2 . 1 )$ with initial condition given at time 0. Let $h ( y )$ be a Borel-measurable function, fix $T > 0$ , and let ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb t } , { \pmb x } )$ be given by $( 6 . 3 . 1 )$ . Then the stochastic process 

$$
g (t, X (t)), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

is a martingale. 

PROOF: Let $0 \leq s \leq t \leq T$ be given. Theorem 6.3. 1 implies 

$$
\mathbb {E} \big [ h (X (T)) \big | \mathcal {F} (s) \big ] = g (s, X (s)),
$$

$$
\mathbb {E} \big [ h (X (T)) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ] = g (t, X (t)).
$$

Take conditional expectations of the second equation, using iterated conditioning and the first equation, to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathbb {E} \big [ g (t, X (t)) \big | \mathcal {F} (s) \big ] & = \mathbb {E} \big [ \mathbb {E} \big [ h (X (T)) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ] \big | \mathcal {F} (s) \big ] \\ & = \mathbb {E} \big [ h (X (T)) \big | \mathcal {F} (s) \big ] \\ & = g (s, X (s)). \end{array}
$$

OUTLINE OF PROOF OF THEOREM 6.4. 1 : Let $X ( t )$ be the solution to the stochastic diferential equation (6.2 . 1 ) starting at time zero. Since $g ( t , X ( t ) )$ is a martingale, the net dt term in the diferential $d g ( t , X ( t ) )$ must be zero. If it were positive at any time, then ${ \mathbf { } } g ( t , X ( t ) )$ would have a tendency to rise at that time; if it were negative, ${ \mathbf { } } g ( t , X ( t ) )$ would have a tendency to fall. Omitting the argument $( t , X ( t ) )$ in several places below, we compute 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d g (t, X (t)) = g _ {t} d t + g _ {x} d X + \frac {1}{2} g _ {x x} d X d X} \\ & {\qquad = g _ {t} d t + \beta g _ {x} d t + \gamma g _ {x} d W + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} g _ {x x} d t} \\ & {\qquad = \left[ g _ {t} + \beta g _ {x} + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} g _ {x x} \right] d t + \gamma g _ {x} d W.} \end{array}
$$

Setting the dt term to zero and putting back the argument $( t , X ( t ) )$ , we obtain 

$$
g _ {t} (t, X (t)) + \beta (t, X (t)) g _ {x} (t, X (t)) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, X (t)) g _ {x x} (t, X (t)) = 0
$$

along every path of X . Therefore, 

$$
g _ {t} (t, x) + \beta (t, x) g _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, x) g _ {x x} (t, x) = 0
$$

at every point $( t , \pmb { x } )$ that can be reached by $( t , X ( t ) )$ . For example, if $X ( t )$ is a geometric Brownian motion, then (6.4. 1) must hold for every $t \in [ 0 , T )$ and every $\pmb { x } > 0 .$ . On the other hand, if $X ( t )$ is a Hull-White interest rate process, which can take any positive or negative value, then (6.4. 1) must hold for every $t \in [ 0 , T )$ and every ${ \pmb x } \in \mathbb { R }$ D 

The general principle behind the proof of the Feynman-Kac theorem is: 

1 . find the martingale, 

2. take the diferential, and 

3. set the dt term equal to zero. 

This gives a partial diferential equation, which can then be solved numerically. We illustrate this three-step procedure in the following theorem and subsequent examples. 

Theorem 6.4.3 (Discounted Feynman-Kac) . Consider the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d X (u) = \beta (u, X (u)) d u + \gamma (u, X (u)) d W (u).\tag{6.2.1}
$$

Let $h ( y )$ be a Borel-measumble function and let r be constant. Fix $T > 0 ,$ , and let $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ be given. Define the function 

$$
f (t, x) = \mathbb {E} ^ {t, x} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} h (X (T)) \right].\tag{6.4.3}
$$

$( W e$ assume that $| \mathbb { E } ^ { t , x } | h ( X ( T ) ) | < \infty$ for all t and x .) Then ${ f } ( t , x )$ satisfies the partial diferential equation 

$$
f _ {t} (t, x) + \beta (t, x) f _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, x) f _ {x x} (t, x) = r f (t, x)\tag{6.4.4}
$$

and the terminal condition 

$$
f (T, x) = h (x) \text {   for   all   } x.\tag{6.4.5}
$$

OuTLINE OF PROOF: Let X(t) be the solution to the stochastic diferential equation (6.2 . 1 ) starting at time zero. Then 

$$
f (t, X (t)) = \mathbb {E} \big [ e ^ {- r (T - t)} h (X (T)) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ].
$$

However, it is not the case that $f ( t , X ( t ) )$ is a martingale. Indeed, if $0 \leq s \leq$ $t \leq T$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathbb {E} \big [ f (t, X (t)) \big | \mathcal {F} (s) \big ] & = \mathbb {E} \big [ \mathbb {E} \big [ e ^ {- r (T - t)} h (X (T)) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ] \big | \mathcal {F} (s) \big ] \\ & = \mathbb {E} \big [ e ^ {- r (T - t)} h (X (T)) \big | \mathcal {F} (s) \big ], \end{array}
$$

which is not the same as 

$$
f (s, X (s)) = \mathbb {E} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - s)} h (X (T)) \mid \mathcal {F} (s) \right]
$$

because of the difering discount terms. The dificulty here is that in order to get the martingale property from iterated conditioning, we need the random variable being estimated not to depend on t, the time of the conditioning. To achieve this, we "complete the discounting," observing that 

$$
e ^ {- r t} f (t, X (t)) = \mathbb {E} \left[ e ^ {- r T} h (X (T)) \mid \mathcal {F} (t) \right].
$$

We may now apply iterated conditioning to show that $e ^ { - r t } f ( t , X ( t ) )$ is a martingale. The diferential of this martingale is 

$$
\begin{array}{r} d \big (e ^ {- r t} f (t, X (t)) \big) = e ^ {- r t} \Big [ - r f d t + f _ {t} d t + f _ {x} d X + \frac {1}{2} f _ {x x} d X d X \Big ] \\ = e ^ {- r t} \Big [ - r f + f _ {t} + \beta f _ {x} + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} f _ {x x} \Big ] d t + e ^ {- r t} \gamma f _ {x} d W. \end{array}
$$

Setting the dt term equal to zero, we obtain (6.4.4) . 

Example $6 . 4 . 4$ {Options on a geometric Brownian motion). Let $h ( S ( T ) )$ be the payof at time $_ { T }$ of a derivative security whose underlying asset is the geometric Brownian motion 

$$
d S (u) = \alpha S (u) d u + \sigma S (u) d W (u).\tag{6.4.6}
$$

We may rewrite this as 

$$
d S (u) = r S (u) d u + \sigma S (u) d \widetilde {W} (u),\tag{6.4.7}
$$

where $\widetilde { W } ( u )$ is a Brownian motion under the risk-neutral probability measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ Here we assume that $\pmb { \sigma }$ and the interest rate $\pmb { r }$ are constant. According to the risk-neutral pricing formula (5.2.31 ) , the price of the derivative security at time t is 

$$
V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- r (T - t)} h (S (T)) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ].\tag{6.4.8}
$$

Because the stock price is Markov and the payof is a function of the stock price alone, there is a function $v ( t , x )$ such that $V ( t ) = v ( t , S ( t ) )$ . Moreover, the function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } )$ must satisfy the discounted partial diferential equation (6.4.4) . This is the Black-Scholes-Merton equation 

$$
v _ {t} (t, x) + r x v _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} x ^ {2} v _ {x x} (t, x) = r v (t, x).\tag{6.4.9}
$$

When the underlying asset is a geometric Brownian motion, this is the right pricing equation for a European call, a European put, a forward contract, and any other option that pays of some function of $s ( T )$ at time ${ \mathbf { } } T .$ 

Note that to derive (6.4.9) we use the discounted partial diferential equation (6.4.4) when the stochastic diferential equation for the underlying process is (6.4.7) rather than (6.4.6) (i.e. , we have ${ r x v } _ { x } ( t , x )$ in (6.4.9) rather than $\alpha x v _ { x } ( t , x ) )$ . This is because we are computing the conditional expectation in (6.4.8) under the risk-neutral measure $\bar { \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } }$ and hence must use the diferential <sub>�</sub>uation that represents $\boldsymbol { S } ( \boldsymbol { u } )$ in terms of $\widetilde { W } ( u )$ , the Brownian motion under $\underline { { \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } } .$ In other words, we are using the Discounted Feynman-Kac Theorem with $\widetilde { W } ( u )$ replacing $W ( u )$ and $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ replacing $\mathbb { P } .$ D 

In the previous example, if $\pmb { \sigma }$ were a function of time and stock price (i.e. , $\sigma ( t , x ) )$ , then the stock price would no longer be a geometric Brownian motion and the Black-Scholes-Merton formula would no longer apply. However, one can still solve for the option price by solving the partial diferential equation ( 6.4. 9) , where now the constant $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ is replaced by $\sigma ^ { 2 } ( t , x )$ 

$$
v _ {t} (t, x) + r x v _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (t, x) x ^ {2} v _ {x x} (t, x) = r v (t, x).\tag{6.4.10}
$$

This equation is not dificult to solve numerically. 

It has been observed in markets that if one assumes a constant volatility, the parameter $\pmb { \sigma }$ that makes the theoretical option price given by (6.4.9) agree with the market price, the so-called implied volatility, is diferent for options having diferent strikes . In fact , this implied volatility is generally a convex function of the strike price. One refers to this phenomenon as the volatility smile. 

One simple model with nonconstant volatility is the constant elasticity of variance (CEV) model, in which $\sigma ( t , x ) = \sigma x ^ { \delta - 1 }$ depends on x but not t. The parameter $\delta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ is chosen so that the model gives a good fit to option prices across diferent strikes at a single expiration date. For this model, the stock price is governed by the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d S (t) = r S (t) d t + \sigma S ^ {\delta} (t) d \widetilde {W} (t).
$$

The volatility $\sigma S ^ { \delta - 1 } ( t )$ is a decreasing function of the stock price. 

When one wishes to account for diferent volatilities implied by options expiring at diferent dates as well as diferent strikes, one needs to allow u to depend on t as well as x. This function $\sigma ( t , \boldsymbol { x } )$ is called the volatility surface (see Exercise 6 . 10) . 

## 6.5 Interest Rate Models

The simplest models for fixed income markets begin with a stochastic diferential equation for the interest rate, e.g. , 

$$
d R (t) = \beta (t, R (t)) d t + \gamma (t, R (t)) d \widetilde {W} (t),\tag{6.5.1}
$$

where $\widetilde { W } ( t )$ is a Brownian motion under a risk-neutral probability measure ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } .$ In these models, one begins with a risk-neutral measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ and uses the riskneutral pricing formula to price all assets. This guarantees that discounted asset prices are martingales under the risk-neutral measure, and hence there is no arbitrage. The issue of calibration of these models (i.e. , choosing the model and the model parameters so that they give a good fit to market prices) is not discussed in this text. 

Models for the interest rate $R ( t )$ are sometimes called short-rate models because $R ( t )$ is the interest rate for short-term borrowing. When the interest rate is determined by only one stochastic diferential equation, as is the case in this section, the model is said to have one factor. The primary shortcoming of one-factor models is that they cannot capture complicated yield curve behavior; they tend to produce parallel shifts in the yield curve but not changes in its slope or curvature. 

The discount process is as given in (5.2 . 1 7) , 

$$
D (t) = e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} R (s) d s},
$$

and we denote the money market account price process to be 

$$
\frac {1}{D (t)} = e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {t} R (s) d s}.
$$

This is the value at time t of one unit of currency invested in the money market account at time zero and continuously rolled over at the short-term interest rate $R ( s ) , s \geq 0$ . As discussed following (5.2. 18) , we have the diferential formulas 

$$
d D (t) = - R (t) D (t) d t, \quad d \left(\frac {1}{D (t)}\right) = \frac {R (t)}{D (t)} d t.
$$

A zero-coupon bond is a contract promising to pay a certain "face" amount, which we take to be 1 , at a fixed maturity date $^ { \mathbf { \delta T } } \cdot$ Prior to that, the bond makes no payments. The risk-neutral pricing formula (5.2.30) says that the discounted price of this bond should be a martingale under the risk-neutral measure. In other words, for $0 \leq t \leq T$ , the price of the bond $B ( t , T )$ should satisfy 

$$
D (t) B (t, T) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ D (T) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ].\tag{6.5.2}
$$

(Note that $B ( T , T ) = 1 . )$ This gives us the zero-coupon bond pricing formula 

$$
B (t, T) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} R (s) d s} \mid \mathcal {F} (t) \right],\tag{6.5.3}
$$

which we take as a definition. Once zero-coupon bond prices have been computed, we can define the yield between times t and $_ { T }$ to be 

$$
Y (t, T) = - \frac {1}{T - t} \log B (t, T)
$$

or, equivalently, 

$$
B (t, T) = e ^ {- Y (t, T) (T - t)}.
$$

The yield $Y ( t , T )$ is the constant rate of continuously compounding interest between times t and $_ { \pmb { T } }$ that is consistent with the bond price $B ( t , T )$ . The 30- year rate at time t is $Y ( t , 3 0 + t )$ ; this is an example of a long rate. Notice that once we adopt a model (6.5. 1 ) for the short rate, the long rate is determined by the formulas above; we may not model the long rate separately. 

Since R is given by a stochastic diferential equation, it is a Markov process and we must have 

$$
B (t, T) = f (t, R (t))
$$

for some function $f ( t , r )$ of the dummy variables t and r. This is a slight step beyond the way we have used the Markov property previously because the random variable $e ^ { - \int _ { t } ^ { T } R ( s ) d s }$ being estimated in (6.5.3) depends on the path segment $R ( s ) , t \leq s \leq T ,$ not just on $R ( T )$ . However, the only relevant part of the path of R before time t is its value at time $\mathbf { } ^ { t , \quad }$ and so the bond price $B ( t , T )$ must be a function of time t and $R ( t )$ 

To find the partial diferential equation for the unknown function $f ( t , r )$ we find a martingale, take its diferential, and set the dt term equal to zero. The martingale in this case is $D ( t ) B ( t , T ) = D ( t ) f ( t , R ( t ) )$ . Its diferential is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \big (D (t) f (t, R (t)) \big) = f (t, R (t)) d D (t) + D (t) d f (t, R (t))} \\ & {\qquad = D (t) \left[ - R f d t + f _ {t} d t + f _ {r} d R + \frac {1}{2} f _ {r r} d R d R \right]} \\ & {\qquad = D (t) \left[ - R f + f _ {t} + \beta f _ {r} + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} f _ {r r} \right] d t + D (t) \gamma f _ {r} d \widetilde {W}.} \end{array}
$$

Setting the dt term equal to zero, we obtain the partial diferential equation 

$$
f _ {t} (t, r) + \beta (t, r) f _ {r} (t, r) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, r) f _ {r r} (t, r) = r f (t, r).\tag{6.5.4}
$$

We also have the terminal condition 

$$
f (T, r) = 1 \text {   for   all   } r\tag{6.5.5}
$$

because the value of the bond at maturity is its face value 1 . 

Example 6. 5. 1 (Hull- White interest rate model}. In the Hull-White model, the evolution of the interest rate is given by 

$$
d R (t) = \left(a (t) - b (t) R (t)\right) d t + \sigma (t) d \widetilde {W} (t),
$$

where ${ \pmb a } ( t ) , \ b b ( t )$ , and $\sigma ( t )$ are nonrandom positive functions of time. The partial diferential equation (6.5.4) for the zero-coupon bond price becomes 

$$
f _ {t} (t, r) + \bigl (a (t) - b (t) r \bigr) f _ {r} (t, r) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (t) f _ {r r} (t, r) = r f (t, r).\tag{6.5.6}
$$

We initially guess and subsequently verify that the solution has the form 

$$
f (t, r) = e ^ {- r C (t, T) - A (t, T)}
$$

for some nonrandom functions $C ( t , T )$ and $A ( t , T )$ to be determined. These are functions of $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ ; the maturity $_ { T }$ is fixed. In this case, the yield 

$$
Y (t, T) = - \frac {1}{T - t} \log f (t, r) = \frac {1}{T - t} \left(r C (t, T) + A (t, T)\right)
$$

is an $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { a } } \mathbf { \beta } \mathbf { \beta } \mathbf { \hat { \boldsymbol { a } } } \mathbf { \boldsymbol { n } } e$ function of $r \ ( \mathrm { i . e . , }$ a number times r plus another number) . The Hull-White model is a special case of a class of models called $a f f i n e$ yield models. 

Furthermore, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f _ {t} (t, r) = \big (- r C ^ {\prime} (t, T) - A ^ {\prime} (t, T) \big) f (t, r), \\ f _ {r} (t, r) = - C (t, T) f (t, r), \\ f _ {r r} (t, r) = C ^ {2} (t, T) f (t, r), \end{array}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { C ^ { \prime } ( t , T ) = \frac { \partial } { \partial t } C ( t , T ) } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { A ^ { \prime } ( t , T ) = \frac { \partial } { \partial t } A ( t , T ) } \end{array}$ . Substitution into the partial diferential equation (6.5.6) gives 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left[ \big (- C ^ {\prime} (t, T) + b (t) C (t, T) - 1 \big) r \right.} \\ & {\qquad \left. - A ^ {\prime} (t, T) - a (t) C (t, T) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (t) C ^ {2} (t, T) \right] f (t, r) = 0.} \end{array}\tag{6.5.7}
$$

Because this equation must hold for all $^ { r , }$ the term that multiplies $\pmb { r }$ in this equation must be zero. Otherwise, changing the value of $\pmb { r }$ would change the value of the left-hand side of (6.5.7) , and hence it could not always be equal to zero. This gives us ordinary diferential equation in t: 

$$
C ^ {\prime} (t, T) = b (t) C (t, T) - 1.\tag{6.5.8}
$$

Setting this term equal to zero in (6.5.7) , we now see that 

$$
A ^ {\prime} (t, T) = - a (t) C (t, T) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (t) C ^ {2} (t, T).\tag{6.5.9}
$$

The terminal condition 6.5.5 must hold for all $^ { r , }$ and this implies that $C ( T , T ) = A ( T , T ) = 0 .$ . Equations (6.5.8) and (6.5.9) and these terminal conditions provide enough information to determine the functions $A ( t , T )$ and $c ( t , T )$ for $0 \leq t \leq T$ . They are 

$$
\begin{array}{l} C (t, T) = \int_ {t} ^ {T} e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {s} b (v) d v} d s, \\ A (t, T) = \int_ {t} ^ {T} \left(a (s) C (s, T) - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (s) C ^ {2} (s, T)\right) d s. \end{array}\tag{6.5.10}
$$

(6 . 5 . 1 1 ) 

It is clear that these formulas give functions that satisfy $C ( T , T ) = A ( T , T ) =$ 0. The verification that these formulas provide the unique solutions to (6.5.8) and (6.5.9) is Exercise 6.3. 

In conclusion, we have derived an explicit formula for the price of a zerocoupon bond as a function of the interest rate in the Hull-White model. It is 

$$
B (t, T) = e ^ {- R (t) C (t, T) - A (t, T)}, 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

where $C ( t , T )$ and $A ( t , T )$ are given by (6.5.10) and (6.5. 1 1) . 

Example 6. 5. 2 (Cox-Ingersoll-Ross interest rate model). In the CIR model, the evolution of the interest rate is given by 

$$
d R (t) = \left(a - b R (t)\right) d t + \sigma \sqrt {R (t)} d \widetilde {W} (t),
$$

where $a , \ b ,$ and $\pmb { \sigma }$ are positive constants. The partial diferential equation (6.5.4) for the bond price becomes 

$$
f _ {t} (t, r) + (a - b r) f _ {r} (t, r) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} r f _ {r r} (t, r) = r f (t, r).\tag{6.5.12}
$$

Again, we initially guess and subsequently verify that the solution has the form 

$$
f (t, r) = e ^ {- r C (t, T) - A (t, T)}.
$$

The Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model is another example of an afine yield model. Substitution into the diferential equation (6.5.12) gives 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \big [ \big (- C ^ {\prime} (t, T) + b C (t, T) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} C ^ {2} (t, T) - 1 \big) r \\ - A ^ {\prime} (t, T) - a C (t, T) \big ] f (t, r) = 0. \end{array}\tag{6.5.13}
$$

We can again conclude that the term multiplying r must be zero and then conclude that the other term must also be zero, thereby obtaining two ordinary diferential equations in t: 

$$
C ^ {\prime} (t, T) = b C (t, T) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} C ^ {2} (t, T) - 1,
$$

$$
A ^ {\prime} (t, T) = - a C (t, T).\tag{6.5.14}
$$

(6.5. 15) 

The solutions to these equations satisfying the terminal conditions $C ( T , T ) =$ $A ( T , T ) = 0$ are 

$$
\begin{array}{l} C (t, T) = \frac {\sinh (\gamma (T - t))}{\gamma \cosh (\gamma (T - t)) + \frac {1}{2} b \sinh (\gamma (T - t))}, \\ A (t, T) = - \frac {2 a}{\sigma^ {2}} \log \left[ \frac {\gamma e ^ {\frac {1}{2} b (T - t)}}{\gamma \cosh (\gamma (T - t)) + \frac {1}{2} b \sinh (\gamma (T - t))} \right], \end{array}\tag{6.5.16}
$$

(6.5. 1 7) 

where $\begin{array} { r } { \gamma = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \sqrt { b ^ { 2 } + 2 \sigma ^ { 2 } } } \end{array}$ , sinh $\begin{array} { r } { u = \frac { e ^ { u } - e ^ { - u } } { 2 } } \end{array}$ , and cosh $\begin{array} { r } { u = \frac { e ^ { u } + e ^ { - u } } { 2 } } \end{array}$ . The verification of this assertion is Exercise 6.4. 0 

Example 6. 5. 3 (Option on a bond}. Consider the general short-rate model (6.5. 1 ) . Let $0 \leq t \leq T _ { 1 } < T _ { 2 }$ be given. In this example, the fixed time $T _ { 2 }$ is the maturity date for a zero-coupon bond. The fixed time $T _ { 1 }$ is the expiration date for a European call on this bond. We wish to determine the value of this call at time t . 

Suppose we have solved for the function $f ( t , r )$ satisfying the partial diferential equation (6.5.4) together with the terminal condition (6.5.5) . This gives us the price of the zero-coupon bond as a function of time and the underlying interest rate. 

According to the risk-neutral pricing formula (5.2.31) and the Markov property, the value of the call at time t is 

$$
\begin{array}{r} c (t, R (t)) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T _ {1}} R (s) d s} \Bigl (f (T _ {1}, R (T _ {1})) - K \Bigr) ^ {+} \bigg | \mathcal {F} (t) \right] \\ = \frac {1}{D (t)} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ D (T _ {1}) \Bigl (f (T _ {1}, R (T _ {1})) - K \Bigr) ^ {+} \bigg | \mathcal {F} (t) \right] \end{array}
$$

for some function $c ( t , r )$ of the dummy variables t and $^ { \mathfrak { r } } \cdot$ The discounted call price 

$$
D (t) c (t, R (t)) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ D (T _ {1}) \Big (f (T _ {1}, R (T _ {1})) - K \Big) ^ {+} \bigg | \mathcal {F} (t) \right], 0 \leq t \leq T _ {1},
$$

is a martingale. The diferential of the discounted call price is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \big (D (t) c (t, R (t)) \big) = c (t, R (t)) d D (t) + D (t) d c (t, R (t))} \\ & {\qquad = D \left[ - R c d t + c _ {t} d t + c _ {r} d R + \frac {1}{2} c _ {r r} d R d R \right]} \\ & {\qquad = D \left[ - R c + c _ {t} + \beta c _ {r} + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} c _ {r r} \right] d t + D \gamma c _ {r} d \widetilde {W}.} \end{array}
$$

Setting the dt term to zero, we obtain the partial diferential equation 

$$
c _ {t} (t, r) + \beta (t, r) c _ {r} (t, r) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, r) c _ {r r} (t, r) = r c (t, r).
$$

This is the same partial diferential equation that governs $f ( t , r )$ . However, $c ( t , r )$ and $\textstyle f ( t , r )$ have diferent terminal conditions. The terminal condition for $\boldsymbol { c } ( t , \boldsymbol { r } )$ is 

$$
c (T _ {1}, r) = (f (T _ {1}, r) - K) ^ {+} \text {   for   all   } r.
$$

One can use these conditions to numerically determine the call price function $\boldsymbol { c } ( t , \boldsymbol { r } )$ [] 

## 6.6 Multidimensional Feynman-Kac Theorems

The Feynman-Kac and Discounted Feynman-Kac Theorems, Theorems 6.4. 1 and 6.4.3, have multidimensional versions. The number of diferential equations and the number of Brownian motions entering those diferential equations can both be larger than one and do not need to be the same. We illustrate the general situation by working out the details for two stochastic diferential equations driven by two Brownian motions. 

Let $W ( t ) = ( W _ { 1 } ( t ) , W _ { 2 } ( t ) )$ be a two-dimensional Brownian motion (i.e. , a vector of two independent, one-dimensional Brownian motions) . Consider two stochastic diferential equations 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d X _ {1} (u) = \beta_ {1} (u, X _ {1} (u), X _ {2} (u)) d u + \gamma_ {1 1} (u, X _ {1} (u), X _ {2} (u)) d W _ {1} (u)} \\ & {\qquad + \gamma_ {1 2} (u, X _ {1} (u), X _ {2} (u)) d W _ {2} (u),} \\ & {d X _ {2} (u) = \beta_ {2} (u, X _ {1} (u), X _ {2} (u)) d u + \gamma_ {2 1} (u, X _ {1} (u), X _ {2} (u)) d W _ {1} (u)} \\ & {\qquad + \gamma_ {2 2} (u, X _ {1} (u), X _ {2} (u)) d W _ {2} (u).} \end{array}
$$

The solution to this pair of stochastic diferential equations, starting at $X _ { 1 } ( t ) = x _ { 1 }$ and $X _ { 2 } ( t ) = x _ { 2 }$ , depends on the specified initial time t and the initial positions $\pmb { x } _ { 1 }$ and $\pmb { x _ { 2 } }$ . Regardless of the initial condition, the solution is a Markov process. 

Let a Borel-measurable function $h ( y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } )$ be given. Corresponding to the initial condition $t , x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 }$ , where $0 \leq t \leq T _ { \cdot }$ , we define 

$$
g (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}) = \mathbb {E} ^ {t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}} h (X _ {1} (T), X _ {2} (T)),\tag{6.6.1}
$$

$$
f (t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}) = \mathbb {E} ^ {t, x _ {1}, x _ {2}} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} h (X _ {1} (T), X _ {2} (T)) \right].\tag{6.6.2}
$$

Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} g _ {t} + \beta_ {1} g _ {x _ {1}} + \beta_ {2} g _ {x _ {2}} \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2} (\gamma_ {1 1} ^ {2} + \gamma_ {1 2} ^ {2}) g _ {x _ {1} x _ {1}} + (\gamma_ {1 1} \gamma_ {2 1} + \gamma_ {1 2} \gamma_ {2 2}) g _ {x _ {1} x _ {2}} + \frac {1}{2} (\gamma_ {2 1} ^ {2} + \gamma_ {2 2} ^ {2}) g _ {x _ {2} x _ {2}} = 0, \\ f _ {t} + \beta_ {1} f _ {x _ {1}} + \beta_ {2} f _ {x _ {2}} \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2} (\gamma_ {1 1} ^ {2} + \gamma_ {1 2} ^ {2}) f _ {x _ {1} x _ {1}} + (\gamma_ {1 1} \gamma_ {2 1} + \gamma_ {1 2} \gamma_ {2 2}) f _ {x _ {1} x _ {2}} + \frac {1}{2} (\gamma_ {2 1} ^ {2} + \gamma_ {2 2} ^ {2}) f _ {x _ {2} x _ {2}} = r f. \end{array} \tag {6.6.3}\tag{6.6.4}
$$

Of course, these functions also satisfy the terminal conditions 

$$
g (T, x _ {1}, x _ {2}) = f (T, x _ {1}, x _ {2}) = h (x _ {1}, x _ {2}) \text {   for   all   } x _ {1} \text {   and   } x _ {2}.
$$

Equations (6.6.3) and (6.6.4) are derived by starting the pair of processes $X _ { 1 } , \ X _ { 2 }$ at time zero, observing that the processes $g ( t , X _ { 1 } ( t ) , X _ { 2 } ( t ) )$ and $e ^ { - r t } f ( t , X _ { 1 } ( t ) , X _ { 2 } ( t ) )$ are martingales, taking their diferentials , and setting the dt terms equal to zero. When taking the diferentials, one uses the fact that $W _ { 1 }$ and $W _ { 2 }$ are independent. We leave the details to the reader in Exercise 6.5. This exercise also provides the counterparts of (6.6.3) and (6.6.4) when $W _ { 1 }$ and $W _ { 2 }$ are correlated Brownian motions. 

Example 6. 6. 1 (Asian option). We show by example how the Discounted Feynman-Kac Theorem can be used to find prices and hedges, even for pathdependent options. The option we choose for this example is Asian option. A more detailed discussion of this option is presented in Section 7.5. The payof we consider is 

$$
V (T) = \left(\frac {1}{T} \int_ {0} ^ {T} S (u) d u - K\right) ^ {+},
$$

where $\boldsymbol { S } ( \boldsymbol { u } )$ is a geometric Brownian motion, the expiration time $_ { T }$ is fixed and positive, and K is a positive strike pric� In terms of the Brownian motion $\widetilde { W } ( u )$ under the risk-neutral measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } _ { : }$ , we may write the stochastic diferential equation for $\pmb { S } ( \pmb { u } )$ as 

$$
d S (u) = r S (u) d u + \sigma S (u) d \widetilde {W} (u).\tag{6.6.5}
$$

Because the payof depends on the whole path of the stock price via its integral, at each time t prior to expiration it is not enough to know just the stock price in order to determine the value of the option. We must also know the integral of the stock price, 

$$
Y (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} S (u) d u,
$$

up to the current time t. Similarly, it is not enough to know just the integral $Y ( t )$ . We must also know the current stock price $S ( t )$ . Indeed, for the same value of $Y ( t )$ , the Asian option is worth more for high values of $S ( t )$ than for low values because the high values of $S ( t )$ make it more likely that the option will have a high payof. 

For the process $Y ( u )$ , we have the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d Y (u) = S (u) d u.\tag{6.6.6}
$$

Because the pair of processes $( S ( u ) , Y ( u ) )$ is given by the pair of stochastic diferential equations (6.6.5) and (6.6.6) , the pair of processes $( S ( u ) , Y ( u ) )$ is a two-dimensional Markov process. 

Note that $Y ( u )$ alone is not a Markov process because its stochastic differential equation involves the process $\pmb { S } ( \pmb { u } )$ . However, the pair $( S ( u ) , Y ( u ) )$ is Markov because the pair of stochastic diferential equations for these processes involves only these processes (and, of course, the driving Brownian motion $\widetilde { W } ( u ) )$ . 

If we use (6.6.5) and (6.6.6) t o generate the processes $\boldsymbol { S } ( \boldsymbol { u } )$ and $Y ( u )$ starting with initial values $S ( 0 ) > 0$ and $Y ( 0 ) = 0$ at time zero, then the payof of the Asian option at expiration time $_ { T }$ is $\begin{array} { r } { V ( T ) = ( \frac { 1 } { T } Y ( T ) - K ) ^ { + } } \end{array}$ According to the risk-neutral pricing formula (5.2.31 ) , the value of the Asian option at times prior to expiration is 

$$
V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} \left(\frac {1}{T} Y (T) - K\right) ^ {+} \bigg | \mathcal {F} (t) \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.
$$

Because the pair of processes $( S ( u ) , Y ( u ) )$ is Markov, this can be written as some function of the time variable t and the values at time t of these processes. In other words, there is a function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ such that 

$$
v (t, S (t), Y (t)) = V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} \left(\frac {1}{T} Y (T) - K\right) ^ {+} \mid \mathcal {F} (t) \right].
$$

Note that this function must satisfy the terminal condition 

$$
v (T, x, y) = \left(\frac {y}{T} - K\right) ^ {+} \text {   for   all   } x \text {   and   } y.\tag{6.6.7}
$$

Using iterated conditioning, it is easy to see that the discounted option value $e ^ { - r t } v ( t , S ( t ) , Y ( t ) )$ is martingale. Its diferential is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} {d \big (e ^ {- r t} v (t, S (t), Y (t)) \big)} \\ {= e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r v d t + v _ {t} d t + v _ {x} d S + v _ {y} d Y + \frac {1}{2} v _ {x x} d S d S + v _ {x y} d S d Y \right.} \\ {\left. + \frac {1}{2} v _ {y y} d Y d Y \right]} \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} = e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r v d t + v _ {t} d t + v _ {x} (r S d t + \sigma S d \widetilde {W}) + v _ {y} S d t + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} v _ {x x} d t \right] \\ = e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r v (t, S (t), Y (t)) + v _ {t} (t, S (t), Y (t)) + r S (t) v _ {x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) \right. \\ \left. + S (t) v _ {y} (t, S (t), Y (t)) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) v _ {x x} (t, S (t), Y (T)) \right] d t \\ + e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) v _ {x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d \widetilde {W} (t). \end{array} \tag {6}\tag{6.6.8}
$$

Because the discounted option price is a martingale, the dt term in this differential must be zero. We obtain the partial diferential equation 

$$
v _ {t} (t, x, y) + r x v _ {x} (t, x, y) + x v _ {y} (t, x, y) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} x ^ {2} v _ {x x} (t, x, y) = r v (t, x, y).\tag{6.6.9}
$$

This is an example of the Discounted Feynman-Kac Theorem, a special case of equation (6.6.4) . In particular, (6.6.8) simplifies to 

$$
d \big (e ^ {- r t} v (t, S (t), Y (t)) \big) = e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) v _ {x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d \widetilde {W} (t).\tag{6.6.10}
$$

Recall from (5.2.27) that the discounted value of a portfolio satisfies the equation 

$$
d \left(e ^ {- r t} X (t)\right) = e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) \Delta (t) d \widetilde {W} (t).\tag{6.6.11}
$$

If we sell the Asian option at time zero for ${  { \boldsymbol v } } ( 0 , S ( 0 ) , 0 )$ and use this as the initial capital for a hedging portfolio (i.e. , take $X ( 0 ) = v ( 0 , S ( 0 ) , 0 ) )$ , and at each time t use the portfolio process $\varDelta ( t ) = v _ { x } ( t , S ( t ) , Y ( t ) )$ , then we will have 

$$
d \big (e ^ {- r t} X (t) \big) = d \big (e ^ {- r t} v (t, S (t), Y (t)) \big)
$$

for all times $\mathbf { } ^ { t , }$ and hence 

$$
X (T) = v (T, S (T), Y (T)) = \left(\frac {1}{T} Y (T) - K\right) ^ {+}.
$$

This procedure hedges a short position in the Asian option. We have obtained the usual formula that the number of shares held to hedge a short position in the option is the derivative of the option value with respect to the underlying stock price. However, the Asian option price is the solution to a partial diferential equation that contains a term $x v _ { y } ( t , x , y )$ that does not appear in the partial diferential equation for the price of a European option. 0 

## 6.7 Summary

When the underlying price of an asset is given by a stochastic diferential equation, the asset price is Markov and the price of any non-path-dependent derivative security based on that asset is given by a partial diferential equation. In order to price path-dependent securities, one first seeks to determine the variables on which the path-dependent payof depends and then introduce one or more additional stochastic diferential equations in order to have a system of such equations that describes the relevant variables. If this can be done, then again the price of the derivative security is given by a partial diferential equation. 

This leads to the following four-step procedure for finding the pricing differential equation and for constructing a hedge for a derivative security. 

1 . Determine the variables on which the derivative security price depends. In addition to time t, these are the underlying asset price S(t) and possibly other stochastic processes. We call these stochastic processes the state processes. One must be able to represent the derivative security payof in terms of these state processes. 

2. Write down a system of stochastic diferential equations for the state processes. Be sure that, except for the driving Brownian motions, the only random processes appearing on the right-hand sides of these equations are the state processes themselves. This ensures that the vector of state processes is Markov. 

3. The Markov property guarantees that the derivative security price at each time is a function of time and the state processes at that time. The discounted option price is a martingale under the risk-neutral measure. Compute the diferential of the discounted option price, set the dt term equal to zero, and obtain thereby a partial diferential equation. 

4. The terms multiplying the Brownian motion diferentials in the discounted derivative security price diferential must be matched by the terms multiplying the Brownian motion diferentials in the evolution of the hedging portfolio value; see (5.4.27) . Matching these terms determines the hedge for a short position in the derivative security. 

## 6.8 Notes

Conditions for the existence and uniqueness of solutions to stochastic diferential equations are provided by Karatzas and Shreve [101] , Chapter 5, Section 2, who also show in Chapter 5, Section 4, that solutions to stochastic diferential equations have the Markov property. This is based on work of Stroock and Varadhan [151] . The ideas behind the Feynman-Kac Theorem, although not the presentation we give here, trace back to Feynman [65] and Kac [99] . 

Hull and White presented their interest rate model in [88] , in which they generalized a model of Vasicek [154] to allow time-varying coeficients. The origin of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model is [41] , where one can find a closedform formula for the distribution of the interest rate in the model. These are examples of afine-yield models, a class identified by Dufie and Kan [58] . They are sometimes called multifactor CIR models. 

Example 6.6. 1 obtains a partial diferential equation for the price of an Asian option but does not address computational issues. In the form given here, the equation is dificult to handle numerically. Veeer [156] and Rogers and Shi [139] present transformations of this equation that are numerically more stable. See also Andreasen [4] for an application of the change-of-numeraire idea of Chapter 9 to discretely sampled Asian options. The transformation of Veeer and its use for both continuously sampled and discretely sampled Asian options is presented in Section 7.5. 

The Heston stochastic volatility model of Exercise 6. 7 is taken from Heston [84] . Exercise 6. 10 on implying the volatility surface comes from Dupire [61] . The same idea for binomial trees was worked out by Derman et al. [50] , [51] .

Exercise 6.2 (No-arbitrage derivation of bond-pricing equation) . In Section 6.5, we began with the stochastic diferential equation (6.5. 1) for the interest rate under the risk-neutral measure ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } ,$ , used the risk-neutral pricing formula (6.5.3) to consider a zero-coupon bond maturing at time $_ { \pmb { T } }$ whose price $B ( t , T )$ at time t before maturity is a function $f ( t , R ( t ) )$ of the time and the interest rate, and derived the partial diferential equation (6.5.4) for the function $f ( t , r )$ . In this exercise, we show how to derive this partial differential equation from no-arbitrage considerations rather than by using the risk-neutral pricing formula. 

Suppose the interest rate is given by a stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d R (t) = \alpha (t, R (t)) d t + \gamma (t, R (t)) d W (t),\tag{6.9.1}
$$

where $W ( t )$ is a Brownian motion under a probability measure $\mathbb { P }$ not assumed to be risk-neutral. Assume further that , for each $^ { T , }$ the T-maturity zerocoupon bond price is a function $f ( t , R ( t ) , T )$ of the current time $t ,$ the current interest rate $R ( t )$ , and the maturity of the bond ${ \mathbf { } } T .$ . We do not assume that this bond price is given by the risk-neutral pricing formula (6.5.3) . 

Assume for the moment that $f _ { r } ( t , r , T ) \neq 0$ for all values of $\pmb { r }$ and ${ \bf 0 } \le t \le$ $^ { T , }$ so we can define 

$$
\beta (t, r, T) = - \frac {1}{f _ {r} (t , r , T)} \left[ - r f (t, r, T) + f _ {t} (t, r, T) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, r) f _ {r r} (t, r, T) \right],\tag{6.9.2}
$$

and then have 

$$
f _ {t} (t, r, T) + \beta (t, r, T) f _ {r} (t, r, T) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, r) f _ {r r} (t, r, T) = r f (t, r, T).\tag{6.9.3}
$$

Equation (6.9.3) will reduce to (6.5.4) for the function $f ( t , r , T )$ if we can show that $\beta ( t , r , T )$ does not depend on ${ \mathbf { } } T .$ 

(i) Consider two maturities $0 < T _ { 1 } < T _ { 2 }$ , and consider a portfolio that at each time $t \leq T _ { 1 }$ holds $\varDelta _ { 1 } ( t )$ bonds maturing at time $T _ { 1 }$ and $\varDelta _ { 2 } ( t )$ bonds maturing at time $T _ { 2 }$ , financing this by investing or borrowing at the interest rate $R ( t )$ . Show that the value of this portfolio satisfies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \big (D (t) X (t) \big) \\ = \varDelta_ {1} (t) D (t) \left[ - R (t) f (t, R (t), T _ {1}) + f _ {t} (t, R (t), T _ {1}) \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \left. + \alpha (t, R (t)) f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {1}) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, R (t)) f _ {r r} (t, R (t), T _ {1}) \right] d t \\ \qquad + \varDelta_ {2} (t) D (t) \left[ - R (t) f (t, R (t), T _ {2}) + f _ {t} (t, R (t), T _ {2}) \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \left. + \alpha (t, R (t)) f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {2}) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, R (t)) f _ {r r} (t, R (t), T _ {2}) \right] d t \\ \qquad + D (t) \gamma (t, R (t)) \big [ \varDelta_ {1} (t) f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {1}) + \varDelta_ {2} (t) f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {2}) \big ] d W (t) \\ = \varDelta_ {1} (t) D (t) \big [ \alpha (t, R (t)) - \beta (t, R (t), T _ {1}) \big ] f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {1}) d t \\ \qquad + \varDelta_ {2} (t) D (t) \big [ \alpha (t, R (t)) - \beta (t, R (t), T _ {2}) \big ] f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {2}) d t \\ \qquad + D (t) \gamma (t, R (t)) \big [ \varDelta_ {1} (t) f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {1}) + \varDelta_ {2} (t) f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {2}) \big ] d W (t). \end{array}\tag{6.9.4}
$$

(ii) Denote 

$$
\operatorname{sign} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text {if x > 0 ,} \\ 0 & \text {if x = 0 ,} \\ - 1 & \text {if x <   0 ,} \end{array} \right.
$$

and 

$$
S (t) = \operatorname{sign} \left\{\left[ \beta (t, R (t), T _ {2}) - \beta (t, R (t), T _ {1}) \right] f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {1}) f _ {r} (t, R (t), T _ {2}) \right\}
$$

Show that the portfolio processes $\varDelta _ { 1 } ( t ) = S ( t ) f _ { r } ( t , R ( t ) , T _ { 2 } )$ and $\varDelta _ { 2 } ( t ) =$ $- S ( t ) f _ { r } ( t , R ( t ) , T _ { 1 } )$ result in arbitrage unless $\beta ( t , R ( t ) , T _ { 1 } ) = \beta ( t , R ( t ) , T _ { 2 } )$ Since $\pmb { T _ { 1 } }$ and $\boldsymbol { T _ { 2 } }$ are arbitrary, we conclude that $\beta ( t , r , T )$ does not depend on ${ \pmb T } .$ . 

(iii) Now let a maturity $T > 0$ be given and consider a portfolio $\varDelta ( t )$ that invests only in the bond of maturity $^ { T , }$ financing this by investing or borrowing at the interest rate $R ( t )$ . Show that the value of this portfolio satisfies

\begin{array}{l} d (D (t) X (t)) \\ = \Delta (t) D (t) [ - R (t) f (t, R (t), T) + f _ {t} (t, R (t), T) \\ \quad + \alpha (t, R (t)) f _ {r} (t, R (t), T) + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} (t, R (t)) f _ {r r} (t, R (t), T) ] d t \\ \quad + D (t) \Delta (t) \gamma (t, R (t)) f _ {r} (t, R (t), T) d W (t). \end{array} \tag {6}\tag{6.9.5}

In conclusion, we have shown that if trading in the zero-coupon bonds presents no arbitrage opportunity, then for all $t , r ,$ and $_ { T }$ such that $f _ { r } ( t , r , T ) \neq 0 ,$ , we can define $\beta ( t , r )$ by (6.9.2) because the right-hand side of (6.9.2) does not depend on T. We then have

which is (6.5.4) for the T-maturity bond. If $f _ { r } ( t , r , T ) = 0 ,$ then (6.9.6) holds , so (6.9.7) must still hold, no matter how $\beta ( t , r )$ is defined. If we now change to a measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ under which

\widetilde {W} (t) = W (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {1}{\gamma (u , R (u))} [ \alpha (u, R (u)) - \beta (u, R (u)) ] d u

is a Brow�ian motion, then (6.9. 1 ) can be rewritten as (6.5. 1 ) . The probability measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ is risk-neutral.

Exercise 6.6 (Moment-generating function for Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process) .

is a Brownian motion. In other words, R(t) is a Cox-Ingersoll-Ross interest rate process (Example 6.5.2) . (Hint: Use Levy's Theorem, Theorem 4.6.4, to show that $B ( t )$ is a Brownian motion. )

Remark 6. 9. 1 {Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process hitting zero). Although we have derived (6.9.22) under the assumption that d is a positive integer, the second line of (6.9.22) is expressed in terms of only the parameters $a , b ,$ and $\pmb { \sigma }$ entering (6.9. 19) , and this formula is valid for all $a > 0 , b > 0 ,$ and $\sigma > 0$ . When $d \geq 2$ $\begin{array} { r } { ( \mathrm { i } . \mathrm { e } . , \pmb { \alpha } \geq \frac { 1 } { 2 } \sigma ^ { 2 } ) } \end{array}$ , the multidimensional process $\left( X _ { 1 } ( t ) , \ldots , X _ { d } ( t ) \right)$ never hits the origin $\mathbf { i n } \ \bar { \mathbb { R } } ^ { d } .$ , and hence $R ( t )$ is never zero. If $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < \alpha < \frac { 1 } { 2 } \sigma ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , then $R ( t )$ hits zero repeatedly but after each hit becomes positive again. 

Exercise 6.7 (Heston stochastic volatility model) . Suppose that under a risk-neutral measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ a stock price is governed by 

$$
d S (t) = r S (t) d t + \sqrt {V (t)} S (t) d \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t),\tag{6.9.23}
$$

where the interest rate $\pmb { r }$ is constant and the volatility $\sqrt { V ( t ) }$ ( is itself a stochastic process governed by the equation 

$$
d V (t) = \left(a - b V (t)\right) d t + \sigma \sqrt {V (t)} d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t).\tag{6.9.24}
$$

The parameters $a , b ,$ , and $\pmb { \sigma }$ are positive constants, and $\widetilde { W } _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $\widetilde { W } _ { 2 } ( t )$ are correlated Brownian motions under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ with 

$$
d \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) = \rho d t
$$

for some $\rho \in ( - 1 , 1 )$ . Because the two-dimensional process $( S ( t ) , V ( t ) )$ is governed by the pair of stochastic diferential equations (6.9.23) and (6.9.24) , it is a two-dimensional Markov process. 

So long as trading takes place only in the stock and money market account, this model is incomplete. One can create a one-parameter family of risk-neutral measures by changing the dt term in (6.9.24) without afecting (6 . 9 .23) . 

At time $\mathbf { } t ,$ the risk-neutral _price of a call expiring at time $T \geq t$ in this stochastic volatility model is $\widetilde { \mathbb { E } } [ e ^ { - r ( T - t ) } ( S ( T ) - K ) ^ { \breve { + } } | \mathcal { F } ( t ) ]$ . Because of the Markov property, there is a function $c ( t , s , v )$ such that 

$$
c (t, S (t), V (t)) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} (S (T) - K) ^ {+} \mid \mathcal {F} (t) \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{6.9.25}
$$

This problem shows that the function $c ( t , s , v )$ satisfies the partial diferential equation 

$$
c _ {t} + r s c _ {s} + (a - b v) c _ {v} + \frac {1}{2} s ^ {2} v c _ {s s} + \rho \sigma s v c _ {s v} + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} v c _ {v v} = r c\tag{6.9.26}
$$

in the region $0 \leq t < T , s \geq 0$ , and $v \geq 0 .$ . The function $c ( t , s , v )$ also satisfies the boundary conditions 

$$
c (T, s, v) = (s - K) ^ {+} \text {   for   all   } s \geq 0, v \geq 0,\tag{6.9.27}
$$

$$
c (t, 0, v) = 0 \text {   for   all   } 0 \leq t \leq T, v \geq 0,\tag{6.9.28}
$$

$$
c (t, s, 0) = \left(s - e ^ {- r (T - t)} K\right) ^ {+} \text {   for   all   } 0 \leq t \leq T, s \geq 0,\tag{6.9.29}
$$

$$
\lim _ {s \rightarrow \infty} \frac {c (t , s , v)}{s - K} = 1 \text {   for   all   } 0 \leq t \leq T, v \geq 0,\tag{6.9.30}
$$

$$
\lim _ {v \to \infty} c (t, s, v) = s \text {   for   all   } 0 \leq t \leq T, s \geq 0.\tag{6.9.31}
$$

In this problem, we shall be concerned only with (6.9.27) . 

(i) Show that $e ^ { - r t } c ( t , S ( t ) , V ( t ) )$ is a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } ,$ and use this fact to obtain (6.9.26) .

Exercise 6.9 (Kolmogorov forward equation) . (Also called the Fokker-Planck equation) . We begin with the same stochastic diferential equation, 

$$
d X (u) = \beta (u, X (u)) d u + \gamma (u, X (u)) d W (u),\tag{6.9.46}
$$

as in Exercise 6.8, use the same notation $p ( t , T , x , y )$ for the transition density, and again assume that $p ( t , T , x , y ) = 0$ for $0 \leq t < T$ and $y \leq 0 .$ In this problem, we show that $p ( t , T , x , y )$ satisfies the Kolmogorov forward equation 

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial T} p (t, T, x, y) = - \frac {\partial}{\partial y} (\beta (t, y) p (t, T, x, y)) + \frac {1}{2} \frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial y ^ {2}} (\gamma^ {2} (T, y) p (t, T, x, y)).\tag{6.9.47}
$$

In contrast to the Kolmogorov backward equation, in which T and y were held constant and the variables were t and x, here t and x are held constant and the variables are y and T. The variables t and x are sometimes called the backward variables, and $_ { \pmb { T } }$ and y are called the forward vanables. 

(i) Let b be a positive constant and let $h _ { b } ( y )$ be a function with continuous first and second derivatives such that $h _ { b } ( { \pmb x } ) = 0$ for all $\pmb { x } \le 0 , h _ { b } ^ { \prime } ( \pmb { x } ) = 0$ for all $x \geq b ,$ and $h _ { b } ( b ) = h _ { b } ^ { \prime } ( b ) = 0 .$ Let $X ( u )$ be the solution to the stochastic diferential equation with initial condition $X ( t ) = x \in ( 0 , b )$ and use $\mathbf { I t } \hat { \mathbf { o } } \ ' \mathbf { s }$ formula to compute $d h _ { b } \big ( X ( u ) \big )$ 

(ii) Let $0 \leq t < T$ be given, and integrate the equation you obtained in (i) from t to T. Take expectations and use the fact that $X ( u )$ has density $p ( t , { \boldsymbol { u } } , { \boldsymbol { x } } , { \boldsymbol { y } } )$ in the y-variable to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {b} h _ {b} (y) p (t, T, x, y) d y = h _ {b} (x) + \int_ {t} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {b} \beta (u, y) p (t, u, x, y) h _ {b} ^ {\prime} (y) d y d u \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {t} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {b} \gamma^ {2} (u, y) p (t, u, x, y) h _ {b} ^ {\prime \prime} (y) d y. \end{array}\tag{6.9.48}
$$

(iii ) Integrate the integrals $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { b } \cdots d y$ on the right-hand side of (6.9.48) by parts to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {b} h _ {b} (y) p (t, T, x, y) d y \\ = h _ {b} (x) - \int_ {t} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {b} \frac {\partial}{\partial y} [ \beta (u, y) p (t, u, x, y) ] h _ {b} (y) d y d u \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {t} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {b} \frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial y ^ {2}} [ \gamma^ {2} (u, y) p (t, u, x, y) ] h _ {b} (y) d y d u. \end{array}\tag{6.9.49}
$$

(iv) Diferentiate (6.9.49) with respect to T to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {0} ^ {b} h _ {b} (y) \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial T} p (t, T, x, y) + \frac {\partial}{\partial y} (\beta (T, y) p (t, T, x, y)) \right. \\ \left. - \frac {1}{2} \frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial y ^ {2}} (\gamma^ {2} (T, y) p (t, T, x, y)) \right] d y = 0. \end{array}\tag{6.9.50}
$$

(v) Use (6.9.50) to show that there cannot be numbers $0 < y _ { 1 } < y _ { 2 }$ such that 

$$

# Exotic Options

## 7.1 Introduction

The European calls and puts considered thus far in this text are sometimes called vanilla or even plain vanilla options. Their payofs depend only on the final value of the underlying asset. Options whose payofs depend on the path of the underlying asset are called path-dependent or exotic. 

In this chapter, we present three types of exotic options on a geometric Brownian motion asset and work out a detailed analysis for one option of each type. The types considered are barier options, lookback options, and Asian options. In each case, we work out the standard partial diferential equation governing the option price. The first two options have explicit pricing formulas, which are based on the reflection principle for Brownian motion. Such a formula for Asian options is not known. However, for the Asian option there is a change-of-numeraire argument that reduces the pricing partial diferential equation to a simple form that can easily be solved numerically. We present this argument in Subsection 7.5.3. 

## 7.2 Maximum of Brownian Motion with Drift

In this section, we derive the joint density for a Brownian motion with drift and its maximum to date. This density is used in Sections 7.3 and 7.4 to obtain explicit pricing formulas for a barrier option and a lookback option. To derive this formula, we begin with a Brownian motion $\widetilde { W } ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T .$ defined on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , { \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } )$ . Under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ the Brownian motion $\widetilde { W } ( t )$ has zero drift (i.e. , it is a martingale) . Let a be a given number, and define 

$$

$$

This Brownian motion $\widehat W ( t )$ has drift a under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ . We further define 

$$

Because $\widehat { \cal W } ( 0 ) = 0 ,$ we have ${ \widehat { M } } ( T ) ~ \geq ~ 0$ . We also have ${ \widehat W } ( T ) \leq { \widehat M } ( T )$ Therefore, the pair of random variables $( \widehat { M } ( t ) , \widehat { W } ( T ) )$ takes values in the set $\{ ( m , w ) ; w \leq m , m \geq 0 \}$ shown in Figure 7.2.1.
