## 7.3 Knock-out Barrier Options

There are several types of barrier options. Some "knock out" when the underlying asset price crosses a barrier (i.e. , they become worthless) . If the underlying asset price begins below the barrier and must cross above it to cause the knock-out, the option is said to be up-and-out. A down-and-out option has the barrier below the initial asset price and knocks out if the asset price falls below the barrier. Other options "knock in" at a barrier (i.e. , they pay of zero unless they cross a barrier) . Knock-in options also fall into two classes, up-and-in and down-and-in. The payof at expiration for barrier options is typically either that of a put or a call. More complex barrier options require the asset price to not only cross a barrier but spend a certain amount of time across the barrier in order to knock in or knock out. 

In this section, we treat an up-and-out call on a geometric Brownian motion. The methodology we develop works equally well for up-and-in, downand-out, and down-and-in puts and calls. 

## 7.3.1 Up-and-Out Call

Our underlying risky asset is geometric Brownian motion 

$$
d S (t) = r S (t) d t + \sigma S (t) d \widetilde {W} (t),
$$

where $\widetilde { W } ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T ,$ , is a Brownian motion under the risk-neutral measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ . Consider a European call, expiring at time $^ { T , }$ with strike price K and upand-out barrier B. We assume $K < B ;$ otherwise, the option must knock out in order to be in the money and hence could only pay of zero. The solution to the stochastic diferential equation for the asset price is 

$$
S (t) = S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widetilde {W} (t) + (r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}) t} = S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {W} (t)},\tag{7.3.1}
$$

where $\widehat W ( t ) = \alpha t + \widetilde W ( t )$ , and 

$$
\alpha = \frac {1}{\sigma} \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right).
$$

We define $\widehat { M } ( T ) = \operatorname* { m a x } _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } \widehat { W } ( t )$ , so 

$$
\max _ {0 \leq t \leq T} S (t) = S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {M} (T)}.
$$

The option knocks out if and only if $S ( 0 ) e ^ { \sigma \widehat { M } ( T ) } > B ; \mathrm { i f } \ : S ( 0 ) e ^ { \sigma \widehat { M } ( T ) } \leq B ,$ the option pays of 

$$
\left(S (T) - K\right) ^ {+} = \left(S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {W} (T)} - K\right) ^ {+}.
$$

In other words, the payof of the option is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & V (T) = \left(S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {W} (T)} - K\right) ^ {+} \mathbb {I} _ {\{S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {M} (T)} \leq B \}} \\ & \quad = \left(S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {W} (T)} - K\right) \mathbb {I} _ {\{S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {W} (T)} \geq K, S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {M} (T)} \leq B \}} \\ & \quad = \left(S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {W} (T)} - K\right) \mathbb {I} _ {\{\widehat {W} (T) \geq k, \widehat {M} (T) \leq b \}}, \end{array}\tag{7.3.2}
$$

where 

$$
k = \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {K}{S (0)}, \quad b = \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {B}{S (0)}.\tag{7.3.3}
$$

## 7.3.2 Black-Scholes-Merton Equation

The price of an up-and-out call satisfies a Black-Scholes-Merton equation that has been modified to account for the barrier. This equation can be used to solve for the price. In this particular case, we do not need to find the price this way because it can be computed analytically (see Subsection 7.3.3}. However, we provide the equation and its derivation because this methodology works in situations where analytical solutions cannot be obtained. 

Theorem 7.3.1. Let ${ \boldsymbol v } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ denote the price at time t of the up-and-out call under the assumption that the call has not knocked out prior to time t and $\begin{array} { r } { { \pmb S } ( t ) = { \pmb x } . } \end{array}$ . Then $v ( t , x )$ satisfies the Black-Scholes-Merton partial diferential equation 

$$
v _ {t} (t, x) + r x v _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} x ^ {2} v _ {x x} (t, x) = r v (t, x)\tag{7.3.4}
$$

in the rectangle $\{ ( t , x ) ; 0 \leq t < T , 0 \leq x \leq B \}$ and satisfies the boundary conditions 

$$
v (t, 0) = 0, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{7.3.5}
$$

$$
v (t, B) = 0, \quad 0 \leq t <   T,\tag{7.3.6}
$$

$$
v (T, x) = (x - K) ^ {+}, \quad 0 \leq x \leq B.\tag{7.3.7}
$$

The lower boundary condition (7.3.5) follows as in the usual Black-Scholes-Merton framework: If the asset price begins at zero, it stays there and the option expires out of the money. The upper boundary condition follows from the fact that when the geometric Brownian $S ( t )$ hits the level B, it immediately rises above B. In fact, because it has nonzero quadratic variation, the asset price $S ( t )$ oscillates, rising and falling across the level B infinitely many times immediately after hitting it. The option price is zero when the asset price hits B because the option is on the verge of knocking out. The only exception to this is if the level B is first reached at the expiration time $T ,$ for then there is no time left for the knock-out . In this case, the option price is given by the terminal condition (7.3.7) . In particular, the function ${ \boldsymbol v } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ is not continuous at the corner of its domain where $t = T$ and $x = B$ . It is continuous everywhere else in the rectangle $\left\{ ( t , x ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T , 0 \leq x \leq B \right\}$ 

Exercise 7.8 outlines the steps to verify the Black-Scholes-Merton equation by direct computation, starting with the analytical formula (7.3.20) obtained in Subsection 7.3.3. Here we derive this partial diferential equation (7.3.4) by the simpler but more generally applicable argument used previously: ( 1) find the martingale, (2) take the diferential, and (3) set the dt term equal to zero. 

Let us begin with an initial asset price ${ \cal S } ( 0 ) \in ( 0 , B )$ . We then define the option payof $V ( T )$ by (7.3.2) . The price of the option at time t between initiation and expiration is given by the risk-neutral pricing formula 

$$
V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} V (T) \Big | \mathcal {F} (t) \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{7.3.8}
$$

The usual iterated conditioning argument (e.g. , (5.3.3) ) shows that 

$$
e ^ {- r t} V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r T} V (T) \mid \mathcal {F} (t) \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{7.3.9}
$$

is a martingale. We would like to use the Markov property as we did in Example 6.4.4 to say that $V ( t ) = v \big ( t , S ( t ) \big )$ , where ${ \boldsymbol v } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ is the function in Theorem 7.3. 1 . However, this equation does not hold for all values of t along all paths. Recall that $v ( t , S ( t ) )$ is the value of the option under the assumption that it has not knocked out prior to t, whereas $V ( t )$ is the value of the option without any assumption. In particular, if the underlying asset price rises above the barrier $B$ and then returns below the barrier by time $\mathbf { } t ,$ then $V ( t )$ will be zero because the option has knocked out, but $v ( t , S ( t ) )$ will be strictly positive because ${ \boldsymbol v } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ given by (7.3.20) is strictly positive for all values of $0 \leq t < T$ and $0 < x < B$ . The process $V ( t )$ is path-dependent and remembers that the option has knocked out. The process $v \left( t , S ( t ) \right)$ is not path-dependent, and when $S ( t ) < B ,$ it gives the price of the option under the assumption that it has not knocked out, even if that assumption is incorrect. 

We resolve this annoyance by defining $\pmb { \rho }$ to be the first time t at which the asset price reaches the barrier B. In other words, $\rho$ is chosen in a pathdependent way so that $S ( t ) < B$ for $0 \leq t \leq \rho$ and $S ( \rho ) = B _ { \cdot }$ . Since the asset price almost surely exceeds the barrier immediately after reaching $\mathbf { i t } ,$ we may regard $\rho$ as the time of knock-out. If the asset price does not reach the barrier before expiration, we set $\rho = \infty .$ . If the asset price first reaches the barrier at time $^ { T , }$ then $\rho = T$ but knock-out does not occur because there is no time left for the asset price to exceed the barrier. However, the probability that the asset price first reaches the barrier at time $_ { T }$ is zero, so this anomaly does not matter. 

The random variable $\pmb { \rho }$ is a stopping time because it chooses its value based on the path of the asset price up to time $\rho .$ . Stopping times in the binomial model were defined in Definition 4.3. 1 of Volume I. The Optional Sampling Theorem, Theorem 4.3.2 of Volume I, asserts that a martingale stopped at a stopping time is still a martingale. The same is true in continuous time. In particular, the process 

$$
e ^ {- r (t \wedge \rho)} V (t \wedge \rho) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} e ^ {- r t} V (t) & \text {if} 0 \leq t \leq \rho , \\ e ^ {- r \rho} V (\rho) & \text {if} \rho <   t \leq T, \end{array} \right.\tag{7.3.10}
$$

is a $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ martingale. Before t gets to ${ \boldsymbol { \rho } } ,$ this is j ust the martingale $e ^ { - r t } V ( t )$ Once t gets to $\rho ,$ although the time parameter t can march on, the value of the process is frozen at $e ^ { - r \rho } V ( \rho )$ . A process that does not move is trivially a martingale. The only way the martingale property could be ruined would be if $\pmb { \rho }$ "looked ahead" when deciding to stop the process. If $\rho$ stopped at a time because the process was about to go up and let the process continue if it was about to go down, the stopped process would have a downward tendency. So long as $\rho$ makes the decision to stop at the current time based only on the path up to and perhaps including the current time, the act of stopping a martingale at time $\pmb { \rho }$ preserves the martingale property. 

## Lemma 7.3.2. We have

$$
V (t) = v \bigl (t, S (t) \bigr), \quad 0 \leq t \leq \rho .\tag{7.3.11}
$$

In particular, $e ^ { - r t } v \big ( t , S ( t ) \big )$ is a $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ -martingale up t o time $\rho , o r ,$ put another way, the stopped process 

$$
e ^ {- r (t \wedge \rho)} v (t \wedge \rho , S (t \wedge \rho)), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{7.3.12}
$$

is a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ 

SKETCH OF PROOF: Because $v ( t , S ( t ) )$ is the value of the up-and-out call under the assumption that it has not knocked out before time t, and for $t \leq \rho$ this assumption is correct, we have (7.3. 1 1) for $t \leq \rho .$ . From (7.3. 1 1 ) , we conclude that the process in (7.3. 12) is the i-martingale ( 7.3. 10) . D 

PROOF OF THEOREM 7.3. 1 : We compute the diferential 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \left(e ^ {- r t} v (t, S (t))\right) = e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r v (t, S (t)) d t + v _ {t} (t, S (t)) d t + v _ {x} (t, S (t)) d S (t) \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{2} v _ {x x} (t, S (t)) d S (t) d S (t) \right] \\ = e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r v (t, S (t)) + v _ {t} (t, S (t)) + r S (t) v _ {x} (t, S (t)) \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) v _ {x x} (t, S (t)) \right] d t \\ \left. + e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) v _ {x} (t, S (t)) d \widetilde {W} (t). \right. \end{array} \tag {7.3.13}
$$

The dt term must be zero for $0 \leq t \leq \rho , \ : ( \mathrm { i . e . }$ , before the option knocks out) . But since $\left( t , S ( t ) \right)$ can reach any point in $\left\{ ( t , x ) ; 0 \leq t < T , 0 \leq x \leq B \right\}$ before the option knocks out, the Black-Scholes-Merton equation (7.3.4) must hold for every $t \in [ 0 , T )$ and $x \in [ 0 , B ]$ D 

Remark 7. 9. 9. From Theorem 7.3. 1 and its proof, we see how to construct a hedge, at least theoretically. Setting the dt term in (7.3.13) equal to zero, we obtain 

$$
d \big (e ^ {- r t} v \big (t, S (t) \big) \big) = e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) v _ {x} \big (t, S (t) \big) d \widetilde {W} (t), \quad 0 \leq t \leq \rho .\tag{7.3.14}
$$

The discounted value of a portfolio that at each time t holds $\varDelta ( t )$ shares of the underlying asset is given by (see (5.2.27)) 

$$
d \big (e ^ {- r t} X (t) \big) = e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) \Delta (t) d \widetilde {W} (t).
$$

At least theoretically, if an agent begins with a short position in the up-and-out call and with initial capital $X ( 0 ) = v { \big ( } 0 , S ( 0 ) { \big ) }$ , then the usual delta-hedging formula 

$$
\Delta (t) = v _ {x} \big (t, S (t) \big)\tag{7.3.15}
$$

will cause her portfolio value $X ( t )$ to track the option value $v \left( t , S ( t ) \right)$ up to the time $\rho$ of knock-out or up to expiration $^ { T , }$ whichever comes first. 

In practice, the delta hedge is impossible to implement if the option has not knocked out and the underlying asset price approaches the barrier near expiration of the option. The function ${ \pmb v } ( { \pmb T } , { \pmb x } )$ is discontinuous at $x = B$ jumping from $B - K$ to 0 at that point . For t near $_ { T }$ and x just below $B ,$ the function ${ \boldsymbol v } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ is approaching a discontinuity and has large negative delta $v _ { x } ( t , x )$ and large negative gamma $v _ { x x } ( t , x )$ values. Near expiration near the barrier, the delta-hedging formula (7.3. 1 5) requires the agent to take a large short position in the underlying asset and to make large adjustments in the position (because of the large negative gamma) whenever the asset price moves. The Black-Scholes-Merton model assumes the bid-ask spread is zero, and here that assumption is a poor model of reality. The delta-hedging formula calls for such a large amount of trading that the bid-ask spread becomes significant. The common industry practice is to price and hedge the up-and-out call as if the barrier were at a level slightly higher than B. In this way, the large delta and gamma values of the option occur in the region above the contractual barrier $B ,$ and the hedging position will be closed out upon knock-out at the contractual barrier before the asset price reaches this region. 0 

## 7.3.3 Computation of the Price of the Up-and-Out Call

The risk-neutral price at time zero of the up-and-out call with payof $V ( T )$ given by (7.3.2) is $V ( 0 ) = \widetilde { \mathbb { E } } [ e ^ { - r T } V ( T ) ]$ . We use the density formula (7.2.3) to compute this. If $\pmb { k } \geq \mathbf 0 .$ , we must integrate over the region $\{ ( m , w ) ; k \le$ $w \leq m \leq b \}$ . On the other hand, if $k < 0 ,$ , we integrate over the region $\{ ( m , w ) ; k \leq w \leq m , 0 \leq m \leq b \}$ . In both cases, the region can be described as $\left\{ ( m , w ) ; k \leq w \leq b , w ^ { + } \leq m \leq b \right\}$ ; see Figure 7.3. 1 . We assume here that $S ( 0 ) \le B$ so that $b > 0 .$ . Otherwise, the region over which we integrate has zero area, and the time-zero value of the call is zero rather than the integral computed below. We also assume $S ( 0 ) > 0$ so that b and k are finite. 

When $0 < S ( 0 ) \le B$ , the time-zero value of the up-and-out call is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V (0) = \int_ {k} ^ {b} \int_ {w ^ {+}} ^ {b} e ^ {- r T} \big (S (0) e ^ {\sigma w} - K \big) \frac {2 (2 m - w)}{T \sqrt {2 \pi T}} e ^ {\alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {1}{2 T} (2 m - w) ^ {2}} d m d w \\ = - \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {- r T} \big (S (0) e ^ {\sigma w} - K \big) \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \left. e ^ {\alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {1}{2 T} (2 m - w) ^ {2}} \right| _ {m = w ^ {+}} ^ {m = b} d w \\ = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} \big (S (0) e ^ {\sigma w} - K \big) e ^ {- r T + \alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {1}{2 T} w ^ {2}} d w \\ - \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} \big (S (0) e ^ {\sigma w} - K \big) e ^ {- r T + \alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {1}{2 T} (2 b - w) ^ {2}} d w \\ = S (0) I _ {1} - K I _ {2} - S (0) I _ {3} + K I _ {4}, \end{array}
$$

where 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/f0ea9bfa-fb56-4ab7-9807-cfaaee673bf0/9768f8ba73191d34361256b9b089fff9951901b3cc5cc74ad6fdd2860839b32a.jpg)



Fig. 7.3. 1 . Regions of integration for $\pmb { k } \geq \mathbf { 0 }$ and $k < 0 .$


$$
I _ {1} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {\sigma w - r T + \alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {1}{2 T} w ^ {2}} d w,
$$

$$
I _ {2} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {- r T + \alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {1}{2 T} w ^ {2}} d w,
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & I _ {3} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {\sigma w - r T + \alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {1}{2 T} (2 b - w) ^ {2}} d w, \\ & \quad = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {\sigma w - r T + \alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {2}{T} b ^ {2} + \frac {2}{T} b w - \frac {1}{2 T} w ^ {2}} d w, \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r} I _ {4} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {- r T + \alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {1}{2 T} (2 b - w) ^ {2}} d w \\ = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {- r T + \alpha w - \frac {1}{2} \alpha^ {2} T - \frac {2}{T} b ^ {2} + \frac {2}{T} b w - \frac {1}{2 T} w ^ {2}} d w. \end{array}
$$

Each of these integrals is of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {\beta + \gamma w - \frac {1}{2 T} w ^ {2}} d w = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {- \frac {1}{2 T} (w - \gamma T) ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} T + \beta} d w \\ = e ^ {\frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} T + \beta} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi}} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sqrt {T}} (k - \gamma T)} ^ {\frac {1}{\sqrt {T}} (b - \gamma T)} e ^ {- \frac {1}{2} y ^ {2}} d y, \end{array}\tag{7.3.16}

where we have made the change of variable $\begin{array} { r } { y = \frac { w - \gamma T } { \sqrt { T } } } \end{array}$ . Using the standard cumulative normal distribution property $N ( z ) = 1 - \bar { N } ( - z )$ and (7.3.3), we continue, writing 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi T}} \int_ {k} ^ {b} e ^ {\beta + \gamma w - \frac {w ^ {2}}{2 T}} d w} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {\frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} T + \beta} \left[ N \left(\frac {b - \gamma T}{\sqrt {T}}\right) - N \left(\frac {k - \gamma T}{\sqrt {T}}\right) \right]} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {\frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} T + \beta} \left[ N \left(\frac {- k + \gamma T}{\sqrt {T}}\right) - N \left(\frac {- b + \gamma T}{\sqrt {T}}\right) \right]} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {\frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} T + \beta} \left[ N \left(\frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {T}} \left[ \log \frac {S (0)}{K} + \gamma \sigma T \right]\right) \right.} \\ & {\qquad \qquad \left. - N \left(\frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {T}} \left[ \log \frac {S (0)}{B} + \gamma \sigma T \right]\right) \right].} \end{array}\tag{7.3.17}
$$

Set 

$$
\delta_ {\pm} (\tau , s) = \frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {\tau}} \left[ \log s + \left(r \pm \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) \tau \right].\tag{7.3.18}
$$

The integral $I _ { 1 }$ is of the form (7.3.17) with $\begin{array} { r } { \beta = - r T - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \alpha ^ { 2 } T } \end{array}$ and $\gamma = \alpha + \sigma ,$ so ${ \scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \gamma ^ { 2 } T + \beta = 0$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \gamma \sigma = r + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \sigma ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ . Therefore, 

$$
I _ {1} = N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(T, \frac {S (0)}{K}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(T, \frac {S (0)}{B}\right)\right).
$$

The integral $I _ { 2 }$ is of the form (7.3.17) with $\begin{array} { r } { \beta = - r T - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \alpha ^ { 2 } T } \end{array}$ and $\gamma = \alpha$ , so $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \gamma ^ { 2 } T + \bar { \beta } = - \bar { r } T$ and $\scriptstyle \gamma \sigma = r - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \sigma ^ { 2 }$ . Therefore, 

$$
I _ {2} = e ^ {- r T} \left[ N \left(\delta_ {-} \left(T, \frac {S (0)}{K}\right)\right) - N \left(d _ {-} \left(T, \frac {S (0)}{B}\right)\right) \right].
$$

For $I _ { 3 }$ , we have $\begin{array} { r } { \beta = { - r T - \frac { 1 } { 2 } \alpha ^ { 2 } T - \frac { 2 b ^ { 2 } } { T } } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \gamma = \alpha + \sigma + \frac { 2 b } { T } } \end{array}$ , so 

$$
\frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} T + \beta = \log \left(\frac {S (0)}{B}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} - 1},
$$

$$
\gamma \sigma T = \left(r + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) T + \log \left(\frac {B}{S (0)}\right) ^ {2}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
I _ {3} = \left(\frac {S (0)}{B}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} - 1} \left[ N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(T, \frac {B ^ {2}}{K S (0)}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(T, \frac {B}{S (0)}\right)\right) \right].
$$

Finally, for $I _ { 4 }$ , we have $\begin{array} { r } { \beta = { - r T - \frac { 1 } { 2 } \alpha ^ { 2 } T - \frac { 2 b ^ { 2 } } { T } } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \gamma = \alpha + \frac { 2 b } { T } } \end{array}$ , so 

$$
\frac {1}{2} \gamma^ {2} T + \beta = - r T + \log \left(\frac {S (0)}{B}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} + 1},
$$

$$
\gamma \sigma T = \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) T + \log \left(\frac {B}{S (0)}\right) ^ {2}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
I _ {4} = e ^ {- r T} \left(\frac {S (0)}{B}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} + 1} \left[ N \left(\delta_ {-} \left(T, \frac {B ^ {2}}{K S (0)}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {-} \left(T, \frac {B}{S (0)}\right)\right) \right].
$$

Putting all this together, under the assumption $0 < S ( 0 ) \le B _ { \cdot }$ , we have the up-and-out call price formula 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & V (0) \\ & = S (0) \left[ N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(T, \frac {S (0)}{K}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(T, \frac {S (0)}{B}\right)\right) \right] \\ & \quad - e ^ {- r T} K \left[ N \left(\delta_ {-} \left(T, \frac {S (0)}{K}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {-} \left(T, \frac {S (0)}{B}\right)\right) \right] \\ & \quad - B \left(\frac {S (0)}{B}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}}} \left[ N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(T, \frac {B ^ {2}}{K S (0)}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(T, \frac {B}{S (0)}\right)\right) \right] \\ & \quad + e ^ {- r T} K \left(\frac {S (0)}{B}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} + 1} \left[ N \biggl (\delta_ {-} \left(T, \frac {B ^ {2}}{K S (0)}\right) \biggr) - N \biggl (\delta_ {-} \left(T, \frac {B}{S (0)}\right) \biggr) \right]. \end{array}\tag{7.3.19}
$$

Now let $t \in [ 0 , T )$ be given, and assume the underlying asset price at time t is $\begin{array} { r } { S ( t ) = x . } \end{array}$ . As above, we assume $0 < x \leq B _ { \cdot }$ . If the call has not knocked out prior to time $\mathbf { } ^ { t , \quad }$ its price at time t is obtained by replacing $_ { x }$ by the time to expiration $\tau = T - t$ and replacing $S ( 0 )$ by x in (7.3. 19) . This gives us the cal price as a function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } )$ of the two variables t and x: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} v (t, x) = x \left[ N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{K}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{B}\right)\right) \right] \\ \quad - e ^ {- r \tau} K \left[ N \left(\delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{K}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{B}\right)\right) \right] \\ \quad - B \left(\frac {x}{B}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}}} \left[ N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {B ^ {2}}{K x}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {B}{x}\right)\right) \right] \\ \quad + e ^ {- r \tau} K \left(\frac {x}{B}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} + 1} \left[ N \left(\delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {B ^ {2}}{K x}\right)\right) - N \left(\delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {B}{x}\right)\right) \right], \\ \quad 0 \leq t <   T, 0 <   x \leq B. \end{array} \tag {7.3.}\tag{7.3.20}
$$

Formula (7.3.20) was derived under the assumption that $\tau > 0 \left( \mathrm { i . e . , } t < T \right)$ and $\mathbf { 0 } < \pmb { x } \le B$ . For $0 \leq t \leq T$ and $\pmb { x } > B$ , we have $v ( t , x ) = 0$ because the option knocks out when the asset price exceeds the barrier B. Indeed, if the asset price reaches the barrier before expiration, then it will immediately exceed the barrier almost surely, and so $v ( t , B ) = 0$ for $0 \leq t < T$ . However, ${ \pmb v } ( T , B ) = B - K$ . We also have $v ( t , 0 ) = 0$ because geometric Brownian motion starting at 0 stays at zero, and hence the call expires out of the money. Finally, if the option does not knock out prior to expiration, then its payof is that of a European call $( \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } v ( T , x ) = ( x - K ) ^ { + } )$ In summary, ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } )$ satisfies the boundary conditions $( 7 . 3 . 5 ) - ( 7 . 3 . 7 )$ . Formula (7.3.6) can be obtained by substitution of $\textbf { \em x } = \textbf { \em B }$ in (7.3.20) , but for $\textbf { \em x } > \textbf { \em B }$ , the right-hand side of (7.3.20) is not $v ( t , x ) = 0 .$ . Formula (7.3.20) was derived under the assumption $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < x \le B , } \end{array}$ and it is incorrect if $\pmb { x } > B .$ Formulas (7.3.5) and (7.3.7) cannot be obtained by substitution of $\pmb { x } = \mathbf { 0 }$ and $t = T \ ( \tau = 0 )$ into (7.3.20) because this leads to zeroes in denominators, but it can be shown that (7.3.20) gives these formulas as limits as $\pmb { x } \downarrow 0$ and $\tau \downarrow 0 ;$ see Exercise 7.2. 

## 7.4 Look back Options

An option whose payof is based on the maximum that the underlying asset price attains over some interval of time prior to expiration is called a lookback option. In this section we price a floating strike lookback option. The payof of this option is the diference between the maximum asset price over the time between initiation and expiration and the asset price at expiration. The discussion of this option introduces a new type of diferential, a diferential that is neither dt nor $d \widetilde { W } ( t )$ 

## 7.4.1 Floating Strike Lookback Option

We begin with a geometric Brownian motion asset price, which may be written as in (7.3. 1 ) as 

$$
S (t) = S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {W} (t)},\tag{7.4.1}
$$

where, as in Subsection 7.3. 1 , $\widehat { W } ( t ) = \alpha t + \widetilde { W } ( t )$ and 

$$
\alpha = \frac {1}{\sigma} \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right).
$$

With 

$$
\widehat {M} (t) = \max _ {0 \leq u \leq t} \widehat {W} (u), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,\tag{7.4.2}
$$

we may write the maximum of the asset price up to time t as 

$$
Y (t) = \max _ {0 \leq u \leq t} S (u) = S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {M} (t)}.\tag{7.4.3}
$$

The lookback option considered in this section pays of 

$$
V (T) = Y (T) - S (T)\tag{7.4.4}
$$

at expiration time T. This payof is nonnegative because $Y ( T ) \ge S ( T )$ 

Let $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ be given. At time $\mathbf { } ^ { t , \mathrm { ~ ~ } }$ the risk-neutral price of the lookback option is 

$$
V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} \bigl (Y (T) - S (T) \bigr) \Big | \mathcal {F} (t) \right].\tag{7.4.5}
$$

Because the pair of processes $( S ( t ) , Y ( t ) )$ has the Markov property (see Exercise 7.3) , there must exist a function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , y )$ such that 

$$
V (t) = v \big (t, S (t), Y (t) \big).
$$

In Subsection 7.4.2, we characterize this function by the Black-Scholes-Merton equation. In Subsection 7.4.3, we compute it explicitly. 

## 7.4.2 Black-Scholes-Merton Equation

Theorem 7.4.1. Let ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , y )$ denote the price at time t of the floating strike lookback option under the assumption that $\mathbf { } S ( t ) = x$ and $Y ( t ) = y$ . Then ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , y )$ satisfies the Black-Scholes-Merton partial diferential equation 

$$
v _ {t} (t, x, y) + r x v _ {x} (t, x, y) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} x ^ {2} v _ {x x} (t, x, y) = r v (t, x, y)\tag{7.4.6}
$$

in the region $\{ ( t , x , y ) ; 0 \leq t < T , 0 \leq x \leq y \}$ and satisfies the boundary conditions 

$$
v (t, 0, y) = e ^ {- r (T - t)} y, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, y \geq 0,\tag{7.4.7}
$$

$$
v _ {y} (t, y, y) = 0, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, y > 0,\tag{7.4.8}
$$

$$
v (T, x, y) = y - x, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y.\tag{7.4.9}
$$

Iterated conditioning implies that $e ^ { - r t } V ( t ) = e ^ { - r t } v ( t , S ( t ) , Y ( t ) )$ , where $V ( t )$ is given by (7.4.5) , is a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ . We compute its diferential and set the dt term equal to zero to obtain (7.4.6) . However, when we do this, the term $d Y ( t )$ appears. This is diferent from the term $d S ( t )$ , because $S ( t )$ has nonzero quadratic variation, whereas $Y ( t )$ has zero quadratic variation. This is because $Y ( t )$ is continuous and nondecreasing in t. Let $0 = t _ { 0 } < t _ { 1 } <$ $\cdots < t _ { m } = T$ be a partition of $[ 0 , T ]$ · Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \left(Y (t _ {j}) - Y (t _ {j - 1})\right) ^ {2} \\ \leq \max _ {j = 1, \ldots , m} \left(Y (t _ {j}) - Y (t _ {j - 1})\right) \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \left(Y (t _ {j}) - Y (t _ {j - 1})\right) \\ = \max _ {j = 1, \ldots , m} \left(Y (t _ {j}) - Y (t _ {j - 1})\right) \cdot \left(Y (T) - Y (0)\right), \end{array}\tag{7.4.10}
$$

and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m a x } _ { j = 1 , \dots , m } \left( Y ( t _ { j } ) - Y ( t _ { j - 1 } ) \right) } \end{array}$ has limit zero as ma $\mathfrak { c } _ { j = 1 , \dots , m } ( t _ { j } - t _ { j - 1 } )$ goes to zero because $\dot { Y } ( t )$ is continuous. We conclude that $Y ( t )$ accumulates zero quadratic variation on $[ 0 , T ]$ , a fact we record by writing 

$$
d Y (t) d Y (t) = 0.\tag{7.4.11}
$$

This argument works because $Y ( t _ { j } ) - Y ( t _ { j - 1 } )$ is nonnegative, and hence we do not need to take the absolute value of these terms in (7.4. 10) . This argument shows that on any interval in which a function is continuous and nondecreasing, it will accumulate zero quadratic variation. 

On the other hand, $d Y ( t )$ is not a $\scriptstyle { d t }$ term: there is no process $\Theta ( t )$ such that $d Y ( t ) = \theta ( t ) d t$ . In other words, we cannot write $Y ( t )$ as 

$$
Y (t) = Y (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Theta (u) d u.\tag{7.4.12}
$$

If we could, then $\boldsymbol { \Theta } ( \boldsymbol { u } )$ would be zero whenever u is in a "flat spot" of $Y ( t )$ which occurs whenever $S ( t )$ drops below its maximum to date (see Figure 7.4. 1 ) . Figure ${ \bf 7 . 4 . 1 }$ suggests that there are time intervals in which $Y ( t )$ is strictly increasing, but in fact no such interval exists. Such an interval can occur only if $S ( t )$ is strictly increasing on the interval, and if there were such an interval, then $S ( t )$ would accumulate zero quadratic variation on the interval (see the argument in the previous paragraph) . This is not the case because $d S ( t ) d S ( t ) = \sigma S ^ { 2 } ( t )$ dt is positive for all t. Thus, despite the suggestion of Figure 7.4. 1 , the lengths of the "flat spots" of $Y ( t )$ on any time interval $[ 0 , T ]$ sum to T. Therefore, if (7.4. 12) were to hold, we would need to have $\boldsymbol { \theta } ( \boldsymbol { u } ) = 0$ for Lebesgue almost every u in $[ 0 , T ]$ . This would result in $Y ( t ) = Y ( 0 )$ for $0 \leq t \leq T$ . But in fact $Y ( t ) > Y ( 0 )$ for all $t > 0$ . We conclude that $Y ( t )$ cannot be represented in the form (7.4. 12) ; $d Y ( t )$ is not a dt term. 

The paths of $Y ( t )$ increase over time, but they do so on a set of times having zero Lebesgue measure. Each time interval $[ 0 , T ]$ contains a sequence of subintervals whose lengths sum to T, and on each of these subintervals, $Y ( t )$ is constant. The particular subintervals depend on the path, but regardless of the path, the lengths of these subintervals sum to T. A similar situation is described in Appendix A, Section A.3. In the case discussed there, $T = 1$ and the subintervals are explicitly exhibited. Their union is the Cantor set. It is verified that although the lengths of these subintervals sum to 1, there are uncountably many points not contained in these intervals. The function ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ described in Section A.3 increases, but only on the complement of the Cantor set. Furthermore, ${ \pmb F } ( { \pmb x } )$ is continuous. Functions of this kind are said to be singularly continuous. 

Fortunately, we can work with the diferential of $Y ( t )$ . We have already argued that $d Y ( t ) d Y ( t ) = 0 .$ Similarly, we have 

$$
d Y (t) d S (t) = 0\tag{7.4.13}
$$

(see Exercise 7.4) . We now provide the proof of Theorem 7.4. 1 . 

PROOF O F THEOREM 7.4. 1 : We use the lt6-Doeblin formula and (7.4. 1 1) and (7.4. 13) to diferentiate the martingale $e ^ { - r t } v \big ( t , S ( t ) , Y ( t ) \big )$ to obtain

Fig. 7.4. 1 . Geometric Brownian motion and its maximum to date.


$$
\begin{array}{l} d \left(e ^ {- r t} v (t, S (t), Y (t))\right) \\ = e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r v (t, S (t), Y (t)) d t + v _ {t} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d t \right. \\ \left. + v _ {x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d S (t) + \frac {1}{2} v _ {x x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d S (t) d S (t) \right. \\ \left. + v _ {y} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d Y (t) \right] \\ = e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r v (t, S (t), Y (t)) + v _ {t} (t, S (t), Y (t)) + r S (t) v _ {x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) v _ {x x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) \right] d t \\ + e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) v _ {x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d \widetilde {W} (t) \\ + e ^ {- r t} v _ {y} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d Y (t). \end{array} \tag {7.4}\tag{7.4.14}
$$

In order to have a martingale, the dt term must be zero, and this gives us the Black-Scholes-Merton equation (7.4.6) . The new feature is that the term $e ^ { - r t } v _ { y } ( t , S ( t ) , Y ( t ) ) d Y ( t )$ must also be zero. It cannot be canceled by the dt term nor by the $d \widetilde { W } ( t )$ term because it is fundamentally diferent from both of these terms. The $d Y ( t )$ term is naturally zero on the "flat spots" of $Y ( t )$ (i.e . , when $S ( t ) < Y ( t ) )$ . However, at the times when $Y ( t )$ increases, which are the times when $S ( t ) = Y ( t )$ , the term $e ^ { - r t } v _ { y } \big ( t , S ( t ) , Y ( t ) \big )$ must be zero because $d Y ( t )$ is "positive." This gives us the boundary condition (7.4.8) . 

The boundary condition (7.4.9) is the payof of the option. If at any time t we have $\begin{array} { r } { S ( t ) = 0 , } \end{array}$ , then we will have $S ( T ) = 0 \quad$ . FUrthermore, Y will be constant on $[ t , T ] ; { \mathrm { i f ~ } } Y ( t ) = y ,$ then $Y ( T ) = y$ and the price of the option at time t is this value discounted from T back to t. This gives us the boundary condition (7.4.7) . 0 

Remark 1.4 . 2. The proof of Theorem 7.4. 1 shows that 

$$
d \left(e ^ {- r t} v (t, S (t), Y (t))\right) = e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) v _ {x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d \widetilde {W} (t).
$$

Just as in Remark 7.3.3, this equation implies that the delta-hedging formula (7.3. 15) works. In contrast to the situation in Remark 7.3.3, here the function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ is continuous and we have no problems with large delta and gamma values. 0 

## 7.4.3 Reduction of Dimension

The price of the floating strike lookback option has a linear scaling property: 

$$
v (t, \lambda x, \lambda y) = \lambda v (t, x, y) \text {   for   all   } \lambda > 0.\tag{7.4.15}
$$

This is because scaling both $S ( t )$ and $Y ( t )$ by the same positive constant at a time t prior to expiration results in the payof $Y ( T ) - S ( T )$ being scaled by the same constant. In particular, if we know the function of two variables 

$$
u (t, z) = v (t, z, 1), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, 0 \leq z \leq 1,\tag{7.4.16}
$$

then we can easily determine the function of three variables ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , y )$ by the formula 

$$
v (t, x, y) = y v \left(t, \frac {x}{y}, 1\right) = y u \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right), \quad 0 \leq t \leq T, 0 \leq x \leq y, y > 0.\tag{7.4.17}
$$

From (7.4. 17) , we can compute the partial derivatives: 

$$
v _ {t} (t, x, y) = y u _ {t} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right),
$$

$$
v _ {x} (t, x, y) = y u _ {z} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) \cdot \frac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\frac {x}{y}\right) = u _ {z} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right),
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {v _ {x x} (t, x, y) = u _ {z z} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) \cdot \frac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\frac {x}{y}\right) = \frac {1}{y} u _ {z z} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right),} \\ & {v _ {y} (t, x, y) = u \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) + y u _ {z} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) \frac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\frac {x}{y}\right)} \\ & {\qquad = u \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) - \frac {x}{y} u _ {z} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right).} \end{array}
$$

Substitution into the Black-Scholes-Merton equation (7.4.6) yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = - r v (t, x, y) + v _ {t} (t, x, y) + r x v _ {x} (t, x, y) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} x ^ {2} v _ {x x} (t, x, y) \\ = y \left[ - r u \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) + u _ {t} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) + r \left(\frac {x}{y}\right) u _ {z} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} \left(\frac {x}{y}\right) ^ {2} u _ {z z} \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) \right]. \end{array}
$$

Canceling y and making the change of variable $\begin{array} { r } { z = \frac { x } { y } } \end{array}$ , we see that $u ( t , z )$ satisfies the Black-Scholes-Merton equation 

$$
u _ {t} (t, z) + r z u _ {z} (t, z) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} z ^ {2} u _ {z z} (t, z) = r u (t, z), \quad 0 \leq t <   T, 0 <   z <   1.\tag{7.4.18}
$$

Boundary conditions for $u ( t , z )$ can be obtained from the boundary conditions (7.4.7)-(7.4.9) for ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ . In particular, 

$$
e ^ {- r (T - t)} y = v (t, 0, y) = y u (t, 0)
$$

implies 

$$
u (t, 0) = e ^ {- r (T - t)}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{7.4.19}
$$

Furthermore, 

$$
0 = v _ {y} (t, y, y) = u (t, 1) - u _ {z} (t, 1)
$$

implies 

$$
u (t, 1) = u _ {z} (t, 1), \quad 0 \leq t <   T.\tag{7.4.20}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\boldsymbol {y} - \boldsymbol {x} = v (T, \boldsymbol {x}, \boldsymbol {y}) = y u \left(T, \frac {\boldsymbol {x}}{\boldsymbol {y}}\right)
$$

implies 

$$
u (T, z) = 1 - z, \quad 0 \leq z \leq 1.\tag{7.4.21}
$$

Equation (7.4. 18) and the boundary conditions (7.4. 19)-(7.4.21) uniquely determine the function $u ( t , z )$ . As a consequence, we see that the Black-Scholes-Merton equation and boundary conditions in Theorem 7.4. 1 uniquely determine the function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , y )$ 

## 7 . 4 . 4 Computation of the Price of the Look back Option

In this subsection, we compute the function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ of Theorem 7.4. 1. We do this for $0 \leq t < T$ and $\ 0 < \pmb { x } \le \pmb { y }$ . Because $Y ( t ) \geq S ( t )$ for all t, we do not need to compute values of ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , y )$ for $\mathscr { x } > y$ . The reader is invited in Exercise 7.5 to compute the partial derivatives of ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , y )$ and verify that the Black-Scholes-Merton equation and boundary conditions in Theorem 7.4. 1 are satisfied. 

For $0 \leq t < T$ and $\tau = T - t ,$ we observe that 

$$
Y (T) = S (0) e ^ {\sigma \widehat {M} (t)} e ^ {\sigma (\widehat {M} (T) - \widehat {M} (t))} = Y (t) e ^ {\sigma (\widehat {M} (T) - \widehat {M} (t))}.
$$

If $\operatorname * { m a x } _ { t \leq u \leq T } \widehat { W } ( u ) > \widehat { M } ( t ) \ ( \mathrm { i . e . }$ , if $\widehat { W }$ attains a new maximum in $[ t , T ] )$ , then 

$$
\widehat {M} (T) - \widehat {M} (t) = \max _ {t \leq u \leq T} \widehat {W} (u) - \widehat {M} (t).
$$

On the other hand, if $\operatorname* { m a x } _ { t \leq u \leq T } \widehat { W } ( u ) \leq \widehat { M } ( t )$ , then ${ \widehat { M } } ( T ) = { \widehat { M } } ( t )$ and 

$$
\widehat {M} (T) - \widehat {M} (t) = 0.
$$

In either case, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \widehat {M} (T) - \widehat {M} (t) = \left[ \max _ {t \leq u \leq T} \widehat {W} (u) - \widehat {M} (t) \right] ^ {+} \\ = \left[ \max _ {t \leq u \leq T} \left(\widehat {W} (u) - \widehat {W} (t)\right) - \left(\widehat {M} (t) - \widehat {W} (t)\right) \right] ^ {+}. \end{array}
$$

Multiplying this equation by $\pmb { \sigma }$ and using (7.4. 1 ) and (7.4.3) , we obtain 

$$
\sigma \big (\widehat {M} (T) - \widehat {M} (t) \big) = \left[ \max _ {t \leq u \leq T} \sigma \big (\widehat {W} (u) - \widehat {W} (t) \big) - \log \frac {Y (t)}{S (t)} \right] ^ {+}.\tag{7.4.22}
$$

Therefore, $V ( t )$ in (7.4.5) is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V (t) = e ^ {- r \tau} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ Y (t) \exp \left\{\left[ \max _ {t \leq u \leq T} \sigma (\widehat {W} (u) - \widehat {W} (t)) - \log \frac {Y (t)}{S (t)} \right] ^ {+} \right\} \mid \mathcal {F} (t) \right] \\ - e ^ {r t} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r T} S (T) \mid \mathcal {F} (t) \right]. \end{array} \tag {7.4.2}
$$

Because the discounted asset price is a martingale under ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } ,$ the second term in (7.4.23) is $- e ^ { r t } e ^ { - r t } S ( t ) = S ( t )$ . For the first term, we can "take out what is known" (see Theorem 2.3.2(ii)) to obtain 

$$
e ^ {- r \tau} Y (t) \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ \exp \left\{\left[ \max _ {t \leq u \leq T} \sigma (\widehat {W} (u) - \widehat {W} (t)) - \log \frac {Y (t)}{S (t)} \right] ^ {+} \right\} \Bigg | \mathcal {F} (t) \right].\tag{7.4.24}
$$

Because $Y ( t )$ and $S ( t )$ are $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ -measurable and max ${ \dot { \substack { \cdot t \leq u \leq T } } } \sigma { \bigl ( } { \widehat { W } } ( u ) - { \widehat { W } } ( t ) { \bigr ) }$ is independent of $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ , we can use the Independence Lemma, Lemma 2.3.4, to write the conditional expectation in $( 7 . 4 . 2 4 )$ as $g \bigl ( S ( t ) , Y ( t ) \bigr )$ , where 

$$
g (x, y) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \exp \left\{\left[ \max _ {t \leq u \leq T} \sigma (\widehat {W} (u) - \widehat {W} (t)) - \log \frac {y}{x} \right] ^ {+} \right\}.\tag{7.4.25}
$$

Note that the expectation in (7.4.25) is no longer conditioned on $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ . Putting this all together, we have 

$$
V (t) = e ^ {- r \tau} Y (t) g (S (t), Y (t)) - S (t)
$$

or, equivalently, 

$$
v (t, x, y) = e ^ {- r \tau} y g (x, y) - x.\tag{7.4.26}
$$

It remains to compute the function ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ . Because 

$$
\max _ {t \leq u \leq T} \sigma \big (\widehat {W} (u) - \widehat {W} (t) \big) = \sigma \max _ {t \leq u \leq T} \big (\widehat {W} (u) - \widehat {W} (t) \big),
$$

and $\operatorname* { m a x } _ { t \leq u \leq T } ( \widehat { W } ( u ) - \widehat { W } ( t ) )$ has the same unconditional distribution under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ as $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m a x } _ { 0 \leq u \leq \tau } \left( \widehat { W } ( u ) - \widehat { W } ( 0 ) \right) = \widehat { M } ( \tau ) } \end{array}$ , the function ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ of (7.4.25) can also be written as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} g (x, y) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \exp \left\{\left[ \sigma \widehat {M} (\tau) - \log \frac {y}{x} \right] ^ {+} \right\} \\ = \widetilde {\mathbb {P}} \left\{\widehat {M} (\tau) \leq \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x} \right\} + \frac {x}{y} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {\sigma \widehat {M} (\tau)} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\widehat {M} (\tau) \geq \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x} \}} \right]. \end{array}\tag{7.4.27}
$$

We compute both terms on the right-hand side of (7.4.27) . 

In order to compute the first term on the right-hand side of (7.4. 27) , we use (7.2.6) with $_ { \pmb { T } }$ replaced by $\tau$ and m replaced by $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { \sigma } } \log { \frac { y } { x } }$ · With these replacements, the arguments of $N$ appearing on the right-hand side of (7.2.6) are 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \frac {1}{\sqrt {\tau}} \left[ \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x} - \alpha \tau \right] & = \frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {\tau}} \left[ \log \frac {y}{x} - \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) \tau \right] \\ & = - \frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {\tau}} \left[ \log \frac {x}{y} + \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) \tau \right] \\ & = - \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right), \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r} \frac {1}{\sqrt {\tau}} \left[ - \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x} - \alpha \tau \right] = \frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {\tau}} \left[ - \log \frac {y}{x} - \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) \tau \right] \\ = - \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {y}{x}\right), \end{array}
$$

where $\delta _ { \pm } ( \tau , s )$ is defined by (7.3. 18) . The term $e ^ { 2 \alpha m }$ appearing on the righthand side of (7.2.6) becomes
