$$

It follows from (7.2.6) that 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {P}} \left\{\widehat {M} (\tau) \leq \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x} \right\} = N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right) - \left(\frac {y}{x}\right) ^ {\frac {2 \tau}{\sigma^ {2}} - 1} N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {y}{x}\right)\right)\tag{7.4.28}
$$

The second term on the right-hand side of (7.4.27) is computed using the density for $\widehat { M } ( \tau )$ under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ given by (7.2.7) with T replacing ${ \mathbf { } } T .$ . Indeed, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\frac {x}{y} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {\sigma \widehat {M} (\tau)} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\widehat {M} (\tau) \geq \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x} \}} \right]} \\ & {\quad = \frac {x}{y} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\sigma m} \widetilde {f} _ {\widehat {M} (\tau)} (m) d m} \\ & {\quad = \frac {x}{y} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {\infty} \frac {2}{\sqrt {2 \pi \tau}} e ^ {\sigma m - \frac {1}{2 \tau} (m - \alpha \tau) ^ {2}} d m} \\ & {\qquad - \frac {x}{y} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {\infty} 2 \alpha e ^ {(\sigma + 2 \alpha) m} N \left(\frac {- m - \alpha \tau}{\sqrt {\tau}}\right) d m.} \end{array}\tag{7.4.29}
$$

We compute the first integral on the right-hand side of (7.4.29). Because 

$$
\begin{array}{l} {r \tau - \frac {1}{2 \tau} (m - \alpha \tau - \sigma \tau) ^ {2}} \\ {\quad = r \tau - \frac {1}{2 \tau} (m - \alpha \tau) ^ {2} + \sigma (m - \alpha \tau) - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} \tau} \\ {\quad = r \tau - \frac {1}{2 \tau} (m - \alpha \tau) ^ {2} + \sigma m - \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) \tau - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} \tau} \\ {\quad = \sigma m - \frac {1}{2 \tau} (m - \alpha \tau) ^ {2},} \end{array}
$$

we may write the first term on the right-hand side of (7.4.29) as 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\frac {x}{y} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {\infty} \frac {2}{\sqrt {2 \pi \tau}} e ^ {\sigma m - \frac {1}{2 \tau} (m - \alpha \tau) ^ {2}} d m} \\ & {\qquad = \frac {2 x e ^ {r \tau}}{y \sqrt {2 \pi \tau}} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- \frac {1}{2 \tau} (m - \alpha \tau - \sigma \tau) ^ {2}} d m.} \end{array}\tag{7.4.30}
$$

We make the change of variable $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { \xi } = \frac { \alpha \tau + \sigma \tau - m } { \sqrt { \tau } } } \end{array}$ ' so the lower limit of integration $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { \sigma } }$ log $\textstyle { \frac { y } { x } }$ becomes 

$$
\frac {1}{\sqrt {\tau}} \left(\alpha \tau + \sigma \tau - \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}\right) = \frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {\tau}} \left(\log \frac {x}{y} + r \tau + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} \tau\right) = \delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right).
$$

With this change of variable in the integral on the right-hand side of (7.4.30) , we obtain the following formula for the first term on the right-hand side of ( 7. 4 . 29 ) : 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \frac {x}{y} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {\infty} \frac {2}{\sqrt {2 \pi \tau}} e ^ {\sigma m - \frac {1}{2 \tau} (m - \alpha \tau) ^ {2}} d m = \frac {2 x e ^ {r \tau}}{y \sqrt {2 \pi}} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\delta_ {+} (\tau , \frac {x}{y})} e ^ {- \frac {1}{2} \xi^ {2}} d \xi \\ = \frac {2 x e ^ {r \tau}}{y} N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right). \end{array}\tag{7.4.31}
$$

The second term on the right-hand side of (7.4.29) requires a reversal of the order of integration over the region shown in Figure 7.4.2. Because $\begin{array} { r } { \sigma + 2 \alpha = \frac { 2 r } { \sigma } } \end{array}$ , this term is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {- \frac {x}{y} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {x}{y}} ^ {\infty} 2 \alpha e ^ {(\sigma + 2 \alpha) m} N \left(\frac {- m - \alpha \tau}{\sqrt {\tau}}\right) d m} \\ & {\qquad = - \frac {2 \alpha x}{y \sqrt {2 \pi}} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {\infty} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\frac {1}{\sqrt {\tau}} (- m - \alpha \tau)} e ^ {\frac {2}{\sigma} r m - \frac {1}{2} \xi^ {2}} d \xi d m} \\ & {\qquad = - \frac {2 \alpha x}{y \sqrt {2 \pi}} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {- \delta_ {-} (\tau , \frac {y}{x})} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {- \xi \sqrt {\tau} - \alpha \tau} e ^ {\frac {2}{\sigma} r m - \frac {1}{2} \xi^ {2}} d m d \xi .} \end{array}\tag{7.4.32}
$$

The inner integral in (7.4.32) can be evaluated. Indeed, 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/f0ea9bfa-fb56-4ab7-9807-cfaaee673bf0/348317cf00c41f132b0a79a29dba07adb78851b78ee3b363bb3f68366fc400c1.jpg)



Fig. 7.4.2. Reversal of integration in (7.4.32) .


$$
\begin{array}{r} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {- \xi \sqrt {\tau} - \alpha \tau} e ^ {\frac {2 r m}{\sigma} - \frac {\xi^ {2}}{2}} d m = \frac {\sigma}{2 r} \left. e ^ {\frac {2 r m}{\sigma} - \frac {\xi^ {2}}{2}} \right| _ {m = \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {m = - \xi \sqrt {\tau} - \alpha \tau} \\ = \frac {\sigma}{2 r} e ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma} (- \xi \sqrt {\tau} - \alpha \tau) - \frac {1}{2} \xi^ {2}} - \frac {\sigma}{2 r} e ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} \log \frac {y}{x} - \frac {1}{2} \xi^ {2}}. \end{array}
$$

But 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \frac {2 r}{\sigma} (- \xi \sqrt {\tau} - \alpha \tau) - \frac {\xi^ {2}}{2} & = - \frac {\xi^ {2}}{2} - \frac {2 r \xi \sqrt {\tau}}{\sigma} - \frac {2 r \alpha \tau}{\sigma} \\ & = - \frac {1}{2} \left(\xi + \frac {2 r \sqrt {\tau}}{\sigma}\right) ^ {2} + \frac {2 r ^ {2} \tau}{\sigma^ {2}} - \frac {2 r \alpha \tau}{\sigma} \\ & = - \frac {1}{2} \left(\xi + \frac {2 r \sqrt {\tau}}{\sigma}\right) ^ {2} + \frac {2 r \tau}{\sigma^ {2}} (r - \sigma \alpha) \\ & = - \frac {1}{2} \left(\xi + \frac {2 r \sqrt {\tau}}{\sigma}\right) ^ {2} + r \tau \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
e ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} \log \frac {y}{x} - \frac {\xi^ {2}}{2}} = \left(\frac {y}{x}\right) ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}}} e ^ {- \frac {\xi^ {2}}{2}}.
$$

Therefore, the inner integral in (7.4.32) is 

$$
\int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {- \xi \sqrt {\tau} - \alpha \tau} e ^ {\frac {2 r m}{\sigma} - \frac {\xi^ {2}}{2}} d m = \frac {\sigma}{2 r} e ^ {r \tau - \frac {1}{2} (\xi + \frac {2 r \sqrt {\tau}}{\sigma}) ^ {2}} - \frac {\sigma}{2 r} \left(\frac {y}{x}\right) ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}}} e ^ {- \frac {\xi^ {2}}{2}}.
$$

We continue (7.4.32) , making this substitution for the inner integral: 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {- \frac {x}{y} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {\infty} 2 \alpha e ^ {(\sigma + 2 \alpha) m} N \left(\frac {- m - \alpha \tau}{\sqrt {\tau}}\right) d m} \\ & {\qquad = - \frac {\alpha \sigma x}{r y \sqrt {2 \pi}} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {- \delta_ {-} (\tau , \frac {y}{x})} e ^ {r \tau - \frac {1}{2} (\xi + \frac {2 r \sqrt {\tau}}{\sigma}) ^ {2}} d \xi} \\ & {\qquad + \frac {\alpha \sigma}{r \sqrt {2 \pi}} \left(\frac {y}{x}\right) ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} - 1} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {- \delta_ {-} (\tau , \frac {y}{x})} e ^ {- \frac {\xi^ {2}}{2}} d \xi} \\ & {\qquad = - \frac {\alpha \sigma x e ^ {r \tau}}{r y \sqrt {2 \pi}} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {- \delta_ {-} (\tau , \frac {y}{x})} e ^ {- \frac {1}{2} (\xi + \frac {2 r \sqrt {\tau}}{\sigma}) ^ {2}} d \xi} \\ & {\qquad + \frac {\alpha \sigma}{r} \left(\frac {y}{x}\right) ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} - 1} N \left(- \delta_ {-} (\tau , \frac {y}{x})\right).} \end{array}\tag{7.4.33}
$$

In the first integral on the right-hand side of (7.4.33) , we make the change of variable $\begin{array} { r } { \eta = \xi + \frac { 2 r \sqrt { \tau } } { \sigma } } \end{array}$ , and the upper limit of integration becomes 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {y}{x}\right) + \frac {2 r \sqrt {\tau}}{\sigma} = \frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {\tau}} \left[ - \log \frac {y}{x} - \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) \tau + 2 r \tau \right]} \\ & {\qquad = \frac {1}{\sigma \sqrt {\tau}} \left[ \log \frac {x}{y} + \left(r + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) \tau \right]} \\ & {\qquad = \delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right).} \end{array}
$$

We conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - \frac {x}{y} \int_ {\frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {y}{x}} ^ {\infty} 2 \alpha e ^ {(\sigma + 2 \alpha) m} N \left(\frac {- m - \alpha \tau}{\sqrt {\tau}}\right) d m \\ = - \frac {\alpha \sigma x}{r y} e ^ {r \tau} N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right) + \frac {\alpha \sigma}{r} \left(\frac {y}{x}\right) ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} - 1} N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {y}{x}\right)\right). \end{array}\tag{7.4.34}
$$

We put all the pieces together. The function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ for $0 \leq t < T$ and $\ 0 < x \le y$ is given by (7.4.26) , where ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ is given by (7.4.27) . We have computed both terms on the right-hand side of (7.4.27) . The first term is given by (7.4.28), and the second term is itself the sum of the two terms in ( 7.4.29) . These two terms are given by (7.4.31) and (7.4.34) . Furthermore, the term $\frac { \alpha \sigma } { r }$ appearing in these formulas is equal to $\textstyle 1 - { \frac { \sigma ^ { 2 } } { 2 r } }$ . We conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} v (t, x, y) = e ^ {- \tau \tau} y \left[ N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right) - \left(\frac {y}{x}\right) ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} - 1} N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {y}{x}\right)\right) \right. \\ \qquad + 2 \left(\frac {x}{y}\right) e ^ {r \tau} N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right) \\ \qquad - \left(1 - \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 r}\right) \left(\frac {x}{y}\right) e ^ {r \tau} N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right) \\ \qquad + \left(1 - \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 r}\right) \left(\frac {y}{x}\right) ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}} - 1} N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {y}{x}\right)\right) \Big ] - x. \end{array}
$$

Simplification results in the formula 

$$
\begin{array}{c} v (t, x, y) = \left(1 + \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 r}\right) x N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right) + e ^ {- r \tau} y N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right) \\ - \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 r} e ^ {- r \tau} \left(\frac {y}{x}\right) ^ {\frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}}} x N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {y}{x}\right)\right) - x, 0 \leq t <   T, 0 <   x \leq y. \end{array}\tag{7.4.35}
$$

The function related to v by (7.4. 16) satisfies 

$$
\begin{array}{r} u \left(t, \frac {x}{y}\right) = \left(1 + \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 r}\right) \left(\frac {x}{y}\right) N \left(\delta_ {+} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right) + e ^ {- r \tau} N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {x}{y}\right)\right) \\ - \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 r} e ^ {- r \tau} \left(\frac {x}{y}\right) ^ {1 - \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}}} N \left(- \delta_ {-} \left(\tau , \frac {y}{x}\right)\right) - \frac {x}{y}. \end{array}
$$

Making the change of variable $\begin{array} { r } { z = \frac { x } { y } } \end{array}$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & u (t, z) = \left(1 + \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 r}\right) z N \big (\delta_ {+} (\tau , z) \big) + e ^ {- r \tau} N \big (- \delta_ {-} (\tau , z) \big) \\ & \qquad - \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2 r} e ^ {- r \tau} z ^ {1 - \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}}} N \big (- \delta_ {-} (\tau , z ^ {- 1}) \big) - z, 0 \leq t <   T, 0 <   z \leq 1. \end{array}\tag{7.4.36}
$$

## 7.5 Asian Options

An Asian option is one whose payof includes a time average of the underlying asset price. The average may be over the entire time period between initiation and expiration or may be over some period of time that begins later than the initiation of the option and ends with the option's expiration. The average may be from continuous sampling, 

$$
\frac {1}{T} \int_ {0} ^ {T} S (t) d t,
$$

or may be from discrete sampling, 

$$
\frac {1}{m} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} S (t _ {j}),
$$

where $0 < t _ { 1 } < t _ { 2 } \dots < t _ { m } = T$ . The primary reason to base an option payof on an average asset price is to make it more dificult for anyone to significantly afect the payof by manipulation of the underlying asset price. 

The price of Asian options is not known in closed form. Therefore, in this section we discuss two ways to derive partial diferential equations for Asian option prices. The first of these was briefly presented in Example 6.6. 1. The other method for computing Asian option prices is Monte Carlo simulation. 

## 7.5.1 Fixed-Strike Asian Call

Once again, we begin with a geometric Brownian motion $S ( t )$ given by 

$$
d S (t) = r S (t) d t + \sigma S (t) d \widetilde {W} (t),\tag{7.5.1}
$$

<sub>�</sub>here $\widetilde { W } ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ , is a Brownian motion under the risk-neutral measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ . Consider a fixed-strike Asian call whose payof at time $_ { T }$ is 

$$
V (T) = \left(\frac {1}{T} \int_ {0} ^ {T} S (t) d t - K\right) ^ {+},\tag{7.5.2}
$$

where the strike price K is a nonnegative constant. The price at times t prior to the expiration time $_ { T }$ of this call is given by the risk-neutral pricing formula 

$$
V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} V (T) \Big | \mathcal {F} (t) \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{7.5.3}
$$

The usual iterated conditioning argument shows that 

$$
e ^ {- r t} V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r T} V (T) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

is a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ . This is the quantity we wish to compute. In the next two subsections, we describe two diferent ways to undertake this. 

## 7.5.2 Augmentation of the State

The Asian option payof $V ( T )$ in (7.5.2) is path-dependent. The price of the option at time t depends not only on t and $S ( t )$ , but also on the path that the asset price has followed up to time t. In particular, we cannot invoke the Markov property to claim that $V ( t )$ is a function of t and $S ( t )$ because $V ( T )$ is not a function of $_ { T }$ and $S ( T ) ; V ( T )$ depends on the whole path of S. 

To overcome this dificulty, we augment the state $S ( t )$ by defining a second process 

$$
Y (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} S (u) d u.\tag{7.5.4}
$$

The stochastic diferential equation for $Y ( t )$ is thus 

$$
d Y (t) = S (t) d t.\tag{7.5.5}
$$

Because the pair of processes $( S ( t ) , Y ( t ) )$ is governed by the pair of stochastic diferential equations (7.5.1) and (7.5.5) , they constitute a two-dimensional Markov process (Corollary 6.3.2) . Furthermore, the call payof $V ( T )$ is a function of $_ { T }$ and the final value $\left( S ( T ) , Y ( T ) \right)$ of this process. Indeed, $V ( T )$ depends only on $_ { T }$ and $Y ( T )$ , by the formula 

$$
V (T) = \left(\frac {1}{T} Y (T) - K\right) ^ {+}.\tag{7.5.6}
$$

This implies that there must exist some function ${ \boldsymbol v } ( t , x , y )$ such that the Asian call price (7.5.3) is given as 

$$
\begin{array}{c} v \big (t, S (t), Y (t) \big) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} \left(\frac {1}{T} Y (T) - K\right) ^ {+} \Bigg | \mathcal {F} (t) \right] \\ = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r (T - t)} V (T) \Big | \mathcal {F} (t) \right]. \end{array}\tag{7.5.7}
$$

The function ${ \boldsymbol v } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } , y )$ satisfies a partial diferential equation. This equation and three boundary conditions are provided in the next theorem. However, in order to numerically solve this equation, it would normally be necessary to also specify the behavior of ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ as x approaches o and y approaches either $\infty \ { \mathfrak { o r } } \ { - } \infty$ . This can be avoided by the method discussed in Subsection 7.5.3; see Remark 7.5.4 below. 

Theorem 7.5.1. The Asian call price function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ of (7. 5. 7} satisfies the partial diferential equation 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} v _ {t} (t, x, y) + r x v _ {x} (t, x, y) + x v _ {y} (t, x, y) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} x ^ {2} v _ {x x} (t, x, y) & = r v (t, x, y), \\ 0 \leq t <   T, x \geq 0, y \in \mathbb {R}, \end{array} \tag {7.}\tag{7.5.8}
$$

and the boundary conditions 

$$
v (t, 0, y) = e ^ {- r (T - t)} \left(\frac {y}{T} - K\right) ^ {+}, 0 \leq t <   T, y \in \mathbb {R},\tag{7.5.9}
$$

$$
\lim _ {y \downarrow - \infty} v (t, x, y) = 0, 0 \leq t <   T, x \geq 0,\tag{7.5.10}
$$

$$
v (T, x, y) = \left(\frac {y}{T} - K\right) ^ {+}, x \geq 0, y \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{7.5.11}
$$

PROOF: Using the stochastic diferential equations (7.5. 1) and (7.5.5) and noting that $d \bar { S } ( t ) d Y ( t ) = d Y ( t ) d Y ( t ) = 0 ,$ we take the diferential of the $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } _ { - \mathrm { m a r t i n g } }$ ale $e ^ { - r t } V ( t ) = e ^ { - r t } v ( t , S ( t ) , Y ( t ) )$ . This diferential is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \left(e ^ {- r t} v (t, S (t), Y (t))\right)} \\ & {= e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r v d t + v _ {t} d t + v _ {x} d S + v _ {y} d Y + \frac {1}{2} v _ {x x} d S d S \right]} \\ & {= e ^ {- r t} \left[ - r v + v _ {t} + r S v _ {x} + S v _ {y} + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} v _ {x x} \right] d t} \\ & {\qquad + e ^ {- r t} \sigma S v _ {x} d \widetilde {W} (t).} \end{array}\tag{7.5.12}
$$

In order for this to be a martingale, the dt term must be zero, which implies 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & v _ {t} \big (t, S (t), Y (t) \big) + r S (t) v _ {x} \big (t, S (t), Y (t) \big) + S (t) v _ {y} \big (t, S (t), Y (t) \big) \\ & \qquad + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) v _ {x x} \big (t, S (t), Y (t) \big) = r v \big (t, S (t), Y (t) \big). \end{array}
$$

Replacing S(t) by the dummy variable x and $Y ( t )$ by the dummy variable ${ \pmb y } .$ we obtain (7.5.8) . 

We note that $S ( t )$ must always be nonnegative, and so (7.5.8) holds for $\pmb { x } \geq 0$ . If $S ( t ) = 0$ and $Y ( t ) = y$ for some value of t, then $\pmb { S } ( \pmb { u } ) = \pmb { 0 }$ for all $u \in [ t , T ]$ , and so $Y ( u )$ is constant on $[ t , T ]$ . Therefore, $\begin{array} { r } { Y ( T ) = y , } \end{array}$ and the value of the Asian call at time t is $\left( { \frac { y } { T } } - K \right) ^ { + }$ , discounted from T back to t. This gives us the boundary condition (7.5.9) . 

In contrast , it is not the case that if $Y ( t ) = 0$ for some time $\mathbf { } ^ { t , \quad }$ then $Y ( u ) = 0$ for all $u \geq 0 .$ Therefore, we cannot easily determine the value of ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , 0 )$ , and we do not provide a condition on the boundary $y = 0 .$ . Indeed, at least mathematicaly there is no problem with allowing y to be negative. If at time t we set $Y ( t ) = y .$ , then $Y ( T )$ is defined by (7.5.5). In integrated form, this formula is T 

$$
Y (T) = y + \int_ {t} ^ {T} S (u) d u.\tag{7.5.13}
$$

Even if y is negative, this makes sense, and in this case we could still have $Y ( T ) > 0$ or even $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { T } Y ( T ) - K > 0 , } \end{array}$ so that the call expires in the money. When using the diferential equations (7.5. 1) and (7.5.5) to describe the "state" processes $S ( t )$ and $Y ( t )$ , there is no reason to require that $Y ( t )$ be nonnegative. (We still require that $S ( t )$ be nonnegative because $\pmb { x } = \pmb { 0 }$ is a natural boundary for $S ( t ) . )$ For this reason, we do not restrict the values of y in the partial diferential equation (7.5.8) . The natural boundary for y is $y = - \infty$ . If $Y ( t ) =$ $y , S ( t ) = x ,$ and holding x fixed we let $y \to - \infty$ , then $Y ( T )$ approaches -o (see (7.5.13) ) , the probability that the call expires in the money approaches zero, and the option price approaches zero. The natural boundary for $\pmb { y }$ is $y = - \infty$ , and the boundary condition there is (7.5.10) . 

The boundary condition (7.5. 1 1) is just the payof of the call. 

Remark 7. 5. 2. After we set the dt term in (7.5. 12) equal to zero, we see that 

$$
d \left(e ^ {- r t} v (t, S (t), Y (t))\right) = e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) v _ {x} (t, S (t), Y (t)) d \widetilde {W} (t).\tag{7.5.14}
$$

The discounted value of a portfolio that at each time t holds $\varDelta ( t )$ shares of the underlying asset is given by (see (5.2.27)) 

$$
d \big (e ^ {- r t} X (t) \big) = e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) \Delta (t) d \widetilde {W} (t).\tag{7.5.15}
$$

To hedge a short position in the Asian call, an agent should equate these two diferentials, which leads to the delta-hedging formula 

$$
\Delta (t) = v _ {x} \big (t, S (t), Y (t) \big).
$$

## 7.5.3 Change of Numeraire

In this subsection we present a partial diferential equation whose solution leads to Asian option prices. We work this out for both continuous and discrete averaging. The derivation of this equation involves a change of numeraire, a concept discussed systematically in Chapter 9. In this section, we derive formulas under the assumption that the interest rate $\pmb { r }$ is not zero. The case $\pmb { r } = \mathbf { 0 }$ is treated in Exercise 7.8. 

We first consider the case of an Asian call with payof 

$$
V (T) = \left(\frac {1}{c} \int_ {T - c} ^ {T} S (t) d t - K\right) ^ {+},\tag{7.5.16}
$$

where c is a constant satisfying $0 < c \leq T$ and $\kappa$ is a nonnegative constant. If $c = T .$ , this is the Asian call (7.5.2) considered in Subsection 7.5.2. Here we also admit the possibility that the averaging is over less than the full time between initiation and expiration of the call. 

To price this call, we create a portfolio process whose value at time $_ { T }$ is 

$$
X (T) = \frac {1}{c} \int_ {T - c} ^ {T} S (u) d u - K.
$$

We begin with a nonrandom function of time $\gamma ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T ,$ which will be the number of shares of the risky asset held by our portfolio. There will be no Brownian motion term in $\gamma ( t )$ , and because of this it will satisfy $\mathop { d \gamma } ( t ) \mathop { d \gamma } ( t ) =$ $d \gamma ( t ) d S ( t ) = 0 .$ This implies that 

$$
d \big (\gamma (t) S (t) \big) = \gamma (t) d S (t) + S (t) d \gamma (t),\tag{7.5.17}
$$

which further implies 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d \big (e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t) S (t) \big) = e ^ {r (T - t)} d \big (\gamma (t) S (t) \big) - r e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t) S (t)   d t \\ = e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t)   d S (t) + e ^ {r (T - t)} S (t)   d \gamma (t) \\ - r e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t) S (t)   d t. \end{array}\tag{7.5.18}
$$

Rearranging terms in (7.5. 18) , we obtain 

$$
e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t) (d S (t) - r S (t) d t) = d \left(e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t) S (t)\right) - e ^ {r (T - t)} S (t) d \gamma (t).\tag{7.5.19}
$$

An agent who holds $\gamma ( t )$ shares of the risky asset at each time t and finances this by investing or borrowing at the interest rate $\pmb { r }$ will have a portfolio whose value evolves according to the equation 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d X (t) = \gamma (t)   d S (t) + r \bigl (X (t) - \gamma (t) S (t) \bigr) d t \\ = r X (t)   d t + \gamma (t) \bigl (d S (t) - r S (t)   d t \bigr). \end{array}\tag{7.5.20}
$$

Using this equation and (7.5. 19) , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \big (e ^ {r (T - t)} X (t) \big) = - r e ^ {r (T - t)} X (t) d t + e ^ {r (T - t)} d X (t)} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t) \big (S (t) - r S (t) d t \big)} \\ & {\qquad = d \big (e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t) S (t) \big) - e ^ {r (T - t)} S (t) d \gamma (t).} \end{array}\tag{7.5.21}
$$

To study the Asian call with payof (7.5.16) , we take $\gamma ( t )$ to be 

$$
\gamma (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{r c} \big (1 - e ^ {- r c} \big), \qquad 0 \leq t \leq T - c, \\ \frac {1}{r c} \big (1 - e ^ {- r (T - t)} \big),   T - c \leq t \leq T, \end{array} \right.\tag{7.5.22}
$$

and we take the initial capital to be 

$$
X (0) = \frac {1}{r c} \left(1 - e ^ {- r c}\right) S (0) - e ^ {- r T} K.\tag{7.5.23}
$$

In the time interval $[ 0 , T - c ]$ , the process $\gamma ( t )$ mandates a buy-and-hold strategy. At time zero, we buy $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { r c } } \left( 1 - e ^ { - r c } \right)$ shares of the risky asset, which costs $\begin{array} { r } { { \frac { 1 } { r c } } ( 1 - e ^ { - r c } ) { \underline { { S } } } ( 0 ) } \end{array}$ . Our initial capital is insuficient to do this, and we must borrow $e ^ { - r T } K$ from the money market account. For $0 \leq t \leq T - c ,$ the value of our holdings in the risky asset is $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { r c } \big ( 1 - e ^ { - r c } \big ) S ( t ) } \end{array}$ and we owe $e ^ { - r ( T - t ) } K$ to the money market account. Therefore, 

$$
X (t) = \frac {1}{r c} \big (1 - e ^ {- r c} \big) S (t) - e ^ {- r (T - t)} K, 0 \leq t \leq T - c.\tag{7.5.24}
$$

In particular, 

$$
X (T - c) = \frac {1}{r c} \left(1 - e ^ {- r c}\right) S (T - c) - e ^ {- r c} K.\tag{7.5.25}
$$

For $T - c \leq t \leq T$ , we have $\begin{array} { r } { d \gamma ( t ) = - \frac { 1 } { c } e ^ { - r ( T - t ) } } \end{array}$ and we compute X (t) by first integrating (7.5.21) from $\pmb { T } - \pmb { c }$ to t and using (7.5.25) and (7.5.22) to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & e ^ {r (T - t)} X (t) \\ & = e ^ {r c} X (T - c) + \int_ {T - c} ^ {t} d \bigl (e ^ {r (T - u)} \gamma (u) S (u) \bigr) - \int_ {T - c} ^ {t} e ^ {r (T - u)} S (u) d \gamma (u) \\ & = \frac {1}{r c} e ^ {r c} \bigl (1 - e ^ {- r c} \bigr) S (T - c) - K + e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t) S (t) \\ & \qquad - \frac {1}{r c} e ^ {r c} \bigl (1 - e ^ {- r c} \bigr) S (T - c) + \frac {1}{c} \int_ {T - c} ^ {t} S (u) d u \\ & = - K + e ^ {r (T - t)} \gamma (t) S (t) + \frac {1}{c} \int_ {T - c} ^ {t} S (u) d u. \end{array}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
X (t) = \frac {1}{r c} \bigl (1 - e ^ {- r (T - t)} \bigr) S (t) + e ^ {- r (T - t)} \frac {1}{c} \int_ {T - c} ^ {t} S (u) d u - e ^ {- r (T - t)} K,\tag{7.5.26}
$$

In particular, 

$$
X (T) = \frac {1}{c} \int_ {T - c} ^ {T} S (u) d u - K,\tag{7.5.27}
$$

as desired, and 

$$
V (T) = X ^ {+} (T) = \max \{X (T), 0 \}.\tag{7.5.28}
$$

The price of the Asian call at time t prior to expiration is 

$$
V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- r (T - t)} V (T) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ] = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- r (T - t)} X ^ {+} (T) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ].\tag{7.5.29}
$$

The calculation of the right-hand side of (7.5.29) uses a change-of-numeraire argument, which we now exlain. Let us define 

$$
Y (t) = \frac {X (t)}{S (t)} = \frac {e ^ {- r t} X (t)}{e ^ {- r t} S (t)}.
$$

This is the value of the portfolio denominated in units of the risky asset rather than in dollars. We have changed the numeraire, the unit of account, from dollars to the risky asset. 

We work out the diferential of $Y ( t )$ . Note first that 

$$
d \big (e ^ {- r t} S (t) \big) = - r e ^ {- r t} S (t) d t + e ^ {- r t} d S (t) = \sigma e ^ {- r t} S (t) d \widetilde {W} (t).\tag{7.5.30}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \left[ \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 1} \right]} \\ & {= - \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 2} d \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) + \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 3} d \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) d \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right)} \\ & {= - \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 2} \sigma \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) d \widetilde {W} (t) + \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 3} \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} d t} \\ & {= - \sigma \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 1} d \widetilde {W} (t) + \sigma^ {2} \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 1} d t.} \end{array}
$$

On the other hand, (7.5.20) and (7.5.30) imply 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} d \big (e ^ {- r t} X (t) \big) & = - r e ^ {- r t} X (t) d t + e ^ {- r t} d X (t) \\ & = \gamma (t) e ^ {- r t} \big (d S (t) - r S (t) \big) d t \\ & = \gamma (t) \sigma e ^ {- r t} S (t) d \widetilde {W} (t). \end{array}
$$

Ito's product rule implies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d Y (t) = d \left[ \left(e ^ {- r t} X (t)\right) \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 1} \right] \\ = e ^ {- r t} X (t) d \left[ \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 1} \right] + \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 1} d \left(e ^ {- r t} X (t)\right) \\ \quad + d \left(e ^ {- r t} X (t)\right) d \left[ \left(e ^ {- r t} S (t)\right) ^ {- 1} \right] \\ = - \sigma Y (t) d \widetilde {W} (t) + \sigma^ {2} Y (t) d t + \sigma \gamma (t) d \widetilde {W} (t) - \sigma^ {2} \gamma (t) d t \\ = \sigma [ \gamma (t) - Y (t) ] [ d \widetilde {W} (t) - \sigma d t ]. \end{array}\tag{7.5.31}
$$

The process Y(t) is not a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ because its diferential (7.5.31) has a dt term. However, we can change measure so that $Y ( t )$ is a martingale, and this will simplify (7.5.3 1 ) . We set 

$$
\widetilde {W} ^ {S} (t) = \widetilde {W} (t) - \sigma t\tag{7.5.32}
$$

and then have 

$$
d Y (t) = \sigma [ \gamma (t) - Y (t) ] d \widetilde {W} ^ {S} (t).\tag{7.5.33}
$$

Accordil_!g to Girsanov's Theorem, Theorem 5.2.3, we can change the measure so that $\widetilde { W } ^ { s } ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T ,$ , is a Brownian motion. In this situation, $- \sigma$ plays the role of $\boldsymbol { \Theta }$ in Theorem 5.2.3, and $\widetilde { W }$ and $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ play the roles of $W$ and P. The Radon-Nikodym derivative process of (5.2 . 1 1) is 

$$
Z (t) = \exp \left\{\sigma \widetilde {W} (t) - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} t \right\}.
$$

In other words, 

$$
Z (t) = \frac {e ^ {- r t} S (t)}{S (0)}.\tag{7.5.34}
$$

Under the probability measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } ^ { s }$ defined by 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {P}} ^ {S} (A) = \int_ {A} Z (T) d \widetilde {\mathbb {P}} \mathrm{forall} A \in \mathcal {F},
$$

$\widetilde { W } ^ { S } ( t )$ is a Brownian motion and $Y ( t )$ is a martingale. 

Under the probability measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } ^ { s }$ , the process $Y ( t )$ is Markov. It is given by the stochastic diferential equation (7.5.33) , and because $\gamma ( t )$ is nonrandom, the term multiplying $d \widetilde { W } ^ { S } ( t )$ in (7.5.33) is a function of t and $Y ( t )$ and has no source of randomness other than $Y ( t )$ . Equation (7. 5.33) is a stochastic differential equation of the type (6.2.1) , and solutions to such equations are Markov (see Corollary 6.3.2) . 

We return to the option price $V ( t )$ of (7.5.29) and use Lemma 5.2.2 to write (7.5.29) as 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & V (t) = e ^ {r t} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- r T} X ^ {+} (T) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ] \\ & \qquad = \frac {S (t)}{e ^ {- r t} S (t)} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r T} S (T) \left(\frac {e ^ {- r T} X (T)}{e ^ {- r T} S (T)}\right) ^ {+} \bigg | \mathcal {F} (t) \right] \\ & \qquad = \frac {S (t)}{Z (t)} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ Z (T) Y ^ {+} (T) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \right] \\ & \qquad = S (t) \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} ^ {S} \left[ Y ^ {+} (T) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \right], \end{array}\tag{7.5.35}
$$

where $\widetilde { \mathbb { E } } ^ { s } [ \cdot \cdot \cdot | \mathcal { F } ( t ) ]$ denotes conditional expectation under the probability measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } ^ { s }$ . Because $Y$ is Markov under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } ^ { s }$ , there must be some function ${ \pmb g } ( t , y )$ such that 

$$
g (t, Y (t)) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} ^ {S} [ Y ^ {+} (T) | \mathcal {F} (t) ].\tag{7.5.36}
$$

From (7.5.36) , we see that 

$$
g (T, Y (T)) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} ^ {S} [ Y ^ {+} (T) | \mathcal {F} (T) ] = Y ^ {+} (T).\tag{7.5.37}
$$

We note that $\begin{array} { r } { Y ( T ) = \frac { X ( T ) } { S ( T ) } } \end{array}$ can take any value since the numerator $X ( T )$ given by (7.5.27) , can be either positive or negative, and the denominator $s ( T )$ can be any positive number. Therefore, (7.5.37) leads to the boundary condition 

$$
g (T, y) = y ^ {+}, \quad y \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{7.5.38}
$$

The usual iterated conditioning argument shows that the right-hand side of (7.5.36) is a martingale under $\tilde { \mathbb { P } } ^ { \tilde { s } }$ , and so the diferential of $g \big ( t , Y ( t ) \big )$ should have only a $d \widetilde { W } ^ { S } ( t )$ term. This diferential is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d g (t, Y (t)) = g _ {t} (t, Y (t)) d t + g _ {y} (t, Y (t)) d Y (t)} \\ & {\qquad + \frac {1}{2} g _ {y y} (t, Y (t)) d Y (t) d Y (t)} \\ & {\qquad = \left[ g _ {t} (t, Y (t)) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (\gamma (t) - Y (t)) ^ {2} g _ {y y} (t, Y (t)) \right] d t} \\ & {\qquad + \sigma (\gamma (t) - Y (t)) g _ {y} (t, Y (t)) d \widetilde {W} ^ {S} (t).} \end{array}
$$

We conclude that $\scriptstyle g ( t , y )$ satisfies the partial diferential equation 

$$
g _ {t} (t, y) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (\gamma (t) - y) ^ {2} g _ {y y} (t, y) = 0, \quad 0 \leq t <   T, y \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{7.5.39}
$$

We summarize this discussion with the following theorem. 

Theorem 7.5.3 (Vecef). For $0 \leq t \leq T$ , the price $V ( t )$ at time t of the continuously averaged Asian call with payof {7. 5. 1 6} at time $_ { T }$ is 

$$
V (t) = S (t) g \left(t, \frac {X (t)}{S (t)}\right),\tag{7.5.40}
$$

where ${ \mathbf { } } g ( t , y )$ satisfies {7. 5. 99} and $X ( t )$ is given by (7. 5. 24} and {7. 5. 26}. The boundary conditions for $\scriptstyle g ( t , y )$ are {7. 5. 98} and 

$$
\lim _ {y \to - \infty} g (t, y) = 0, \quad \lim _ {y \to \infty} [ g (t, y) - y ] = 0, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{7.5.41}
$$

Remark 7. 5.4 (Boundary conditions). Let $0 \ \leq \ t \ \leq \ T$ be given. The first boundary condition in (7.5.41) can be derived from the fact that when $Y ( t )$ is very negative, the probability that $Y ( T )$ also is negative is near one and therefore the probability that $\dot { Y } ^ { + } ( T ) = \dot { 0 }$ is near one. This causes $g ( t , Y ( t ) )$ in (7.5.36) to be near zero. The second boundary condition in (7.5.41) is a consequence of that fact that when $Y ( t )$ is large, then the probability that $Y ( T ) > 0$ is near one. Therefore, $g \big ( t , Y ( t ) \big )$ given by (7.5.36) is approximately equal to $\widetilde { \mathbb E } ^ { s } \left[ Y ( T ) \vert \mathcal F ( t ) \right]$ , and because $Y ( T )$ is a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb P } ^ { s }$ , this conditional expectation is $Y ( t )$ 

It is easier to derive these boundary conditions at ${ \pmb y } = \pm \infty$ for ${ \mathfrak { g } } ( t , y )$ than it is to derive the boundary conditions for ${ \boldsymbol { v } } ( t , { \boldsymbol { x } } , y )$ in Theorem 7.5. 1 because ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } , { \pmb y } )$ has two variables, x and $^ { y , }$ that can become large. For example, it is not at all clear how ${ \boldsymbol v } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } , y )$ behaves as $\pmb { x }  \infty$ and $y  - \infty$ . The reduction of the Asian option pricing problem provided by Theorem 7.5.3 reduces the dimensionality of the problem and simplifies the boundary conditions. It also removes a so-called "degeneracy" in equation (7.5.8) created by the absence of the $v _ { y y } ( t , x , y )$ term. This degeneracy complicates the numerical solution of (7.5.8) . 0 

In the remainder of this subsection, we adapt the arguments just given to treat a discretely sampled Asian call. Assume we are given times $0 = t _ { 0 } <$ $t _ { 1 } < t _ { 2 } \dots < t _ { m } = T$ and the Asian call payof is 

$$
V (T) = \left(\frac {1}{m} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} S (t _ {j}) - K\right) ^ {+}.\tag{7.5.42}
$$

We wish to create a portfolio process so that 

$$
X (T) = \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} S (t _ {j}) - K.
$$

In place of (7.5.22) , we define 

$$
\gamma (t _ {j}) = \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {i = j} ^ {m} e ^ {- r (T - t _ {i})}, \quad j = 0, 1, \dots , m.\tag{7.5.43}
$$

Then 

$$
\gamma (t _ {j}) = \gamma (t _ {j - 1}) - \frac {1}{m} e ^ {- r (T - t _ {j - 1})}, \quad j = 1, \dots , m,\tag{7.5.44}
$$

and $\begin{array} { r } { \gamma ( T ) = \gamma ( t _ { m } ) = \frac { 1 } { m } } \end{array}$ . We complete the definition of $\gamma ( t )$ by setting 

$$
\gamma (t) = \gamma (t _ {j}), \quad t _ {j - 1} <   t \leq t _ {j}.\tag{7.5.45}
$$

This defines $\gamma ( t )$ for all $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ . In this situation, (7.5.21) still holds, but now $d \gamma ( t ) = 0$ in each subinterval $( t _ { j - 1 } , t _ { j } )$ · Integrating (7.5.21 ) from $t _ { j - 1 }$ to $t _ { j }$ and using (7.5.44) and the fact that $\gamma ( t ) = \gamma ( t _ { j } )$ for $t \in ( t _ { j - 1 } , t _ { j } ]$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & e ^ {r (T - t _ {j})} X (t _ {j}) - e ^ {r (T - t _ {j - 1})} X (t _ {j - 1}) \\ & = \gamma (t _ {j}) \big [ e ^ {r (T - t _ {j})} S (t _ {j}) - e ^ {r (T - t _ {j - 1})} S (t _ {j - 1}) \big ] \\ & = \gamma (t _ {j}) e ^ {r (T - t _ {j})} S (t _ {j}) - \bigg (\gamma (t _ {j - 1}) - \frac {1}{m} e ^ {- r (T - t _ {j - 1})} \bigg) e ^ {r (T - t _ {j - 1})} S (t _ {j - 1}) \\ & = \gamma (t _ {j}) e ^ {r (T - t _ {j})} S (t _ {j}) - \gamma (t _ {j - 1}) e ^ {r (T - t _ {j - 1})} S (t _ {j - 1}) + \frac {1}{m} S (t _ {j - 1}). \end{array}
$$

Summing this equation from $j = 1 \ { \mathsf { t o } } \ j = k$ , we see that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} e ^ {r (T - t _ {k})} X (t _ {k}) - e ^ {r T} X (0) \\ = \gamma (t _ {k}) e ^ {r (T - t _ {k})} S (t _ {k}) - \gamma (0) e ^ {r T} S (0) + \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} S (t _ {j - 1}) \\ = \gamma (t _ {k}) e ^ {r (T - t _ {k})} S (t _ {k}) + \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k - 1} S (t _ {i}) + \left(- \gamma (0) e ^ {r T} + \frac {1}{m}\right) S (0). \end{array}
$$

We set 

$$
X (0) = e ^ {- r T} \left[ \gamma (0) e ^ {r T} - \frac {1}{m} \right] S (0) - e ^ {- r T} K,
$$

so this equation becomes 

$$
e ^ {r (T - t _ {k})} X (t _ {k}) = \gamma (t _ {k}) e ^ {r (T - t _ {k})} S (t _ {k}) + \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k - 1} S (t _ {i}) - K
$$

or, equivalently, 

$$
X (t _ {k}) = \gamma (t _ {k}) S (t _ {k}) + e ^ {- r (T - t _ {k})} \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k - 1} S (t _ {i}) - e ^ {- r (T - t _ {k})} K.\tag{7.5.46}
$$

In particular, 

$$
X (T) = X (t _ {m}) = \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m} S (t _ {i}) - K\tag{7.5.47}
$$

as desired. 

To determine X (t) for $t _ { k } \leq t \leq t _ { k + 1 }$ • we integrate (7.5.21) from $\scriptstyle t _ { k }$ to t to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} e ^ {r (T - t)} X (t) = e ^ {r (T - t _ {k})} X (t _ {k}) + \gamma (t _ {k + 1}) \left[ e ^ {r (T - t)} S (t) - e ^ {r (T - t _ {k})} S (t _ {k}) \right] \\ \qquad = \gamma (t _ {k}) e ^ {r (T - t _ {k})} S (t _ {k}) + \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k - 1} S (t _ {i}) - K + \gamma (t _ {k + 1}) e ^ {r (T - t)} S (t) \\ \qquad - \left(\gamma (t _ {k}) - \frac {1}{m} e ^ {- r (T - t _ {k})}\right) e ^ {r (T - t _ {k})} S (t _ {k}) \\ \qquad = \gamma (t _ {k + 1}) e ^ {r (T - t)} S (t) + \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} S (t _ {i}) - K. \end{array}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
X (t) = \gamma (t _ {k + 1}) S (t) + e ^ {- r (T - t)} \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} S (t _ {i}) - e ^ {- r (T - t)} K, \quad t _ {k} \leq t \leq t _ {k + 1}.\tag{7.5.48}
$$

We now proceed with the change of numeraire as before. This leads again to Theorem 7.5.3 for the discretely sampled Asian call with payof (7.5.42) . 

The price at time t is given by (7.5.40) , where ${ \pmb g } ( { \pmb t } , { \pmb x } )$ satisfies (7.5.39) with boundary conditions (7.5.38) and (7.5.41). The only diference is that now the nonrandom function 7(t) appearing in (7.5.39) is given by (7.5.43) and (7.5.45) and the process X (t) in (7.5.40) is given by (7.5.48) . 

## 7.6 Summary

Three specific exotic options on a geometric Brownian motion have been considered: an up-and-out barrier call, a lookback call, and an Asian call. In each case, the discounted option price is a martingale under the risk-neutral measure, and this leads to a partial diferential equation of the Black-Scholes-Merton type. However, the look back call and the Asian call equations have an additional state variable in this equation. 

For the barrier call and the lookback call, the option price was computed explicitly. The Asian option pricing problem was transformed by a change of numeraire to an equation with a single state variable. This transformation was done both for the continuously sampled and the discretely sampled Asian options. 

## 7.7 Notes

There are scores of diferent exotic options, and the search for explicit pricing formulas can lead to complex computations. Analysis of many exotic options is provided by Zhang [167] and Haug [80] . Papers by a variety of authors who treat exotic options, including some of those cited below, have been collected by Lipton [1 10] . Exotic options are prevalent in foreign exchange markets. Analysis of several instruments appearing in these markets is provided by Hakla and Wystup [76] . Many exotic pricing formulas can be derived from the formulas for distributions related to Brownian motion collected by Borodin and Salminen [18] . 

The analysis of barrier options presented here follows Rubinstein and Reiner [142] . Monte Carlo simulation of barrier options normally obtains the price for the case when barrier crossing is checked only at discrete times. Broadie, Glasserman and Kou [22] provide a correction term to adjust this result to obtain the price for an option in which the barrier is monitored continuously. The problem of large delta and gamma values for barrier options near expiration near the barrier can be ameliorated by placing an a priori constraint on the hedging strategy and pricing this constraint into the option; se Schmock, Shreve, and Wystup [148] . 

The change-of-numeraire approach to Asian options, explained in Subsection 7.5.3, is due to Vecef [155] , [156] . This methodology was extended to jump processes by Vecef and Xl' [157] . Other partial diferential equations for pricing Asian options are provided by Andreasen [4] , Lipton [109] , and Rogers and Shi [139] . 

Geman and Yor [71] obtain a closed-form formula for a Laplace transform of the Asian option price. $\mathbf { F u } ,$ Madan, and Wang [67] compare Monte Carlo and Laplace transform methods for Asian option pricing. 

## 7.8 Exercises

Exercise 7.1 (Black-Scholes-Merton equation for the up-and-out call). This exercise shows by direct calculation that the function ${ \pmb v } ( t , { \pmb x } )$ of (7.3.20) satisfies the Black-Scholes-Merton equation (7.3.4) . 

(i) Recall that $\tau = T - t ,$ so $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { d \tau } { d t } = - 1 } \end{array}$ . Show that $\delta _ { \pm } ( \tau , s )$ given by (7.3. 18) satisfies 

$$

# American Derivative Securities

## 8. 1 Introduction

European option contracts specify an expiration date, and if the option is to be exercised at all, the exercise must occur on the expiration date. An option whose owner can choose to exercise at any time up to and including the expiration date is called American. Because of this early exercise feature, such an option is at least as valuable as its European counterpart. Sometimes the diference in value is negligible or even zero, and then American and European options are close or exact substitutes. We shall see in this chapter that the early exercise feature for a call on a stock paying no dividends is worthless; American and European calls on such a stock have the same price. In other cases, most notably put options, the value of this early exercise feature, the so-called early e<sub>x</sub>ercise premium, can be substantial. An intermediate option between American and European is Bermudan, an option that permits early exercise but only on a contractually specified finite set of dates. 

Because an American option can be exercised at any time prior to its expiration, it can never be worth less than the payof associated with immediate exercise. This is called the intrinsic value of the option. 

In contrast to the case for a European option, whose discounted price process is a martingale under the risk-neutral measure, the discounted price process of an American option is a supermartingale under this measure. The holder of this option may fail to exercise at the optimal exercise date, and in this case the discounted option price has a tendency to fall; hence, the supermartingale property. During any period of time in which it is not optimal to exercise, however, the discounted price process behaves as a martingale. 

To price an American option, just as with a European option, we could imagine selling the option in exchange for some initial capital and then consider how to use this capital to hedge the short position in the option. In this ase, we would need to be ready to pay of the option at all times prior to the expiration date because we do not know when it will be exercised. We could determine when, from our point of view, is the worst time for the owner to exercise the option. From the owner's point of view, this would be the optimal e<sub>x</sub>ercise time, and we shall call it that. We could then compute the initial capital we need in order to be hedged against exercise at the optimal exercise time. Finally, we could show how to invest this capital so that we are hedged even if the owner exercises at a nonoptimal time. In the subsequent sections, we do all these things but begin the analysis at a diferent point than for European options. We define the price of American options using a risk-neutral pricing formula and then show that this price is the smallest initial capital that permits construction of the hedge just described. 

For the binomial model, the program described above was carried out in Chapter 4 of Volume I. Here we revisit these matters in a continuous-time setting. We treat first the perpetual American put (Section <sub>8.3) ,</sub> which is not actually traded. The analysis of this option provides lessons that we apply in the subsequent sections. In Section <sub>8.4,</sub> we discuss the finite-expiration American put, an option that is traded. Section <sub>8.5</sub> treats the American call. In the case of a non-dividend-paying stock, we show that the American and European calls have the same price. However, if the stock pays dividends, these prices can difer. We show how to compute the American call price in this latter case. 

## 8.2 Stopping Times

Throughout this chapter, we need the concept of stopping times. These were defined and discussed in the binomial model in Section 4.3 of Volume I. A stopping time is a random variable T that takes values in [0, o] . The stopping times we shall encounter are the times at which an American option is exercised. The decision of an agent to exercise this option may depend on all the information available at that time but may not depend on future information. We provide a mathematical formulation of this property in Definition 8.2.1 below. Before stating this definition, we seek to motivate it. 

In the N-period model of Volume I, where the filtration is generated by coin tossing and there are only finitely many dates, we defined a stopping time to be a random variable T taking values 0, 1 , . . . , N or o and having the property that if $\tau ( \omega _ { 1 } \dots \omega _ { n } \omega _ { n + 1 } \dots \omega _ { N } ) = n ;$ <sub>,</sub> then $\tau ( \omega _ { 1 } \dots \omega _ { n } \omega _ { n + 1 } ^ { \prime } \dots \omega _ { N } ^ { \prime } ) = n$ for all $\omega _ { n + 1 } ^ { \prime } \ldots \omega _ { N } ^ { \prime }$ . This condition guarantees that the decision to stop at time n does not depend on the coin tosses that come after time <sub>n.</sub> 

One way to try to capture this same idea in continuous time is to require that for each nonrandom $t \geq 0$ <sub>,</sub> the set $\{ \tau = t \} = \{ \omega \in \varOmega ; \tau ( \omega ) = t \}$ should be in $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ (i.e. , the agent stops (exercises the option) at time t based on the information available at time t) . However, we shall be interested in sets of ws of the form $\{ \omega \in \Omega ; T _ { 1 } \le \tau ( \omega ) \le T _ { 2 } \}$ , and these cannot be gotten by taking countable unions of sets of the form $\{ \omega \in \Omega ; \tau ( \omega ) = t \}$ . Therefore, we impose the slightly stronger condition of Definition 8.2.1 below. 

<sub>Definition</sub> <sub>8.2.1 .</sub> A stopping time $\tau$ is a mndom variable taking values in [0, o] and satisfying 

$$
\{\tau \leq t \} \in \mathcal {F} (t) f o r a l l t \geq 0.\tag{8.2.1}
$$

Remark 8. 2. 2. Let $t \geq 0$ be given. Note that (8.2.1) and the properties of $\sigma \mathrm { - }$ algebras imply that $\begin{array} { r } { \left\{ \tau > t - \frac { 1 } { n } \right\} = \left\{ \tau \leq t - \frac { \mathrm { i } } { n } \right\} \in \mathcal { F } \left( t - \frac { 1 } { n } \right) } \end{array}$ for all positive integers <sub>n.</sub> Since every set in $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { F } \left( t - \frac { 1 } { n } \right) } \end{array}$ is also in $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ , we conclude that $\begin{array} { r } { \left\{ \tau > t - \frac { 1 } { n } \right\} } \end{array}$ is in $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ for every <sub>n,</sub> and hence 

$$
\{\tau = t \} = \{\tau \leq t \} \cap \left(\bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left\{\tau > t - \frac {1}{n} \right\}\right)
$$

is also in $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ . In other words, by Definition 8.2.1, a stopping time $\tau$ has the property that the decision to stop at time t must be based on information available at time t. 

Example 8. 2. 3 {First passage time for a continuous process). Let $X ( t )$ be an adapted process with continuous paths, let <sub>m</sub> be a number, and set 

$$
\tau_ {m} = \min \{t \geq 0; X (t) = m \}.\tag{8.2.2}
$$

This is the first time the process $X ( t )$ reaches the level $_ { \pmb { m } . }$ If $X ( t )$ never reaches the level $m ,$ then we interpret $\tau _ { m }$ to be $\infty$ . Intuitively, $\tau _ { m }$ must be a stopping time because the value of $\tau _ { m }$ is determined by the path of $X ( t )$ up to time $\tau _ { m }$ . An agent can exercise an option the first time the underlying asset price reaches a level; this exercise strategy does not require information about the underlying price movements after the exercise time. 

We use Definition 8.2.1 and the properties of a-algebras to show mathematically that $\tau _ { m }$ is a stopping time. Let $t \geq 0$ be given. We need to show that $\{ \tau \leq t \}$ is in $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ 

If $t = 0 ,$ , then $\{ \tau \leq t \} = \{ \tau = 0 \}$ is either fl or <sub>0,</sub> depending On whether $X ( 0 ) = m$ or $X ( 0 ) \neq m$ <sub>.</sub> In either case, $\{ \tau \leq 0 \} \in \mathcal { F } ( 0 )$ 

We consider the case $t > 0$ . Suppose $\omega \in \Omega$ satisfies $\tau ( \omega ) \leq t .$ Then there is some number $s \leq t$ such that $X ( s , \omega ) = m$ <sub>,</sub> where we indicate explicitly the dependence of X on $\omega .$ . For each positive integer $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \mathbf { \eta } ^ { n , } }$ there is an open interval of time containing s for which the process X is in $( m - \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { n } } , m + \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { n } } )$ . In this interval, there is a rational number $q \leq s \leq t .$ Therefore, $\omega$ is in the set 

$$
A = \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \bigcup_ {0 \leq q \leq t, q \text {   rational }} \left\{m - \frac {1}{n} <   X (q) <   m + \frac {1}{n} \right\}.
$$

We have shown that $\{ \tau \leq t \} \subset A$ 

On the other hand, $\operatorname { i f } \omega \in A ,$ <sub>,</sub> then for every positive integer there is a rational number $q _ { n } \leq t$ such that 

$$
m - \frac {1}{n} <   X (q _ {n}, \omega) <   m + \frac {1}{n}.
$$

The infinite sequence $\{ q _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ must have an accumulation point s in the closed, bounded interval $[ 0 , t ]$ . In other words, there must exist a number $s \in [ 0 , t ]$ and a subsequence $\{ q _ { n _ { k } } \} _ { k = 1 } ^ { n }$ such that lim $_ { k  \infty } q _ { n _ { k } } = s$ . But 

$$
m - \frac {1}{n _ {k}} <   X (q _ {n _ {k}}, \omega) <   m + \frac {1}{n _ {k}} \text { for   all } k = 1, 2, \dots .
$$

Letting $k \to \infty$ in these inequalities and using the fact that X has continuous paths, we see that $X ( s , \omega ) = m$ . It follows that $\tau ( \omega ) \leq t .$ We have shown that $A \subset \{ \tau \leq t \}$ . Therefore $A = \{ \tau \leq t \}$ 

Because X is adapted to the filtration, for each positive integer n and rational $q \in [ 0 , t ]$ , the set 

$$
\left\{m - \frac {1}{n} <   X (q) <   m + \frac {1}{n} \right\}
$$

is in $\mathcal { F } ( q )$ and hence in the larger a-algebra $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ . Because there are only countably many rational numbers $\pmb q$ in $[ 0 , t ]$ , they can be arranged in a sequence, and the union 

$$
B _ {n} = \bigcup_ {0 \leq q \leq t, q \text {   rational }} \left\{m - \frac {1}{n} <   X (q) <   m + \frac {1}{n} \right\}
$$

is really a union of a sequence of sets in $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ . The set $B _ { n }$ must therefore also be in $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ . Because $B _ { n }$ is in $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ for every positive integer $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \mathbf { \eta } ^ { n , } }$ the intersection $\cap _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } B _ { n } = A$ is also in $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ . We have already shown that $A = \{ \tau \leq t \}$ . We conclude that $\{ \tau \leq t \} \in \mathcal { F } ( t )$ D 

Suppose now that we have an adapted process $X ( t )$ and a stopping time $\pmb { \tau } .$ We define the stopped process $X ( t \wedge \tau )$ , where <sub>1\</sub> denotes the minimum of two quantities $( \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } t \wedge \tau = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ t , \tau \} )$ . The stopped process $X ( t \wedge \tau )$ agrees with $X ( t )$ up to time $\tau ,$ and thereafter it is frozen at the value of $X ( \tau )$ . See Figure 8.2 . 1 . 

Theorem 8.2.4 (Optional sampling) . A martingale stopped a t a stopping time is a martingale. A supermartingale {or submartingale) stopped at a stopping time is a supermartingale (or submartingale, respectively). 

While the proof of Theorem 8.2.4 is technical and will not be given here, the intuition is clear. If $M ( t )$ is a martingale, then the stopped process $M ( t \land \tau )$ agrees with $M ( t )$ before time T and thus is also a martingale. After time $\tau ,$ the stopped process is frozen (i.e. , it no longer changes with time) , and this is a trivial martingale. A martingale goes neither up nor down "on average." After being frozen, a process goes neither up nor down, path-by-path. The only way the martingale property could be violated is if the stopping decision looked ahead. Suppose that a martingale is stopped (frozen) if it will go up in the near future but is allowed to continue if it will go down. Then stopping introduces a downward bias by removing the upward possibility. Figure 8.2.2 shows a martingale in a discrete-time model under the assumption that the probability of H (an up move) is $\begin{array} { r } { \tilde { p } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ and the probability of $_ { T }$ (a down move) is $\begin{array} { r } { \tilde { q } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ <sub>-</sub> Figures 8.2.2-8.2.4 are taken from Section 4.3 of Volume ${ \mathbf { I } } ,$ where the martingale in Figure 8.2.2 is a discounted stock price under a riskneutral measure. Figure 8.2.3 shows a random time $\pmb { \rho }$ that is not a stopping time; this random time $\pmb { \rho }$ causes stopping at time 0 if there is an $\pmb { H }$ on the first toss (an up move) but lets the process continue if there is a $_ { T }$ on the first toss. Similarly, if there is a $_ { T }$ on the first toss and an $\pmb { H }$ on the second toss, $\pmb { \rho }$ stops the martingale at time 1 but lets it continue to time 2 if there is a $_ { T }$ on the first toss and an $\pmb { H }$ on the second toss. The stopped martingale is shown in Figure 8.2.4, and it is not a martingale. For example,

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} M _ {2 \wedge \rho} = \frac {1}{4} (4 + 4 + 1. 6 0 + 0. 6 4) = 2. 5 6 <   M _ {0} = 4,
$$

whereas the expectation of a martingale does not change over time. Our definition of stopping time rules out this kind of stopping. 

Similar intuition applies to supermartingales. A stopped supermartingale is a supermartingale before being frozen, and after being frozen it is a martingale, which is a special case of a supermartingale. The situation with submartingales is analogous. Again, the stopping must be done at a stopping time.

Looking ahead to make the stopping decision can ruin the supermartingale (respectively, submartingale) property. 

## 8.3 Perpetual American Put

The simplest interesting American option is the perpetual American put. It is interesting because the optimal exercise policy is not obvious, and it is simple because this policy can be determined explicitly. Although this is not a traded option, we begin our discussion with it in order to present in a simple context the ideas behind the subsequent analysis of more realistic options. 

The underlying asset in most of this chapter (except in Subsection 8.5.2, where the asset pays dividends) has the price process $S ( t )$ given by 

$$
d S (t) = r S (t) d t + \sigma S (t) d \widetilde {W} (t),\tag{8.3.1}
$$

where the interest rate r and the volatility $\pmb { \sigma }$ are strictly positive constants and $\widetilde { W } ( t )$ is a Brownian motion under the risk-neutral probability measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ The perpetual American put pays $K - S ( t )$ if it is exercised at time t. This is its intrinsic value. 

Definition 8.3. 1 . Let $\tau$ be the set of all stopping times. The price of the perpetual American put is defined to be 

$$
v _ {*} (x) = \max _ {\tau \in \mathcal {T}} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r \tau} \big (K - S (\tau) \big) \right],\tag{8.3.2}
$$

where $\pmb { x } = \pmb { S } ( \mathbf { 0 } )$ in {8. 3. 2} is the initial stock price. In the event that $\tau = \infty$ we interpret $e ^ { - r \tau } ( K - S ( \tau ) )$ to be zero. 

The idea behind Definition 8.3.1 is that the owner of the perpetual American put can choose an exercise time T, subject only to the condition that she may not look ahead to determine when to exercise. The mathematical formulation of this "not look ahead" restriction is that $\tau$ must be a stopping time. The price of the option at time zero is the risk-neutral expected payof of the option, discounted from the exercise time back to time zero. If the option is never exercised, its payof is zero. This explains the term under the expectation on the right-hand side of (8.3.2) . The owner of the option should choose the exercise strategy that maximizes this expected payof, discounted back to time zero, and thus we define the price of the option to be the maximum over $\tau \in \tau$ of the discounted expected payofs. 

This risk-neutral pricing definition of the perpetual American put price appears to difer from the construction of the price of a European call in Section 4.5. There we took the price to be the initial capital required by an agent holding a short position in the option in order for this agent to hedge the hort position (i.e., invest in the stock and money market account in such a way that at expiration of the option the resulting portfolio value is the payof of the option) . It turns out that ${ \pmb v } _ { \ast } ( { \pmb x } )$ defined above is the initial capital required for an agent to hedge a short position in the American put regardless of the exercise strategy $\tau$ used by the owner of the put; see Corollaries 8.3.6 and 8.3.7. 

The owner of the perpetual American put can exercise at any time. In particular, there is no expiration date after which the put can no longer be exercised. This makes every date like every other date; the time remaining to expiration is always the same (i.e. , infinity) . Because every date is like every other date, it is reasonable to expect that the optimal exercise policy depends only on the value of $S ( t )$ and not on the time variable t. The owner of the put should exercise as soon as S(t) falls "far enough" below K. In other words, it is reasonable to expect that the optimal exercise policy is of the form 

"Exercise the put as soon as $S ( t )$ falls to the level $L _ { * } . ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$ 

We have two questions to answer: 

(i) What is the value of $L _ { * }$ and how do we know it corresponds to optimal exercise? 

(ii) What is the value of the put? 

For the perpetual American put, we can base the answers to these questions on explicit computations. 

## 8.3.1 Price Under Arbitrary Exercise

Theorem 8.3.2 (Laplace transform for first passage time of drifted Brownia motion) . Let $\widetilde { W } ( t )$ be a Brownian motion under a probability measure ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } ,$ let $\pmb { \mu }$ be a real number, and let m be a positive number. Define $X ( t ) = \mu t + \tilde { W } ( t )$ , and set 

$$
\tau_ {m} = \min \{t \geq 0; X (t) = m \},
$$

so that $\tau _ { m }$ is the stopping time of Example 8. 2. 3. If X (t) never reaches the level $^ { m , }$ then we interpret $\tau _ { m }$ to be o. Then 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} e ^ {- \lambda \tau_ {m}} = e ^ {- m (- \mu + \sqrt {\mu^ {2} + 2 \lambda})} f o r a l l \lambda > 0,\tag{8.3.3}
$$

where we interpret $e ^ { - \lambda \tau _ { m } }$ to be zero $i f \tau _ { m } = \infty$ 

PROOF: Define $\sigma = - \mu + \sqrt { \mu ^ { 2 } + 2 \lambda }$ so that $\sigma > 0$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\sigma \mu + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} = - \mu^ {2} + \mu \sqrt {\mu^ {2} + 2 \lambda} + \frac {1}{2} \left(- \mu + \sqrt {\mu^ {2} + 2 \lambda}\right) ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = - \mu^ {2} + \mu \sqrt {\mu^ {2} + 2 \lambda} + \frac {1}{2} \mu^ {2} - \mu \sqrt {\mu^ {2} + 2 \lambda} + \frac {1}{2} \mu^ {2} + \lambda} \\ & {\qquad = \lambda .} \end{array}
$$

Then 

$$
e ^ {\sigma X (t) - \lambda t} = e ^ {\sigma \mu t + \sigma \widetilde {W} (t) - \sigma \mu t - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} t} = e ^ {\sigma \widetilde {W} (t) - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} t},
$$

which is a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ (its diferential has a $d \widetilde { W } ( t )$ term and no <sub>dt</sub> term). According to Theorem 8.2.4 (optional sampling) , the stopped martingale 

$$
M (t) = e ^ {\sigma \widetilde {W} (t \wedge \tau_ {m}) - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} (t \wedge \tau_ {m})}
$$

is also a martingale. Therefore, for each positive integer $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \mathbf { \eta } ^ { n } ; \mathbf { \delta } }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {1 = M (0) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} M (n)} \\ & {\quad = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {\sigma X (n \wedge \tau_ {m}) - \lambda (n \wedge \tau_ {m})} \right]} \\ & {\quad = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda \tau_ {m}} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} \leq n \}} \right] + \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {\sigma X (n) - \lambda n} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} > n \}} \right].} \end{array}\tag{8.3.4}
$$

The nonnegative random variables $e ^ { \sigma m - \lambda \tau _ { m } } \mathbb { I } _ { \{ \tau _ { m } \leq n \} }$ increase with $\mathbf { \delta } _ { \mathbf { \eta } ^ { n , } }$ , and their limit is $e ^ { \sigma m - \lambda \tau _ { m } } \mathbb { I } _ { \{ \tau _ { m } < \infty \} }$ <sub>0</sub> In other words, 

$$
0 \leq e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda \tau_ {m}} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} \leq 1 \}} \leq e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda \tau_ {m}} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} \leq 2 \}} \leq \dots \text { almost   surely },
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda \tau_ {m}} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} \leq n \}} = e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda \tau_ {m}} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} <   \infty \}} \text {   almost   surely.   }
$$

The Monotone Convergence Theorem, Theorem 1 .4.5, implies 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda \tau_ {m}} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} \leq n \}} \right] = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda \tau_ {m}} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} <   \infty \}} \right].\tag{8.3.5}
$$

On the other hand, the random variable $e ^ { \sigma X ( n ) - \lambda n } \mathbb { I } _ { \{ \tau _ { m } > n \} }$ satisfies 

$$
0 \leq e ^ {\sigma X (n) - \lambda n} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} > n \}} \leq e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda n} \leq e ^ {\sigma m} \text {   almost   surely }
$$

because $X ( n ) \leq m$ for $n < \tau _ { m }$ and $\pmb { \sigma }$ is positive. Because A is positive, we have 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} e ^ {\sigma X (n) - \lambda n} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} > n \}} \leq \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda n} = 0.
$$

According to the Dominated Convergence Theorem, Theorem 1 .4.9, 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mathbb {E} \left[ e ^ {\sigma X (n) - \lambda n} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} > n \}} \right] = 0.\tag{8.3.6}
$$

Taking the limit in (8.3.4) and using (8.3.5) and (8.3.6) , we obtain 

$$
1 = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {\sigma m - \lambda \tau_ {m}} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} <   \infty \}} \right]

or, equivalently, 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- \lambda \tau_ {m}} \mathbb {I} _ {\{\tau_ {m} <   \infty \}} \right] = e ^ {- \sigma m} = e ^ {- m (- \mu + \sqrt {\mu^ {2} + 2 \lambda})} \text {   for   all   } \lambda > 0.\tag{8.3.7}
$$

This is (8.3.3) when we interpret $e ^ { - \lambda \tau _ { m } }$ to be zero if $\tau _ { m } = \infty$ 

Remark 8. 3. 3. We used the strict positivity of <sub>A</sub> to derive (8.3.7) , but now that we have it, we can take the limit as $\lambda \downarrow 0 .$ . The random variables $e ^ { - \lambda \tau _ { m } } \mathbb { I } _ { \{ \tau _ { m } < \infty \} }$ are nonnegative and increase to $\mathbb { I } _ { \{ \tau _ { m } < \infty \} }$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0 ,$ , and the Monotone Convergence Theorem allows us to conclude that

On the other hand, if $\mu < 0 ,$ the drift in $X ( t )$ is downward, away from level $m ,$ and $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } \{ \tau _ { m } < \infty \} =$ $\left. e ^ { - 2 m | \mu | } < 1 \right.$ ; there is a positive probability of never reaching <sub>m.</sub> 0 

The solution to (8.3 . 1 ) is 

$$
S (t) = S (0) \exp \left\{\sigma \widetilde {W} (t) + \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) t \right\}.\tag{8.3.8}

Suppose the owner of the perpetual American put sets a positive level $L < K$ and resolves to exercise the put the first time the stock price falls to L. If the initial stock price is at or below $L ,$ she exercises immediately (at time zero<sub>)</sub> . The value of the put in this case is $v _ { L } ( S ( 0 ) ) = K - S ( 0 )$ . If the initial stock price is above $L ,$ she exercises at the stopping time 

$$

$$

where $\tau _ { L }$ is set equal to o if the stock price never reaches the level L. At the time of exercise, the put pays $K - S ( \tau _ { L } ) = K - L .$ . Discounting this back to time zero and taking the risk-neutral expected value, we compute the value of the put under this exercise strategy to be 

$$

On those paths where $\tau _ { L } = \infty ,$ , we interpret $e ^ { - r \tau _ { L } }$ to be zero. <sub>(</sub>Recall our assumption at the beginning of this section that $\pmb { r }$ is strictly positive. ) Although not explicitly indicated by the notation, the distribution of $\tau _ { L }$ depends on the initial stock price $S ( 0 )$ , so the right-hand side (8.3. 10) is a function of S(O) . 

Lemma 8.3.4. The function ${ \pmb v } _ { L } ( { \pmb x } )$ is given b y the formula

v _ {L} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} K - x, & 0 \leq x \leq L, \\ (K - L) \left(\frac {x}{L}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}}}, & x \geq L. \end{array} \right.\tag{8.3.11}

$$
S (t) = x \exp \left\{\sigma \widetilde {W} (t) + \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) \right\}

$$

With these replacements, $\tau _ { m }$ in Theorem 8.3.2 is $\tau _ { L }$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mu^ {2} + 2 \lambda & = \frac {1}{\sigma^ {2}} \left(r ^ {2} - r \sigma^ {2} + \frac {1}{4} \sigma^ {4}\right) + 2 r \\ & = \frac {1}{\sigma^ {2}} \left(r ^ {2} + r \sigma^ {2} + \frac {1}{4} \sigma^ {4}\right) \\ & = \frac {1}{\sigma^ {2}} \left(r + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) ^ {2}. \end{array}

$$
- \mu + \sqrt {\mu^ {2} + 2 \lambda} = \frac {1}{\sigma} \left(r - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) + \frac {1}{\sigma} \left(r + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) = \frac {2 r}{\sigma}.
$$

Equation (8.3.3) implies 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} ^ {- r \tau_ {L}} = \exp \left\{- \frac {1}{\sigma} \log \frac {x}{L} \cdot \frac {2 r}{\sigma} \right\} = \left(\frac {x}{L}\right) ^ {- \frac {2 r}{\sigma^ {2}}}.
$$

The second line in (8.3. 1 1 ) follows.
