Term-Structure Models 

## 10. 1 Introduction

Real markets do not have a single interest rate. Instead, they have bonds of different maturities, some paying coupons and others not paying coupons. From these bonds, yields to diferent maturities can be implied. More specifically, let $0 = T _ { 0 } < T _ { 1 } < T _ { 2 } < \cdots < T _ { n }$ be a given set of dates, and let $B ( 0 , T _ { j } )$ denote the price at time zero of a zero-coupon bond paying 1 at maturity $T _ { j }$ . Consider a coupon-paying bond that makes fixed payments $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 } , \ldots , C _ { j }$ at dates $T _ { 1 } , T _ { 2 } , \ldots , T _ { j }$ , respectively. Each of the numbers $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 } , \dots , C _ { j - 1 }$ represents a coupon (interest payment) , and $C _ { j }$ represents the interest plus principal paid at the maturity $T _ { j }$ of the bond. The price of this bond at time zero can be decomposed as 

$$
\sum_ {j = i} ^ {j} C _ {i} B (0, T _ {i}).\tag{10.1.1}
$$

On the other hand, if one is given the price of a coupon-paying bond of each maturity $T _ { 1 } , T _ { 2 } , \ldots , T _ { n }$ , then using (10. 1 . 1 ) one can solve recursively for $B ( 0 , T _ { 1 } ) , \ldots , B ( 0 , T _ { n } )$ by first observing that $B ( 0 , T _ { 1 } )$ is the price of the $\scriptstyle { \mathbf { } } T _ { 1 } -$ maturity bond divided by the payment it will make at $T _ { 1 }$ , then using this value of $B ( 0 , T _ { 1 } )$ and the price of the T2-maturity bond to solve for $B ( 0 , T _ { 2 } )$ and continuing in this manner. This method of determining zero-coupon bond prices from coupon-paying bond prices is called botstrapping. 

In any event, from market data one can ultimately determine prices of zerocoupon bonds for a number of diferent maturity dates. Each of these bonds has a yield specific to its maturity, where yield is defined to be the constant continuously compounding interest rate over the lifetime of the bond that is consistent with its price: 

$$
\text { price   of   zero - coupon   bond } = \text { face   value } \times e ^ {- \text { yield } \times \text { time   to   maturity }}.
$$

The face value of a zero-coupon bond is the amount it promises to pay upon maturity. The formula above implies that capital equal to the price of the bond, invested at a continuously compounded interest rate equal to the yield would, over the lifetime of the bond, result in a final payment of the face value. In this chapter, we shall normalize zero-coupon bonds by taking the face value to be 1 . 

In summary, instead of having a single interest rate, real markets have a yield curve, which one can regard either as a function of finitely many yields plotted versus their corresponding maturities or more often as a function of a nonnegative real variable (time) obtained by interpolation from the finitely many maturity-yield pairs provided by the market. The interest rate (sometimes called the short mte) is an idealization corresponding to the shortestmaturity yield or perhaps the overnight rate ofered by the government, depending on the particular application. 

We assume throughout this chapter that the bonds have no risk of default. One generally regards U.S. government bonds to be nondefaultable. 

Models for interest rates have already appeared in this text, most notably in Section 6.5, where the partial diferential equation satisfied by zero-coupon bonds in a one-factor short-rate model was developed and the Hull-White and Cox-Ingersoll-Ross models were given as examples. In Section 10.2 of this chapter, we extend these models to permit finitely many factors. These are Markov models in which the state of the model at each time is a multidimensional vector. 

Unlike the models for equities considered heretofore and the Heath-Jarrow-Morton model considered later, the multifactor models in Section 10.2 do not immediately provide a mechanism for evolution of the prices of tradeable assets. In the earlier models , we assume an evolution of the price of a primary asset or the prices of multiple primary assets under the actual measure and then determine the market prices of risk that enable us to switch to a riskneutral measure. In the multifactor models of Section 10.2, we begin with the evolution of abstract "factors," and from these the interest rate is obtained. But the interest rate is not the price of an asset, and we cannot infer a market price of risk from the interest rate alone. If we also had prices of some primary assets, say zero-coupon bonds, we could determine market prices of risk. However, in the models of Section 10.2, the only way to get prices of zero-coupon bonds is to use the risk-neutral pricing formula, and this cannot be done until we have a risk-neutral measure. Therefore, we build these models under the risk-neutral measure from the outset. Zero-coupon bond prices are given by the risk-neutral pricing formula, which implies that discounted zero-coupon bond prices are martingales under the risk-neutral measure. This implies in turn that no arbitrage can be achieved by trading in the zero-coupon bonds and the money market. After these models are built, they are calibrated to market prices for zero-coupon bonds and probably also some fixed income derivatives. The actual probability measure and the market prices of risk never enter the picture. 

In contrast to the models of Section 10.2, the Heath-Jarrow-Morton (HJM) model takes its state at each time to be the forward curve at that time. The forward rate $\textstyle f ( t , T )$ , which is the state of the HJM model, is the instantaneous rate that can be locked in at time t for borrowing at time $T \geq t .$ For fixed t, one calls the function $T \mapsto f ( t , T )$ , defined for $T \geq t ,$ , the forward rate curve. The HJM model provides a mechanism for evolving this curve (a "curve" in the variable T) forward in time (the variable t) . The forward rate curve can be deduced from the zero-coupon bond prices, and the zero-coupon bond prices can be deduced from the forward rate curve. Because zero-coupon bond prices are given directly by the HJM model rather than indirectly by the risk-neutral pricing formula, one needs to be careful that the model does not generate prices that admit arbitrage. Hence, HJM is more than a model because it provides a necessary and suficient condition for a model driven by Brownian motion to be free of arbitrage. Every Brownian-motion-driven model must satisfy the HJM no-arbitrage condition, and to illustrate that point we provide Exercise 10. 10 to verify that the Hull-White and Cox-Ingersoll-Ross models satisfy this condition. 

For practical applications, it would be convenient to build a model where the forward rate had a log-normal distribution. Unfortunately, this is not possible. However, if one instead models the simple interest rate $L ( t , T )$ that one can lock in at time t for borrowing over the interval T to $T { + } \delta$ , where 8 is a positive constant, this problem can be overcome. We call $L ( t , T )$ forward LIBOR (London interbank ofered rate). The constant 8 is typically 0.25 (three-month LIBOR) or 0.50 (six-month LIBOR) . The model that takes forward LIBOR as its state is often called the forward LIBOR model, the market model, or the Brace- Gatarek-Musiela (BGM) model. It is presented in Section 10.4. 

## 10.2 Afine-Yield Models

The one-factor Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and Hull-White models appearing in Section 6.5 are called afine-yield models because in these models the yield for zero-coupon bond prices is an afine (linear plus constant) function of the interest rate. In this section, we develop the two-factor, constant-coeficient versions of these models. (The constant-coeficient version of the Hull-White model is the Vasicek model. ) Models with three or more factors can be developed along the lines of the two-factor models of this section. 

It turns out that there are essentially three diferent two-factor afine-yield models, one in which both factors have constant difusion terms (and hence are Gaussian processes, taking negative values with positive probability) , one in which both factors appear under the square root in difusion terms (and hence must be nonnegative at all times), and one in which only one factor appears under the square root in the difusion terms (and only this factor is nonnegative at all times, whereas the other factor can become negative) . We shall call these the two-factor Vasicek, the two-factor CIR, and the two-factor mixed term-structure models, respectively. For each of these types of models, there is a canonical model (i.e. , a simplest way of writing the model) . 

Two-factor afne yield-models appearing in the literature, which often seem to be more complicated than the canonical models of this section, can always be obtained from one of the three canonical models by changing variables. It is desirable when calibrating a model to first change the variables to put the model into a form having the minimum number of parameters; otherwise, the calibration can be confounded by the fact that multiple sets of parameters yield the same result. The canonical models presented here have the minimmu number of parameters. 

## 10.2.1 Two-Factor Vasicek Model

For the two-factor Vasicek model, we let the factors $X _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $X _ { 2 } ( t )$ be given by the system of stochastic diferential equations 

$$
d X _ {1} (t) = \left(a _ {1} - b _ {1 1} X _ {1} (t) - b _ {1 2} X _ {2} (t)\right) d t + \sigma_ {1} d \widetilde {B} _ {1} (t),\tag{10.2.1}
$$

$$
d X _ {1} (t) = \left(a _ {2} - b _ {2 1} X _ {1} (t) - b _ {2 2} X _ {2} (t)\right) d t + \sigma_ {2} d \widetilde {B} _ {2} (t),\tag{10.2.2}
$$

where the processes $\widetilde { B } _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $\widetilde { B } _ { 2 } ( t )$ are Brownian motions under a riskneutral measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ with constant correlation $\nu \in ( - 1 , 1 ) \ ( \mathrm { i . e . , } \ d \widetilde { B } _ { 1 } ( t ) d \widetilde { B } _ { 2 } ( t ) =$ $\nu d t )$ . The constants $\sigma _ { 1 }$ and $\sigma _ { 2 }$ are assumed to be strictly positive. We further assume that the matrix 

$$
B = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} b _ {1 1} & b _ {1 2} \\ b _ {2 1} & b _ {2 2} \end{array} \right]
$$

has strictly positive eigenvalues $\lambda _ { 1 }$ and $\lambda _ { 2 }$ . The positivity of these eigenvalues causes the factors $X _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $X _ { 2 } ( t )$ , as well as the canonical factors $Y _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $Y _ { 2 } ( t )$ defined below, to be mean-reverting. Finally, we assume the interest rate is an afine function of the factors, 

$$
R (t) = \epsilon_ {0} + \epsilon_ {1} X _ {1} (t) + \epsilon_ {2} X _ {2} (t),\tag{10.2.3}
$$

where $\epsilon _ { 0 } , \epsilon _ { 1 }$ , and $\epsilon _ { 2 }$ are constants. This is the most general two-factor Vasicek model. 

## Canonical Form

As presented above, the two-factor Vasicek model is "overparametrized" (i.e. , diferent choices of the parameters $a _ { i } , \ b _ { i j } , \ \sigma _ { i }$ , and $\epsilon _ { i }$ can lead to the same distribution for the process $R ( t ) )$ . To eliminate this overparametrization, we reduce the model ( 10.2. 1)-(10.2.3) to the canonical two-factor Vasicek model 

$$
d Y _ {1} (t) = - \lambda_ {1} Y _ {1} (t) d t + d \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t),\tag{10.2.4}
$$

$$
d Y _ {2} (t) = - \lambda_ {2 1} Y _ {1} (t) d t - \lambda_ {2} Y _ {2} (t) d t + d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t),\tag{10.2.5}
$$

$$
R (t) = \delta_ {0} + \delta_ {1} Y _ {1} (t) + \delta_ {2} Y _ {2} (t),\tag{10.2.6}
$$

where $\widetilde { W } _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $\widetilde { W } _ { 2 } ( t )$ are independent Brownian motions. 

The canonical two-factor Vasicek model has six parameters: 

$$
\lambda_ {1} > 0, \lambda_ {2} > 0, \lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {0}, \delta_ {1}, \delta_ {2}.
$$

The parameters are used to calibrate the model. In practice, one often permits some of these parameters to be time-varying but nonrandom in order to make the model fit the initial yield curve; see Exercise 10.3. 

To achieve this reduction, we first transform $B$ to its Jordan canonical form by choosing a nonsingular matrix 

$$
P = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} p _ {1 1} & p _ {1 2} \\ p _ {2 1} & p _ {2 2} \end{array} \right]
$$

such that 

$$
K = P B P ^ {- 1} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & 0 \\ \kappa & \lambda_ {2} \end{array} \right].
$$

If $\lambda _ { 1 } \neq \lambda _ { 2 }$ , then the columns of $P ^ { - 1 }$ are eigenvectors of B and $\pmb { \kappa } = \mathbf { 0 } \ ( \mathrm { i . e . , } \ K$ is diagonal) . If $\lambda _ { 1 } = \lambda _ { 2 }$ , then K might be zero, but it can also happen that $\kappa \neq 0 ,$ in which case we may choose P so that $\kappa = 1$ . Using the notation 

$$
X (t) = \left[ \begin{array}{c} X _ {1} (t) \\ X _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right], A = \left[ \begin{array}{c} a _ {1} \\ a _ {2} \end{array} \right], \Sigma = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \sigma_ {1} & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_ {2} \end{array} \right], \widetilde {B} (t) = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \widetilde {B} _ {1} (t) \\ \widetilde {B} _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right],
$$

we may rewrite ( 10.2. 1 ) and ( 10.2.2) in vector notation: 

$$
d X (t) = A d t - B X (t) d t + \Sigma d \widetilde {B} (t).
$$

Multiplying both sides by P and defining $\overline { { X } } ( t ) = P X ( t )$ , we obtain 

$$
d \overline {{X}} (t) = P A d t - K \overline {{X}} (t) d t + P \Sigma d \widetilde {B} (t),
$$

which can be written componentwise as 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \overline {{X}} _ {1} (t) = (p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2}) d t - \lambda_ {1} \overline {{X}} _ {1} (t) d t} \\ & {\qquad + p _ {1 1} \sigma_ {1} d \widetilde {B} _ {1} (t) + p _ {1 2} \sigma_ {2} d \widetilde {B} _ {2} (t),} \\ & {d \overline {{X}} _ {2} (t) = (p _ {2 1} a _ {1} + p _ {2 2} a _ {2}) d t - \kappa \overline {{X}} _ {1} (t) d t - \lambda_ {2} \overline {{X}} _ {2} (t) d t} \\ & {\qquad + p _ {2 1} \sigma_ {1} d \widetilde {B} _ {1} (t) + p _ {2 2} \sigma_ {2} d \widetilde {B} _ {2} (t).} \end{array}\tag{10.2.7}
$$

( 10.2.8) 

Lemma 10.2. 1 . Under our assumptions that $\sigma _ { 1 } > 0 , \sigma _ { 2 } > 0 , - 1 < \nu < 1$ and P is nonsingular, we have 

$$
\gamma_ {i} = p _ {i 1} ^ {2} \sigma_ {1} ^ {2} + 2 \nu p _ {i 1} p _ {i 2} \sigma_ {1} \sigma_ {2} + p _ {i 2} ^ {2} \sigma_ {2} ^ {2}, \quad i = 1, 2,\tag{10.2.9}
$$

are strictly positive, and 

$$
\rho = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1} \gamma_ {2}}} \big (p _ {1 1} p _ {2 1} \sigma_ {1} ^ {2} + \nu (p _ {1 1} p _ {2 2} + p _ {1 2} p _ {2 1}) \sigma_ {1} \sigma_ {2} + p _ {1 2} p _ {2 2} \sigma_ {2} ^ {2} \big)\tag{10.2.10}
$$

is in ( - 1 , 1 ) . 

PROOF: Because $\pmb { \nu } \in ( - 1 , 1 )$ , the matrix 

$$
N = \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \nu \\ \nu & 1 \end{array} \right]
$$

has a matrix square root. Indeed, one such square root is 

$$
\sqrt {N} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} a & \sqrt {1 - a ^ {2}} \\ \sqrt {1 - a ^ {2}} & a \end{array} \right],
$$

where $a = \mathrm { s i g n } ( \nu ) \sqrt { { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } + { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \sqrt { 1 - \nu ^ { 2 } } } $ • Verification of this uses the equation 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} 2 a \sqrt {1 - a ^ {2}} & = 2 \mathrm{sign} (\nu) \sqrt {\frac {1}{2} + \frac {1}{2} \sqrt {1 - \nu^ {2}}} \cdot \sqrt {\frac {1}{2} - \frac {1}{2} \sqrt {1 - \nu^ {2}}} \\ & = 2 \mathrm{sign} (\nu) \sqrt {\frac {1}{4} - \frac {1}{4} (1 - \nu^ {2})} \\ & = 2 \mathrm{sign} (\nu) \cdot \frac {1}{2} | \nu | = \nu . \end{array}
$$

The matrices $\sqrt { N } , \Sigma$ , and $P ^ { \mathrm { t r } }$ are nonsingular, which implies nonsingularity of the matrix 

$$
\sqrt {N} \Sigma P ^ {\mathrm{tr}} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} p _ {1 1} \sigma_ {1} a + p _ {1 2} \sigma_ {2} \sqrt {1 - a ^ {2}} & p _ {2 1} \sigma_ {1} a + p _ {2 2} \sigma_ {2} \sqrt {1 - a ^ {2}} \\ p _ {1 1} \sigma_ {1} \sqrt {1 - a ^ {2}} + p _ {1 2} \sigma_ {2} a & p _ {2 1} \sigma_ {1} \sqrt {1 - a ^ {2}} + p _ {2 2} \sigma_ {2} a \end{array} \right].
$$

Let $c _ { 1 }$ be the first column of this matrix and $c _ { 2 }$ the second column. Because of the nonsingularity of $\sqrt { N } \Sigma P ^ { \mathrm { t r } }$ , these vectors are linearly independent, and hence neither of them is the zero vector, 

Therefore, 

$$
\gamma_ {i} = \left\| c _ {i} \right\| ^ {2} > 0, \quad i = 1, 2.
$$

For linearly independent vectors, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality implies 

$$
- \left\| c _ {1} \right\| \left\| c _ {2} \right\| <   c _ {1} \cdot c _ {2} <   \left\| c _ {1} \right\| \left\| c _ {2} \right\|.
$$

This is equivalent to $- 1 < \rho < 1$ 

We define 

$$
\overline {{{B}}} _ {i} (t) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {i}}} \bigl (p _ {i 1} \sigma_ {1} \widetilde {B} _ {1} (t) + p _ {i 2} \sigma_ {2} \widetilde {B} _ {2} (t) \bigr), \quad i = 1, 2.
$$

The processes $\overline { { B } } _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $\overline { { B } } _ { 2 } ( t )$ are continuous martingales starting at zero. Furthermore, 

$$
d \overline {{{B}}} _ {1} (t) d \overline {{{B}}} _ {1} (t) = d \overline {{{B}}} _ {2} (t) d \overline {{{B}}} _ {2} (t) = d t.
$$

According to Levy's Theorem, Theorem 4.6.4, $\overline { { B } } _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $\overline { { B } } _ { 2 } ( t )$ are Brownian motions. Furthermore, 

$$
d \overline {{{B}}} _ {1} (t) d \overline {{{B}}} _ {2} (t) = \rho d t,
$$

where $\rho$ is defined by ( 10.2.10). We may rewrite ( 10.2.7) and ( 10.2.8) as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \overline {{X}} _ {1} (t) = (p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2})   d t - \lambda_ {1} \overline {{X}} _ {1} (t)   d t + \sqrt {\gamma_ {1}}   d \overline {{B}} _ {1} (t), \\ d \overline {{X}} _ {2} (t) = (p _ {2 1} a _ {1} + p _ {2 2} a _ {2})   d t - \kappa \overline {{X}} _ {1} (t)   d t - \lambda_ {2} \overline {{X}} _ {2} (t)   d t + \sqrt {\gamma_ {2}}   d \overline {{B}} _ {2} (t). \end{array}\tag{10.2.11}
$$

( 10. 2 . 1 2) 

Setting 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widehat {X} _ {1} (t) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1}}} \left(\overline {{X}} _ {1} (t) - \frac {p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}\right), \\ \widehat {X} _ {2} (t) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {2}}} \left(\overline {{X}} _ {2} (t) + \frac {\kappa (p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2})}{\lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {2}} - \frac {p _ {2 1} a _ {1} + p _ {2 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {2}}\right), \end{array}
$$

we may further rewrite ( 10.2. 1 1 ) and ( 10.2. 12) as 

$$
d \widehat {X} _ {1} (t) = - \lambda_ {1} \widehat {X} _ {1} (t) d t + d \overline {{{B}}} _ {1} (t),\tag{10.2.13}
$$

$$
d \widehat {X} _ {2} (t) = - \kappa \sqrt {\frac {\gamma_ {1}}{\gamma_ {2}}} \widehat {X} _ {1} (t) d t - \lambda_ {2} \widehat {X} _ {2} (t) d t + d \overline {{{B}}} _ {2} (t).\tag{10.2.14}
$$

As the last step, we define 

$$
\widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) = \overline {{B}} _ {1} (t), \quad \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2}}} \big [ - \rho \overline {{B}} _ {1} (t) + \overline {{B}} _ {2} (t) \big ].
$$

Both $\widetilde { W } _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $\widetilde { W } _ { 2 } ( t )$ are continuous martingales, and it is easily verified that 

$$
d \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) d \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) = d t, \quad d \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) = 0, \quad d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) = d t.
$$

According to Levy's Theorem, Theorem 4.6.4, $\widetilde { W } _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $\widetilde { W } _ { 2 } ( t )$ are independent Brownian motions. Setting 

$$
Y _ {1} (t) = \widehat {X} _ {1} (t), \quad Y _ {2} (t) = \frac {- \rho \widehat {X} _ {1} (t) + \widehat {X} _ {2} (t)}{\sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2}}},
$$

we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d Y _ {2} (t) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2}}} \left[ - \rho d \widehat {X} _ {1} (t) + d \widehat {X} _ {2} (t) \right] \\ = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2}}} \left[ \left(\rho \lambda_ {1} - \kappa \sqrt {\frac {\gamma_ {1}}{\gamma_ {2}}}\right) \widehat {X} _ {1} (t) - \lambda_ {2} \widehat {X} _ {2} (t) \right] d t \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2}}} \left[ - \rho d \overline {{B}} _ {1} (t) + d \overline {{B}} _ {2} (t) \right] \\ = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2}}} \left(\rho \lambda_ {1} - \rho \lambda_ {2} - \kappa \sqrt {\frac {\gamma_ {1}}{\gamma_ {2}}}\right) Y _ {1} (t) d t - \lambda_ {2} Y _ {2} (t) d t + d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t). \end{array}
$$

We may thus rewrite ( 10.2. 13) and ( 10.2. 14) as 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d Y _ {1} (t) = - \lambda_ {1} Y _ {1} (t) d t + d \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t),} \\ & {d Y _ {2} (t) = - \lambda_ {2 1} Y _ {1} (t) d t - \lambda_ {2} Y _ {2} (t) d t + d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t),} \end{array}
$$

where 

$$
\lambda_ {2 1} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2}}} \left(- \rho \lambda_ {1} + \rho \lambda_ {2} + \kappa \sqrt {\frac {\gamma_ {1}}{\gamma_ {2}}}\right).
$$

These are the canonical equations ( 10.2.4) and (10.2.5) . 

To obtain ( 10.2.6) , we trace back through the changes of variables: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y _ {1} (t) = \widehat {X} _ {1} (t) \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1}}} \left(\overline {{X}} _ {1} (t) - \frac {p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}\right) \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1}}} \left(p _ {1 1} X _ {1} (t) + p _ {1 2} X _ {2} (t) - \frac {p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}\right), \\ Y _ {2} (t) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {1 - \rho^ {2}}} \big (- \rho \widehat {X} _ {1} (t) + \widehat {X} _ {2} (t) \big) \\ \qquad = - \frac {\rho}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1} (1 - \rho^ {2})}} \left(\overline {{X}} _ {1} (t) - \frac {p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}\right) \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {2} (1 - \rho^ {2})}} \left(\overline {{X}} _ {2} (t) + \frac {\kappa (p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2})}{\lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {2}} - \frac {p _ {2 1} a _ {1} + p _ {2 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {2}}\right) \\ \qquad = - \frac {\rho}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1} (1 - \rho^ {2})}} \left(p _ {1 1} X _ {1} (t) + p _ {1 2} X _ {2} (t) - \frac {p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}\right) \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {2} (1 - \rho^ {2})}} \left(p _ {2 1} X _ {1} (t) + p _ {2 2} X _ {2} (t) + \frac {\kappa (p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2})}{\lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {2}} - \frac {p _ {2 1} a _ {1} + p _ {2 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {2}}\right). \end{array}
$$

In vector notation, 

$$
Y (t) = \Gamma \bigl (P X (t) + V \bigr),\tag{10.2.15}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{r l r} & & {Y (t) = \left[ \begin{array}{l} Y _ {1} (t) \\ Y _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right], \quad \varGamma = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1}}} & 0 \\ - \frac {\rho}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {1} (1 - \rho^ {2})}} & \frac {1}{\sqrt {\gamma_ {2} (1 - \rho^ {2}}} \end{array} \right],} \\ & & {V = \left[ \begin{array}{c} - \frac {p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}} \\ \frac {\kappa (p _ {1 1} a _ {1} + p _ {1 2} a _ {2})}{\lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {2}} - \frac {p _ {2 1} a _ {1} + p _ {2 2} a _ {2}}{\lambda_ {2}} \end{array} \right].} \end{array}
$$

We solve ( 10.2.15) for $X ( t )$ : 

$$
X (t) = P ^ {- 1} \left(\Gamma^ {- 1} Y (t) - V\right).
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {R (t) = \epsilon_ {0} + [ \epsilon_ {1} \epsilon_ {2} ] X (t)} \\ & {\qquad = \epsilon_ {0} + [ \epsilon_ {1} \epsilon_ {2} ] P ^ {- 1} \Gamma^ {- 1} Y (t) - [ \epsilon_ {1} \epsilon_ {2} ] P ^ {- 1} V} \\ & {\qquad = \delta_ {0} + [ \delta_ {1} \delta_ {2} ] Y (t),} \end{array}
$$

where 

$$
\delta_ {0} = \epsilon_ {0} - [ \epsilon_ {1} \epsilon_ {2} ] P ^ {- 1} V, \quad [ \delta_ {1} \delta_ {2} ] = [ \epsilon_ {1} \epsilon_ {2} ] P ^ {- 1} \Gamma^ {- 1}.
$$

We have obtained ( 10.2.6) . 

## Bond Prices

We derive the formula for zero-coupon bond prices in the canonical two-factor Vasicek model. According to the risk-neutral pricing formula, the price at time t of a zero-coupon bond paying 1 at a later time $_ { T }$ is 

$$
B (t, T) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} R (u) d u} \mid \mathcal {F} (t) \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.
$$

Because $R ( t )$ given by ( 10.2.6) is a function of the factors $Y _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $Y _ { 2 } ( t )$ and the solution of the system of stochastic diferential equations ( 10.2.4) and {10.2.5) is Markov, there must be some function $f ( t , y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } )$ such that 

$$
B (t, T) = f \big (t, Y _ {1} (t), Y _ {2} (t) \big).\tag{10.2.16}
$$

The discount factor $D ( t ) ~ = ~ e ^ { - \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } R ( u ) d u }$ satisfies $d D ( t ) \ = \ - R ( t ) D ( t )$ dt (se (5.2.18) ) . Iterated conditioning implies that the discounted bond price $D ( t ) B ( t , T )$ is a martingale under ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } .$ Therefore, the diferential of $D ( t ) B ( t , T )$ has dt term zero. We compute this diferential: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \big (D (t) B (t, T) \big) \\ = d \Big (D (t) f \big (t, Y _ {1} (t), Y _ {2} (t) \big) \Big) \\ = - R (t) D (t) f \big (t, Y _ {1} (t), Y _ {2} (t) \big) d t + D (t) d f \big (t, Y _ {1} (t), Y _ {2} (t) \big) \\ = D \left[ - R f d t + f _ {t} d t + f _ {y _ {1}} d Y _ {1} + f _ {y _ {2}} d Y _ {2} \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{2} f _ {y _ {1} y _ {1}} d Y _ {1} d Y _ {1} + f _ {y _ {1} y _ {2}} d Y _ {1} d Y _ {2} + \frac {1}{2} f _ {y _ {2} y _ {2}} d Y _ {2} d Y _ {2} \right]. \end{array}\tag{10.2.17}
$$

We use equations (10.2.4)-( 10.2.6) to take the next step: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \big (D (t) B (t, T) \big) \\ = D \left[ - (\delta_ {0} + \delta_ {1} Y _ {1} + \delta_ {2} Y _ {2}) f + f _ {t} - \lambda_ {1} Y _ {1} f _ {y _ {1}} - \lambda_ {2 1} Y _ {1} f _ {y _ {2}} \right. \\ \left. - \lambda_ {2} Y _ {2} f _ {y _ {2}} + \frac {1}{2} f _ {y _ {1} y _ {1}} + \frac {1}{2} f _ {y _ {2} y _ {2}} \right] d t + D \left[ f _ {y _ {1}} d \widetilde {W} _ {1} + f _ {y _ {2}} d \widetilde {W} _ {2} \right]. \end{array}
$$

Setting the dt term equal to zero, we obtain the partial diferential equation 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & - (\delta_ {0} + \delta_ {1} y _ {1} + \delta_ {2} y _ {2}) f (t, y _ {1}, y _ {2}) + f _ {t} (t, y _ {1}, y _ {2}) \\ & \quad - \lambda_ {1} y _ {1} f _ {y _ {1}} (t, y _ {1}, y _ {2}) - \lambda_ {2 1} y _ {1} f _ {y _ {2}} (t, y _ {1}, y _ {2}) - \lambda_ {2} y _ {2} f _ {y _ {2}} (t, y _ {1}, y _ {2}) \\ & \quad + \frac {1}{2} f _ {y _ {1} y _ {1}} (t, y _ {1}, y _ {2}) + \frac {1}{2} f _ {y _ {2} y _ {2}} (t, y _ {1}, y _ {2}) = 0 \end{array}\tag{10.2.18}
$$

for all $t \in [ 0 , T )$ and all $y _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { R } , y _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R }$ We have also the terminal condition 

$$
f (T, y _ {1}, y _ {2}) = 1 \text {   for   all   } y _ {1} \in \mathbb {R}, y _ {2} \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{10.2.19}
$$

To solve this equation, we seek a solution of the afine-yield form 

$$
f (t, y _ {1}, y _ {2}) = e ^ {- y _ {1} C _ {1} (T - t) - y _ {2} C _ {2} (T - t) - A (T - t)}\tag{10.2.20}
$$

for some functions $C _ { 1 } ( \tau ) , C _ { 2 } ( \tau )$ , and $A ( \tau )$ . Here we define $\tau = T - t$ to be the relative maturity (i.e. , the time until maturity) . So long as the model parameters do not depend on $\mathbf { } ^ { t , \quad }$ zero-coupon bond prices will depend on t and $_ { T }$ only through $\ast .$ The terminal condition ( 10.2. 19) implies that 

$$
C _ {1} (0) = C _ {2} (0) = A (0) = 0.\tag{10.2.21}
$$

We compute derivatives, where ' denotes diferentiation with respect to $\tau$ . We use the fact $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { d } { d t } C _ { i } ( \tau ) = C _ { i } ^ { \prime } ( \tau ) \cdot \frac { d } { d t } \tau = - C _ { i } ^ { \prime } ( \tau ) , i = 1 , 2 } \end{array}$ , and the similar equation $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { d } { d t } A ( \tau ) = - \ddot { A ^ { \prime } } ( \tau ) } \end{array}$ to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f _ {t} = [ y _ {1} C _ {1} ^ {\prime} + y _ {2} C _ {2} ^ {\prime} + A ^ {\prime} ] f, \quad f _ {y _ {1}} = - C _ {1} f, \quad f _ {y _ {2}} = - C _ {2} f, \\ f _ {y _ {1} y _ {1}} = C _ {1} ^ {2} f, \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad f _ {y _ {1} y _ {2}} = C _ {1} C _ {2} f,   f _ {y _ {2} y _ {2}} = C _ {2} ^ {2} f. \end{array}
$$

Equation (10.2. 18) becomes 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left[ (C _ {1} ^ {\prime} + \lambda_ {1} C _ {1} + \lambda_ {2 1} C _ {2} - \delta_ {1}) y _ {1} + (C _ {2} ^ {\prime} + \lambda_ {2} C _ {2} - \delta_ {2}) y _ {2} \right.} \\ & {\qquad \left. + \left(A ^ {\prime} + \frac {1}{2} C _ {1} ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2} C _ {2} ^ {2} - \delta_ {0}\right) \right] f = 0.} \end{array}\tag{10.2.22}
$$

Because (10.2.22) must hold for all $_ { y _ { 1 } }$ and $_ { y _ { 2 } }$ , the term $C _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } + \lambda C _ { 1 } + \lambda _ { 2 1 } C _ { 2 } -$ $\delta _ { 1 }$ multiplying $\pmb { y _ { 1 } }$ must be zero. If it were not , and ( 10.2.22) held for one value of $\pmb { y _ { 1 } }$ , then a change in the value of $_ { y _ { 1 } }$ would cause the equation to be violated. Similarly, the term $C _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } + \lambda _ { 2 } C _ { 2 } - \delta _ { 2 }$ multiplying $_ { y _ { 2 } }$ must be zero, and consequently the remaining term $A ^ { \prime } + { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } C _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } C _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } - \delta _ { 0 }$ must also be zero. This gives us a system of three ordinary diferential equations: 

$$
C _ {1} ^ {\prime} (\tau) = - \lambda_ {1} C _ {1} (\tau) - \lambda_ {2 1} C _ {2} (\tau) + \delta_ {1},\tag{10.2.23}
$$

$$
C _ {2} ^ {\prime} (\tau) = - \lambda_ {2} C _ {2} (\tau) + \delta_ {2},\tag{10.2.24}
$$

$$
A ^ {\prime} (\tau) = - \frac {1}{2} C _ {1} ^ {2} (\tau) - \frac {1}{2} C _ {2} ^ {2} (\tau) + \delta_ {0}.\tag{10.2.25}
$$

The solution of ( 10.2.24) satisfying the initial condition $C _ { 2 } ( 0 ) \ = \ 0$ (see ( 1 0. 2 . 2 1 ) ) is 

$$
C _ {2} (\tau) = \frac {\delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {2}} \left(1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {2} \tau}\right).\tag{10.2.26}
$$

We substitute this into ( 10.2.23) and solve using the initial condition $C _ { 1 } ( 0 ) =$ 0. In particular, ( 10.2.23) implies 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \frac {d}{d \tau} \big (e ^ {\lambda_ {1} \tau} C _ {1} (\tau) \big) & = e ^ {\lambda_ {1} \tau} \big (\lambda_ {1} C _ {1} (\tau) + C _ {1} ^ {\prime} (\tau) \big) \\ & = e ^ {\lambda_ {1} \tau} \big (- \lambda_ {2 1} C _ {2} (\tau) + \delta_ {1} \big) \\ & = e ^ {\lambda_ {1} \tau} \left(- \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {2}} \big (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {2} \tau} \big) + \delta_ {1}\right). \end{array}
$$

If $\lambda _ { 1 } \neq \lambda _ { 2 }$ , integration from 0 to T yields 

$$
C _ {1} (\tau) = \frac {1}{\lambda_ {1}} \left(\delta_ {1} - \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {2}}\right) \left(1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \tau}\right) + \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {2} \left(\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}\right)} \left(e ^ {- \lambda_ {2} \tau} - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \tau}\right).\tag{10.2.27}
$$

If $\lambda _ { 1 } = \lambda _ { 2 }$ , we obtain instead 

$$
C _ {1} (\tau) = \frac {1}{\lambda_ {1}} \left(\delta_ {1} - \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}\right) \left(1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \tau}\right) + \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}} \tau e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \tau}.\tag{10.2.28}
$$

Finally, ( 10.2.25) and the initial condition $A ( 0 ) = 0$ imply 

$$
A (\tau) = \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \left[ - \frac {1}{2} C _ {1} ^ {2} (u) - \frac {1}{2} C _ {2} ^ {2} (u) + \delta_ {0} \right] d u,\tag{10.2.29}
$$

and this can be obtained in closed form by a lengthy but straightforward computation. 

## Short Rate and Long Rate

We fix a positive relative maturity $\overline { { \tau } }$ (say, thirty years) and call the yield at time t on the zero-coupon bond with relative maturity $\overline { { \tau } } \ ( \mathrm { i . e . }$ , the bond maturing at date $t + { \overline { { \tau } } } )$ the long rate $L ( t )$ . Once we have a model for evolution of the short rate R(t) under the risk-neutral measure, then for each $t \geq 0$ the price of the $( t + \overline { { \tau } } )$ -maturity zero-coupon bond is determined by the riskneutral pricing formula, and hence the short-rate model alone determines the long rate. We cannot therefore write down an arbitrary stochastic diferential equation for the long rate. Nonetheless, in any afine-yield model, the long rate satisfies some stochastic diferential equation, and we can work out this equation. 

Consider the canonical two-factor Vasicek model. As we have seen in the previous discussion, zero-coupon bond prices in this model are of the form 

$$
B (t, T) = e ^ {- Y _ {1} (t) C _ {1} (T - t) - Y _ {2} (t) C _ {2} (T - t) - A (T - t)},
$$

where $C _ { 1 } ( \tau ) , C _ { 2 } ( \tau )$ , and $A ( \tau )$ are given by ( 10.2.26)-( 10.2.29) . Thus, the long rate at time t is 

$$
L (t) = - \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} \log B (t, t + \overline {{\tau}}) = \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} \big [ C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) Y _ {1} (t) + C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) Y _ {2} (t) + A (\overline {{\tau}}) \big ],\tag{10.2.30}
$$

which is an afne function of the canonical factors $Y _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $Y _ { 2 } ( t )$ at time t. Because the canonical factors do not have an economic interpretation, we may wish to use $R ( t )$ and $\mathbf { } L ( t )$ as the model factors. We now show how to do this, obtaining a two-factor Vasicek model of the form (10.2. 1 ) , (10.2.2) , and ( 10.2.3) , where $X _ { 1 } ( t )$ is replaced by $R ( t )$ and $X _ { 2 } ( t )$ is replaced by $\mathbf { } L ( t )$ 

We begin by writing the formulas ( 10.2.6) and ( 10.2.30) in vector notation: 

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c} R (t) \\ L (t) \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} Y _ {1} (t) \\ Y _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right] + \left[ \begin{array}{c} \delta_ {0} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} A (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right].\tag{10.2.31}
$$

We wish to solve this system for $( Y _ { 1 } ( t ) , Y _ { 2 } ( t ) )$ 

Lemma 10.2.2. The matrix 

$$
D = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right]
$$

is nonsingular if and only if $\delta _ { 2 } \neq 0$ and 

$$
(\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}) \delta_ {1} + \lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2} \neq 0.\tag{10.2.32}
$$

PROOF: Consider the function $f ( x ) = 1 - e ^ { - x } - x e ^ { - x }$ , for which $\pmb { f } ( 0 ) = \mathbf { 0 }$ and $f ^ { \prime } ( x ) = x e ^ { - x } > 0$ for all $\pmb { x } > 0 .$ . We have $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } ) > \mathbf { 0 }$ for all $\pmb { x } > 0 .$ . Define $\begin{array} { r } { h ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { x } ( 1 - e ^ { - x } ) } \end{array}$ . Since $h ^ { \prime } ( x ) = - x ^ { - 2 } f ( x )$ , which is strictly negative for all ${ \pmb x } > 0 , \hat { h ( { \pmb x } ) }$ is strictly decreasing on $( 0 , \infty )$ 

To examine the nonsingularity of $D ,$ , we consider first the case $\lambda _ { 1 } \neq \lambda _ { 2 }$ . In this case, (10.2.26) and ( 10.2.27) imply 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \det (D) & = \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} \big [ \delta_ {1} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) - \delta_ {2} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) \big ] \\ & = \frac {\delta_ {1} \delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}} \big (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}} \big) - \frac {\delta_ {1} \delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}} \big (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}} \big) \\ & \qquad + \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2} ^ {2}}{(\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}) \lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}} \big [ (\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}) \big (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}} \big) - \lambda_ {1} e ^ {\lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}} + \lambda_ {1} e ^ {\lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}} \big ] \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} = \delta_ {1} \delta_ {2} \left[ \frac {1}{\lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}} (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}}) - \frac {1}{\lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}} (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}}) \right] \\ \qquad + \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2} ^ {2}}{(\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}) \lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}} [ \lambda_ {1} (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}}) - \lambda_ {2} (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}}) ] \\ = \delta_ {2} (\delta_ {1} + \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2}}{(\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2})}) [ \frac {1}{\lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}} (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}}) - \frac {1}{\lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}} (1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}}) ] \\ = \delta_ {2} (\delta_ {1} + \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2}}{(\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2})}) [ h (\lambda_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}) - h (\lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}) ]. \end{array}
$$

Because $\lambda _ { 1 } \neq \lambda _ { 2 }$ and h i s strictly decreasing, $h ( \lambda _ { 2 } \overline { { \tau } } ) \neq h ( \lambda _ { 2 } \overline { { \tau } } )$ . The determinant of $D$ is nonzero if and only if $\delta _ { 2 } \neq 0$ and ( 10.2.32) holds. 

Next consider the case $\lambda _ { 1 } = \lambda _ { 2 }$ . In this case, ( 10.2.26) and ( 10.2.28) imply 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \det (D) = \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} \left[ \delta_ {1} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) - \delta_ {2} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) \right] \\ \qquad = \frac {\delta_ {1} \delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}} \left(1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}}\right) - \frac {\delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}} \left(\delta_ {1} - \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}\right) \left(1 - e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}}\right) - \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2} ^ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}} e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}} \\ \qquad = \frac {\lambda_ {2 1} \delta_ {2} ^ {2}}{\lambda_ {1} ^ {2} \overline {{\tau}}} f (\lambda_ {1} \overline {{\tau}}). \end{array}
$$

Because $\lambda _ { 1 } \overline { { \tau } }$ is positive, $f ( \lambda _ { 1 } { \overline { { \tau } } } )$ is not zero. In this case, (10.2.32) is equivalent to $\delta _ { 2 } \neq 0$ and $\lambda _ { 2 1 } \neq 0 .$ . The determinant of D is nonzero if and only if ( 10.2.32) holds (in which case $\delta _ { 2 } \neq 0$ and $\lambda _ { 2 1 } \neq 0 )$ 0 

Under the assumptions of Lemma 10.2.2, we can invert ( 10.2.31) to obtain 

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c} Y _ {1} (t) \\ Y _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] ^ {- 1} \left(\left[ \begin{array}{c} R (t) \\ L (t) \end{array} \right] - \left[ \begin{array}{c} \delta_ {0} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} A (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right]\right).\tag{10.2.33}
$$

We can compute the diferential in ( 10.2.31) using (10.2.4) and ( 10.2.5) . This leads to a formula in which $Y _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $Y _ { 2 } ( t )$ appear on the right-hand side, but we can then use ( 10.2.33) to rewrite the right-hand side in terms of $R ( t )$ $L ( t )$ . These steps result in the equation 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left[ \begin{array}{l} d R (t) \\ d L (t) \end{array} \right]} \\ & {= \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l} d Y _ {1} (t) \\ d Y _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right]} \\ & {= \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] (- \left[ \begin{array}{l l} \lambda_ {1} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} & \lambda_ {2} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l} Y _ {1} (t) \\ Y _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right] d t + \left[ \begin{array}{l} d \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) \\ d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right])} \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} & \lambda_ {2} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] ^ {- 1} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \delta_ {0} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} A (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] d t \\ & \quad - \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {2 1} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} & \lambda_ {2} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\over {\tau}) \end{array} \right] ^ {- 1} \left[ \begin{array}{c} R (t) \\ L (t) \end{array} \right] d t \\ & \quad + \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} d \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) \\ d \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right]. \end{array}
$$

This is the vector notation for a pair of equations of the form ( 10.2. 1 ) and ( 10.2.2) for a two-factor Vasicek model for the short rate $R ( t )$ and the long rate $\mathbf { } L ( t )$ . The parameters ${ \pmb a } _ { 1 }$ and ${ \pmb a } _ { 2 }$ appearing in ( 10.2 . 1 ) and ( 10.2.2) are given by 

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c} a _ {1} \\ a _ {2} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} & \lambda_ {2} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] ^ {- 1} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \delta_ {0} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} A (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right].
$$

The matrix B is 

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c c} b _ {1 1} & b _ {1 2} \\ b _ {2 1} & b _ {2 2} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} & \lambda_ {2} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \delta_ {1} & \delta_ {2} \\ \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) & \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \end{array} \right] ^ {- 1},
$$

and the eigenvalues of B are $\lambda _ { 1 } > 0 , \lambda _ { 2 } > 0$ . With 

$$
\sigma_ {1} = \sqrt {\delta_ {1} ^ {2} + \delta_ {2} ^ {2}}, \quad \sigma_ {2} = \frac {1}{\overline {{\tau}}} \sqrt {C _ {1} ^ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) + C _ {2} ^ {2} (\overline {{\tau}})},
$$

the processes 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\widetilde {B} _ {1} (t) = \frac {1}{\sigma_ {1}} \big (\delta_ {1} \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) + \delta_ {2} \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) \big),} \\ & {\widetilde {B} _ {2} (t) = \frac {1}{\sigma_ {2} \overline {{\tau}}} \big (C _ {1} (\overline {{\tau}}) \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) + C _ {2} (\overline {{\tau}}) \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) \big),} \end{array}
$$

are the Brownian motions appearing in (10.2. 1 ) and (10.2.2) . Finally, equation ( 10.2.3) takes the form 

$$
R (t) = 0 + 1 \cdot R (t) + 0 \cdot L (t)
$$

(i.e. , E:o <sup>=</sup> €2 <sup>=</sup> 0, €1 <sup>=</sup> 1 ) . 

## Gaussian Factor Processes

The canonical two-factor Vasicek model in vector notation is 

$$
d Y (t) = - \varLambda Y (t) + d \widetilde {W} (t),\tag{10.2.34}
$$

where 

$$
Y (t) = \left[ \begin{array}{c} Y _ {1} (t) \\ Y _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right], \quad \varLambda = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} & \lambda_ {2} \end{array} \right], \quad \widetilde {W} (t) = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \widetilde {W} _ {1} (t) \\ \widetilde {W} _ {2} (t) \end{array} \right].
$$

Recall that $\lambda _ { 1 } > 0 , \lambda _ { 2 } > 0$ . There i s a closed-form solution t o this matrix differential equation. To derive this solution, we first form the matrix exponential $e ^ { \boldsymbol { A } t }$ defined by 

$$
e ^ {\varLambda t} = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} (\varLambda t) ^ {n},
$$

where $( A t ) ^ { 0 } = I ,$ the $2 \times 2$ identity matrix. 

Lemma 10.2.3. If $\lambda _ { 1 } \neq \lambda _ { 2 }$ , then 

$$
e ^ {\varLambda t} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} e ^ {\lambda_ {1} t} & 0 \\ \frac {\lambda_ {2 1}}{\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}} \big (e ^ {\lambda_ {1} t} - e ^ {\lambda_ {2} t} \big) & e ^ {\lambda_ {2} t} \end{array} \right].\tag{10.2.35}
$$

If $\lambda _ { 1 } = \lambda _ { 2 }$ , then 

$$
e ^ {\Lambda t} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} e ^ {\lambda_ {1} t} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} t e ^ {\lambda_ {1} t} & e ^ {\lambda_ {1} t} \end{array} \right].\tag{10.2.36}

where the derivative is defined componentwise, and

where ${ e ^ { - \mathbf { \mathscr { A } } t } }$ is obtained by replacing $\lambda _ { 1 } , \lambda _ { 2 }$ , and $\lambda _ { 2 1 }$ in the formula for $e ^ { \boldsymbol { A } t }$ by $- \lambda _ { 1 } , - \lambda _ { 2 }$ , and $- \lambda _ { 2 1 }$ . respectively.

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {(\varLambda t) ^ {n + 1} = (\varLambda t) (\varLambda t) ^ {n}} \\ & {\qquad = \left[ \begin{array}{l l} \lambda_ {1} t & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} t & \lambda_ {2} t \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} (\lambda_ {1} t) ^ {n} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} t ^ {n} \frac {\lambda_ {1} ^ {n} - \lambda_ {2} ^ {n}}{\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}} & (\lambda_ {2} t) ^ {n} \end{array} \right]} \\ & {\qquad = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} (\lambda_ {1} t) ^ {n + 1} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} t ^ {n + 1} \left(\lambda_ {1} ^ {n} + \lambda_ {2} \frac {\lambda_ {1} ^ {n} - \lambda_ {2} ^ {n}}{\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}}\right) & (\lambda_ {2} t) ^ {n + 1} \end{array} \right]} \\ & {\qquad = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} (\lambda_ {1} t) ^ {n + 1} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} t ^ {n + 1} \frac {\lambda_ {1} ^ {n + 1} - \lambda_ {2} ^ {n + 1}}{\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}} & (\lambda_ {2} t) ^ {n + 1} \end{array} \right],} \end{array}
$$

which is ( 10.2.39) with n replaced by $^ { n + 1 }$ . Having thus established ( 10.2 .39) for all values of $^ { n , }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} e ^ {\varLambda t} & = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} (\varLambda t) ^ {n} \\ & = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} (\lambda_ {1} t) ^ {n} & 0 \\ \frac {\lambda_ {2 1}}{\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}} \left(\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} (\lambda_ {1} t) ^ {n} - \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} (\lambda_ {2} t) ^ {n}\right) & \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} (\lambda_ {2} t) ^ {n} \end{array} \right] \\ & = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} e ^ {\lambda_ {1} t} & 0 \\ \frac {\lambda_ {2 1}}{\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}} (e ^ {\lambda_ {1} t} - e ^ {\lambda_ {2} t}) & e ^ {\lambda_ {2} t} \end{array} \right]. \end{array}

This is ( 1 0.2.35) . 

We next consider the case $\lambda _ { 1 } = \lambda _ { 2 }$ . We claim in this case that

which is ( 10.2.40) with n replaced by $_ { n + 1 }$ . Having thus established ( 1 0.2 .40) for all values of $\mathbf { \eta } _ { n , \mathbf { \lambda } }$ , we have 

$$
e ^ {\varLambda t} = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} (\varLambda t) ^ {n} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} (\lambda_ {1} t) ^ {n} & 0 \\ \lambda_ {2 1} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {n}{n !} \lambda_ {1} ^ {n - 1} t ^ {n} & \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} (\lambda_ {1} t) ^ {n} \end{array} \right].\tag{10.2.41}

Substituting this into ( 10.2.41 ) , we obtain ( 10.2.36) . 

When $\lambda _ { 1 } \neq \lambda _ { 2 }$ , we have 

$$

$$

and 

$$
e ^ {- \Lambda t} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} t} & 0 \\ \frac {\lambda_ {2 1}}{\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {2}} \big (e ^ {- \lambda_ {1} t} - e ^ {- \lambda_ {2} t} \big) & e ^ {- \lambda_ {2} t} \end{array} \right].
$$

When $\lambda _ { 1 } = \lambda _ { 2 }$ 

$$
