## 11.5 Stochastic Calculus for Jump Processes

## 11.5.1 ItO-Doeblin Formula for One Jump Process

For a continuous-path process, the ItO-Doeblin formula is the following. Let 

$$
X ^ {c} (t) = X ^ {c} (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Gamma (s) d W (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Theta (s) d s,\tag{11.5.1}
$$

where $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( \mathfrak { s } )$ and $\pmb \theta ( \pmb s )$ are adapted processes. I n diferential notation, we write 

$$
d X ^ {c} (s) = \Gamma (s) d W (s) + \Theta (s) d s, \quad d X ^ {c} (s) d X ^ {c} (s) = \Gamma^ {2} (s) d s.
$$

Let $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } )$ be a function whose first and second derivatives are defined and continuous. Then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d f \big (X ^ {c} (s) \big) = f ^ {\prime} \big (X ^ {c} (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X ^ {c} (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) d X ^ {c} (s)} \\ & {\qquad = f ^ {\prime} \big (X ^ {c} (s) \big) \Gamma (s) d W (s) + f ^ {\prime} \big (X ^ {c} (s) \big) \Theta (s) d s} \\ & {\qquad + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X ^ {c} (s) \big) \Gamma^ {2} (s) d s.} \end{array}\tag{11.5.2}
$$

We write this in integral form as 

$$
\begin{array}{r} f (X ^ {c} (t)) = f (X ^ {c} (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime} (X ^ {c} (s)) \Gamma (s) d W (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime} (X ^ {c} (s)) \Theta (s) d s \\ + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime \prime} (X ^ {c} (s)) \Gamma^ {2} (s) d s. \end{array}
$$

We now add a right-continuous pure jump term J into ( 1 1 .5.1), setting 

$$
X (t) = X (0) + I (t) + R (t) + J (t),
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { I ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } { \varGamma ( s ) d W ( s ) } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { R ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \theta ( s ) } \end{array}$ ds. As usual, we denote by $X ^ { c } ( t ) = X ( 0 ) + I ( t ) + R ( t )$ the continuous part of $X ( t )$ . Between jumps of $^ { J , }$ the analogue of ( 1 1 .5.2) holds: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d f \big (X (s) \big) = f ^ {\prime} \big (X (s) \big)   d X (s) + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X (s) \big)   d X (s)   d X (s) \\ = f ^ {\prime} \big (X (s) \big) \Gamma (s)   d W (s) + f ^ {\prime} \big (X (s) \big) \Theta (s)   d s \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X (s) \big) \Gamma^ {2} (s)   d s \\ = f ^ {\prime} \big (X (s) \big)   d X ^ {c} (s) + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X (s) \big)   d X ^ {c} (s)   d X ^ {c} (s). \end{array}\tag{11.5.3}
$$

When there is a jump in X from $\pmb { X } ( \pmb { s } - \big )$ to $\pmb { X } ( \pmb { \mathscr { s } } )$ , there is typically also a jump in $f ( X )$ from $f ( X ( s - ) )$ to $\pmb { f } \big ( \pmb { X } ( \pmb { s } ) \big )$ . When we integrate both sides of ( 1 1 .5.3) from 0 to t, we must add in all the jumps that occur between these two times. This leads to the following theorem. 

Theorem 1 1 .5.1 (ItO-Doeblin formula for one jump process) . Let $X ( t )$ be a jump process and $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } )$ a function for which ${ f ^ { \prime } } ( x )$ and $f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x )$ are defined and continuous. Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (X (t)) = f (X (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime} (X (s)) d X ^ {c} (s) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime \prime} (X (s)) d X ^ {c} (s) d X ^ {c} (s) \\ \quad + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} [ f (X (s)) - f (X (s -)) ]. \end{array} \tag {11.5.4}
$$

PROOF: Fix $\omega \in \Omega ,$ , which fixes the path of $X$ , and let $0 < \tau _ { 1 } < \tau _ { 2 } < \cdots <$ $\tau _ { n - 1 } < t$ be the jump times in $[ 0 , t )$ of this path of the process $X$ . We set $\tau _ { 0 } = 0 ,$ which is not a jump time, and $\tau _ { n } = t .$ , which may or may not be a jump time. Whenever $u \ : < \ : v$ are both in the same interval $( \tau _ { j } , \tau _ { j + 1 } )$ , there is no jump between times u and $^ { v , }$ and the ltO-Doeblin formula ( 1 1 .5.3) for continuous processes applies. We thus have 

$$
f (X (v)) - f (X (u)) = \int_ {u} ^ {v} f ^ {\prime} (X (s)) d X ^ {c} (s) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {u} ^ {v} f ^ {\prime \prime} (X (s)) d X ^ {c} (s) d X ^ {c} (s).
$$

Letting $u \downarrow \tau _ { j }$ and $v \uparrow \tau _ { j + 1 }$ and using the right-continuity of $X ,$ , we conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f \big (X (\tau_ {j + 1} -) \big) - f \big (X (\tau_ {j}) \big) \\ = \int_ {\tau_ {j}} ^ {\tau_ {j + 1}} f ^ {\prime} \big (X (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {\tau_ {j}} ^ {\tau_ {j + 1}} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) d X ^ {c} (s). \end{array}\tag{11.5.5}
$$

(Note here that 

$$
\lim _ {v \uparrow \tau_ {j + 1}} \int_ {u} ^ {v} f ^ {\prime} (X (s)) d X ^ {c} (s) = \int_ {v} ^ {\tau_ {j + 1}} f ^ {\prime} (X (s)) d X ^ {c} (s),
$$

but this is not the case if we replace $d X ^ { c } ( s )$ by $d X ( s )$ in this equation. If we made this replacement, the jump in $X$ at time $\tau _ { j + 1 }$ would appear on the right-hand side of the equation but not on the left-hand side. It is for this reason that we integrate with respect to $d X ^ { c } ( \pmb { s } )$ in (11.5.5) .) We now add the jump in $f ( X )$ at time $\tau _ { j + 1 }$ into (1 1 .5.5) , obtaining thereby 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f \big (X (\tau_ {j + 1}) \big) - f \big (X (\tau_ {j}) \big) \\ = \int_ {\tau_ {j}} ^ {\tau_ {j + 1}} f ^ {\prime} \big (X (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {\tau_ {j}} ^ {t _ {j + 1}} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) d X ^ {c} (s) \\ \qquad + f \big (X (\tau_ {j + 1}) \big) - f \big (X (\tau_ {j + 1} -) \big). \end{array}
$$

Summing over $j = 0 , \ldots , n - 1$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f \big (X (t) \big) - f \big (X (0) \big) \\ = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ f \big (X (\tau_ {j + 1}) \big) - f \big (X (\tau_ {j}) \big) \right] \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime} \big (X (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) d X ^ {c} (s) \\ + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} \left[ f \big (X (\tau_ {j + 1}) \big) - f \big (X (\tau_ {j + 1} -) \big) \right], \end{array}
$$

which is (11 .5.4) . Note in this connection that if there is no jump at $\tau _ { n } = t$ then the last term in the sum on the right-hand side, $f \bigl ( X ( \tau _ { n } ) \bigr ) - \bar { f } \bigl ( X ( \tau _ { n } - ) \bigr )$ ， is zero. 0 

It is not always possible to rewrite ( 1 1 .5.4) in diferential form because it is not always possible to find a diferential form for the sum of jumps. We provide one case in which this can be done in the next example. 

Example 1 1 . 5. 2 (Geometric Poisson process). Consider the geometric Poisson process 

$$
S (t) = S (0) \exp \left\{N (t) \log (\sigma + 1) - \lambda \sigma t \right\} = S (0) e ^ {- \lambda \sigma t} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (t)},\tag{11.5.6}
$$

where $\sigma > - 1$ is a constant. If $\sigma > 0$ , this process jumps up and moves down between jumps; if $- 1 < \sigma < 0$ , it jumps down and moves up between jumps. We show that the process is a martingale. 

We may write $S ( t ) = S ( 0 ) f \big ( X ( t ) \big )$ , where $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { x } ) = e ^ { \pmb { x } }$ and 

$$
X (t) = N (t) \log (\sigma + 1) - \lambda \sigma t
$$

has continuous part $X ^ { c } ( t ) = - \lambda \sigma t$ and pure jump part $J ( t ) = N ( t ) \log ( \sigma + 1 )$ According t o the It6-Doeblin formula for jump processes, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S (t) = f (X (t)) \\ \quad = f (X (0)) - \lambda \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime} (X (u)) d u + \sum_ {0 <   u \leq t} [ f (X (u)) - f (X (u -)) ] \\ \quad = S (0) - \lambda \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} S (u) d u + \sum_ {0 <   u \leq t} [ S (u) - S (u -) ]. \end{array} \tag {11.5}\tag{11.5.7}
$$

If there is a jump at time u, then $S ( u ) = ( \sigma + 1 ) S ( u - \ d )$ . Therefore, 

$$
S (u) - S (u -) = \sigma S (u -)\tag{11.5.8}
$$

whenever there is a jump at time u, and of course $S ( u ) - S ( u - \Big ) = 0$ if there is no jump at time u. In either case, we have 

$$
S (u) - S (u -) = \sigma S (u -) \Delta N (u).
$$

This observation permits us to rewrite the sum on the right-hand side of ( 1 1 .5. 7) as 

$$
\sum_ {0 <   u \leq t} [ S (u) - S (u -) ] = \sum_ {0 <   u \leq t} \sigma S (u -) \Delta N (u) = \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} S (u -) d N (u).
$$

It does not matter whether we write the Riemann integral on the righthand side of ( 1 1 .5. 7) as $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } S ( u )$ du or as $\begin{array} { r l } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } S ( u - \ d s ) } \end{array}$ du. The integrands in these two integrals difer at only finitely many times, and when we integrate with respect to $d u ,$ these diferences do not matter. Therefore, we may rewrite ( 1 1 .5. 7) as 

$$
\begin{array}{c} {S (t) = S (0) - \lambda \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} S (u -) d u + \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} S (u -) d N (u)} \\ {= S (0) + \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} S (u -) d M (u),} \end{array}
$$

where M is the compensated Poisson process $M ( u ) = N ( u ) - \lambda u ,$ which is a martingale. Because the integrand $s ( u - )$ is left-continuous, Theorem 1 1 .4.5 guarantees that $S ( t )$ is a martingale. 

In this case, the ltO-Doeblin formula (11 .5.7) has a diferential form, namely, 

$$
d S (t) = \sigma S (t -) d M (t) = - \lambda \sigma S (t) d t + \sigma S (t -) d N (t).\tag{11.5.9}
$$

We were able to obtain this diferential form because in ( 1 1 .5.8) we were able to write the jump in $f ( X )$ (i.e. , the jump in $S )$ at time u in terms of $f ( X ( u - \rangle )$ (i.e. , in terms of $S ( u { - } ) )$ 0 

Corollary 11.5.3. Let $W ( t )$ be a Brownian motion and let $N ( t )$ be a Poisson process with intensity $\lambda > 0 ,$ both defined on the same probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mathbb { P } )$ and relative to the same filtration $\mathcal { F } ( t ) , t \geq 0 .$ Then the processes $W ( t )$ and $N ( t )$ are independent.

$$

$$

We use the ltO-Doeblin formula to show that $Y$ is a martingale. 

To do this, we define 

$$
X (s) = u _ {1} W (s) + u _ {2} N (s) - \frac {1}{2} u _ {1} ^ {2} s - \lambda \bigl (e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1 \bigr) s
$$

and $\begin{array} { r } { f ( \pmb { x } ) = e ^ { \pmb { x } } , } \end{array}$ , so that $Y ( s ) = f { \bigl ( } X ( s ) { \bigr ) }$ . The process $X ( s )$ has Ito integral part $I ( s ) = u _ { 1 } W ( s )$ , Riemann integral part $\begin{array} { r } { R ( s ) = - \frac 1 2 u _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } s - \lambda \big ( e ^ { u _ { 2 } } - 1 \big ) s } \end{array}$ , and pure jump part $J ( s ) = u _ { 2 } N ( s )$ . In particular, 

$$
d X ^ {c} (s) = u _ {1} d W (s) - \frac {1}{2} u _ {1} ^ {2} d s - \lambda \left(e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1\right) d s, \quad d X ^ {c} (s) d X ^ {c} (s) = u _ {1} ^ {2} d s.
$$

We next observe that if Y has a jump at time $s ,$ then 

$$
Y (s) = \exp \left\{u _ {1} W (s) + u _ {2} (N (s -) + 1) - \frac {1}{2} u _ {1} ^ {2} s - \lambda \bigl (e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1 \bigr) s \right\} = Y (s -) e ^ {u _ {2}}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Y (s) - Y (s -) = \big (e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1 \big) Y (s -) \varDelta N (s).
$$

According to the ItO-Doeblin formula for jump processes, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y (t) = f \big (X (t) \big) \\ \quad = f \big (X (0) \big) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime} \big (X (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f ^ {\prime \prime} \big (X (s) \big) d X ^ {c} (s) d X ^ {c} (s) \\ \quad + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} \big [ f \big (X (s) \big) - f \big (X (s -) \big) \big ] \\ = 1 + u _ {1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s) d W (s) - \frac {1}{2} u _ {1} ^ {2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s) d s - \lambda \big (e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1 \big) \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s) d s \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2} u _ {1} ^ {2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s) d s + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} \big [ Y (s) - Y (s -) \big ] \\ = 1 + u _ {1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s) d W (s) - \lambda \big (e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1 \big) \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s -) d s \\ \quad + \big (e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1 \big) \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s -) d N (s) \\ = 1 + u _ {1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s) d W (s) + \big (e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1 \big) \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s -) d M (s), \end{array} \tag {11.5.1}
$$

where $M ( s ) = N ( s ) - \lambda s$ is a compensated Poisson process. Here we have used the fact that because Y has only finitely many jumps, $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } Y ( s ) d s = } \end{array}$ $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } Y ( s - ) d s$ . The Ito integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } Y ( s ) d W ( s )$ in the last line of (11 .5. 10) is a martingale, and the integral of the left-continuous process $Y ( s - )$ with respect to the martingale $M ( s )$ is also. Therefore, Y is a martingale. 

Because $Y ( 0 ) = 1$ and Y is a martingale, we have $\mathbb { E } Y ( t ) = 1$ for all t. In other words, 

$$
\mathbb {E} \exp \left\{u _ {1} W (t) + u _ {2} N (t) - \frac {1}{2} u _ {1} ^ {2} t - \lambda \bigl (e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1 \bigr) t \right\} = 1 \text {for all} t \geq 0.
$$

We have obtained the joint moment-generating function formula 

$$
\mathbb {E} e ^ {u _ {1} W (t) + u _ {2} N (t)} = \exp \left\{\frac {1}{2} u _ {1} ^ {2} t \right\} \cdot \exp \left\{\lambda t \big (e ^ {u _ {2}} - 1 \big) \right\}.
$$

This is the product of the moment-generating function $\mathbb { E } e ^ { u _ { 1 } W ( t ) } = \exp \left\{ { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } u _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } t \right\}$ for $W ( t )$ (see Exercise $\mathbf { 1 . 6 ( i ) } )$ and the moment-generating function $\mathbb { E } e ^ { u _ { 2 } \bar { N } ( t ) } =$ exp $\{ \lambda \dot { t } ( e ^ { \dot { u } _ { 2 } } - 1 ) \}$ for N ( t) (see ( 1 1 .3.4)) . Since the joint moment-generating function factors into the product of moment-generating functions, the random variables $W ( t )$ and N(t) are independent. 

The corollary asserts more than the independence between N ( t) and $W ( t )$ for fixed t, saying that the processes N and W are independent (i.e., anything depending only on the path of W is independent of anything depending only on the path of N). For example, the corollary asserts that $\operatorname* { m a x } _ { 0 \leq s \leq t } W ( s )$ is independent of $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } N ( s ) } \end{array}$ ds. The first step in the proof of this st;te�ent is the one just given, which shows that the random variables $W ( t )$ and N(t) are independent of each fixed t. The next step, which we omit, is to show that for any finite set of times $0 \leq t _ { 1 } < t _ { 2 } < \cdots < t _ { n }$ , the vector of random variables $( W ( t _ { 1 } ) , W ( t _ { 2 } ) , \ldots , W ( t _ { n } ) )$ is independent of the vector of random variables $( N ( t _ { 1 } ) , N ( t _ { 2 } ) , \ldots , N ( t _ { n } ) )$ . The assertion of the corollary follows from this. 0 

## 11.5.2 ItO-Doeblin Formula for Multiple Jump Processes

There is a multidimensional version of the ItO-Doeblin formula for jump processes. We give the two-dimensional version. The formula for higher dimensions follows the same pattern. 

Theorem 11.5.4 (Two-dimensional ItO-Doeblin formula for processes with jumps) . Let $X _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $X _ { 2 } ( t )$ be jump processes, and let $f ( t , x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } )$ be a function whose first and second partial derivatives appearing in the following formula are defined and are continuous. Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f \big (t, X _ {1} (t), X _ {2} (t) \big) \\ = f \big (0, X _ {1} (0), X _ {2} (0) \big) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} f _ {t} \big (s, X _ {1} (s), X _ {2} (s) \big) d s \\ + \int_ {0} ^ {t} f _ {x _ {1}} \big (s, X _ {1} (s), X _ {2} (s) \big) d X _ {1} ^ {c} (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} f _ {x _ {2}} \big (s, X _ {1} (s), X _ {2} (s) \big) d X _ {2} ^ {c} (s) \\ + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f _ {x _ {1}, x _ {1}} \big (s, X _ {1} (s), X _ {2} (s) \big) d X _ {1} ^ {c} (s) d X _ {1} ^ {c} (s) \\ + \int_ {0} ^ {t} f _ {x _ {1}, x _ {2}} \big (s, X _ {1} (s), X _ {2} (s) \big) d X _ {1} ^ {c} (s) d X _ {2} ^ {c} (s) \\ + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f _ {x _ {2}, x _ {2}} \big (s, X _ {1} (s), X _ {2} (s) \big) d X _ {2} ^ {c} (s) d X _ {2} ^ {c} (s) \\ + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} \left[ f \big (s, X _ {1} (s), X _ {2} (s) \big) - f \big (s, X _ {1} (s -), X _ {2} (s -) \big) \right]. \end{array}
$$

Corollary 11.5.5 (Ito's product rule for jump processes) . Let $X _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $X _ { 2 } ( t )$ be jump processes. Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X _ {1} (t) X _ {2} (t) = X _ {1} (0) X _ {2} (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {2} (s) d X _ {1} ^ {c} (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {1} (s) d X _ {2} ^ {c} (s) \\ \qquad + [ X _ {1} ^ {c}, X _ {2} ^ {c} ] (t) + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} \left[ X _ {1} (s) X _ {2} (s) - X _ {1} (s -) X _ {2} (s -) \right] \\ = X _ {1} (0) X _ {2} (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {2} (s -) d X _ {1} (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {1} (s -) d X _ {2} (s) \\ \qquad + [ X _ {1}, X _ {2} ] (t). \end{array} \tag {1}\tag{11.5.11}
$$

PROOF: Take $f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) = x _ { 1 } x _ { 2 }$ so that 

$$
f _ {x _ {1}} = x _ {2}, f _ {x _ {2}} = x _ {1}, f _ {x _ {1} x _ {1}} = 0, f _ {x _ {1} x _ {2}} = 1, f _ {x _ {2} x _ {2}} = 0.
$$

The two-dimensional It6-Doeblin formula implies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X _ {1} (t) X _ {2} (t) = X _ {1} (0) X _ {2} (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {2} (s) d X _ {1} ^ {c} (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {1} (s) d X _ {2} ^ {c} (s) \\ \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} 1 d X _ {1} ^ {c} (s) d X _ {2} ^ {c} (s) + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} \Big [ X _ {1} (s) X _ {2} (s) - X _ {1} (s -) X _ {2} (s -) \Big ]. \end{array}\tag{11.5.12}
$$

The notation $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } 1 d X _ { 1 } ^ { c } ( s ) d X _ { 2 } ^ { c } ( s ) } \end{array}$ in (1 1.5. 12) means $[ X _ { 1 } ^ { c } , X _ { 2 } ^ { c } ] ( t )$ (see Remark 1 1 .4.8) . This establishes the first equality in ( 1 1 . 5. 1 1 ) . 

To obtain the second equality, we denote by $J _ { 1 } ( t ) = X _ { 1 } ( t ) - X _ { 1 } ^ { c } ( t )$ and $J _ { 2 } ( t ) = X _ { 2 } ( t ) - X _ { 2 } ^ { c } ( t )$ the pure jump parts of $X _ { 1 } ( t )$ and $X _ { 2 } ( t )$ , respectively, and begin with the last line of ( 1 1.5. 1 1) , using (1 1 .4. 12) to compute 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & X _ {1} (0) X _ {2} (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {2} (s -) d X _ {1} (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {1} (s -) d X _ {2} (s) + [ X _ {1}, X _ {2} ] (t) \\ & = X _ {1} (0) X _ {2} (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {2} (s -) d X _ {1} ^ {c} (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {2} (s -) d J _ {1} (s) \\ & \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {1} (s -) d X _ {2} ^ {c} (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {1} (s -) d J _ {2} (s) \\ & \qquad + [ X _ {1} ^ {c}, X _ {2} ^ {c} ] (t) + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} \varDelta J _ {1} (s) \varDelta J _ {2} (s) \\ & = X _ {1} (0) X _ {2} (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {2} (s) d X _ {1} ^ {c} (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {1} (s) d X _ {2} ^ {c} (s) + [ X _ {1} ^ {c}, X _ {2} ^ {c} ] (t) \\ & \qquad + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} \big [ X _ {2} (s -) \varDelta X _ {1} (s) + X _ {1} (s -) \varDelta X _ {2} (s) + \varDelta X _ {1} (s) \varDelta X _ {2} (s) \big ]. \end{array}\tag{11.5.13}
$$

We have also used the fact that the jumps in $X _ { i } ( t )$ are the same as the jumps in $J _ { i } ( t )$ . It remains to show that this last sum is the same as the sum 

$$
\sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} \left[ X _ {1} (s) X _ {2} (s) - X _ {1} (s -) X _ {2} (s -) \right]
$$

in the second line of ( 1 1 .5. 1 1 ) . We expand the typical term in the sum in the second line of ( 1 1 .5. 1 1 ) : 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X _ {1} (s) X _ {2} (s) - X _ {1} (s -) X _ {2} (s -) \\ = \left(X _ {1} (s -) + \varDelta X _ {1} (s)\right) \left(X _ {2} (s -) + \varDelta X _ {2} (s)\right) - X _ {1} (s -) X _ {2} (s -) \\ = X _ {1} (s -) X _ {2} (s -) + X _ {1} (s -) \varDelta X _ {2} (s) + \varDelta X _ {1} (s) X _ {2} (s -) + \varDelta X _ {1} (s) \varDelta X _ {2} (s) \\ \qquad - X _ {1} (s -) X _ {2} (s -) \\ = X _ {1} (s -) \varDelta X _ {2} (s) + \varDelta X _ {1} (s) X _ {2} (s -) + \varDelta X _ {1} (s) \varDelta X _ {2} (s). \end{array}
$$

This is the typical term in the sum appearing at the end of ( 1 1 .5. 13) . 

For stochastic calculus without jumps, Girsanov's Theorem tells us how to change the measure using the Radon-Nikodym derivative process 

$$
Z (t) = \exp \Big \{- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Gamma (s) d W (s) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Gamma^ {2} (s) d s \Big \}.
$$

This process satisfies the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d Z (t) = - \Gamma (t) Z (t) d W (t) = Z (t) d X ^ {c} (t),
$$

where $\begin{array} { l } { { X ^ { c } ( t ) ~ = ~ - \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \varGamma ( s ) d W ( s ) } } \end{array}$ and $[ X ^ { c } , X ^ { c } ] ( t ) \ = \ \textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } { \cal T } ^ { 2 } ( s )$ ds. We may rewrite $ { \boldsymbol { Z } } ( t )$ as 

$$
Z (t) = \exp \left\{X ^ {c} (t) - \frac {1}{2} [ X ^ {c}, X ^ {c} ] (t) \right\}.\tag{11.5.14}
$$

In stochastic calculus for processes with jumps, the analogous stochastic diferential equation is 

$$
d Z ^ {X} (t) = Z ^ {X} (t -) d X (t),\tag{11.5.15}
$$

where the integrator X is now allowed to have jumps. The solution to ( 1 1 .5.15) is like ( 1 1 .5.14) , except now, whenever there is a jump in X, ( 1 1 .5. 15) says there is a jump in $z ^ { x }$ of size 

$$
\Delta Z ^ {X} (s) = Z ^ {X} (s -) \Delta X (s).
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Z ^ {X} (s) = Z ^ {X} (s -) + \Delta Z ^ {X} (s) = Z ^ {X} (s -) \bigl (1 + \Delta X (s) \bigr).
$$

The following corollary presents the result. 

Corollary 1 1.5.6. Let X(t) be a jump process. The Doleans-Dade exponential of X is defined to be the process 

$$
Z ^ {X} (t) = \exp \left\{X ^ {c} (t) - \frac {1}{2} [ X ^ {c}, X ^ {c} ] (t) \right\} \prod_ {0 <   s \leq t} \bigl (1 + \varDelta X (s) \bigr).
$$

This process is the solution to the stochastic diferential equation {1 1 . 5. 1 5} with initial condition $z ^ { X } ( 0 ) = 1$ , which in integral form is 

$$
Z ^ {X} (t) = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} Z ^ {X} (s -) d X (s).\tag{11.5.16}
$$

PROOF: We may write $X ( t )$ as $X ( t ) = X ^ { c } ( t ) + J ( t )$ , where 

$$
X ^ {c} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Gamma (s) d W (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Theta (s) d s\tag{11.5.17}
$$

is the continuous part of X and $\boldsymbol { J } ( t )$ is the pure jump part. We define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} Y (t) = \exp \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} \Gamma (s) d W (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Theta (s) d s - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Gamma^ {2} (s) d s \right\} \\ = \exp \left\{X ^ {c} (t) - \frac {1}{2} [ X ^ {c}, X ^ {c} ] (t) \right\}. \end{array}\tag{11.5.18}
$$

From the It6-Doeblin formula for continuous processes, we know that 

$$
d Y (t) = Y (t) d X ^ {c} (t) = Y (t -) d X ^ {c} (t).\tag{11.5.19}
$$

We next define $K ( t ) = 1$ for t between 0 and the time of the first jump of X, and we set 

$$
K (t) = \prod_ {0 <   s \leq t} \left(1 + \Delta X (s)\right)\tag{11.5.20}
$$

for t greater than or equal to the first jump time of X. The process $K ( t )$ is a pure jump process, and $Z ^ { X } ( t ) = Y ( t ) K ( t )$ . If X has a jump at time $\mathbf { } ^ { t , \quad }$ then $K ( t ) = K ( t - ) { \big ( } 1 + \Delta X ( t ) { \big ) }$ . Therefore, 

$$
\Delta K (t) = K (t) - K (t -) = K (t -) \Delta X (t).\tag{11.5.21}
$$

Because $Y ( t )$ is continuous and $K ( t )$ is a pure jump process, $[ Y , K ] ( t ) = 0$ We now use Ito's product rule for jump processes to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Z ^ {X} (t) = Y (t) K (t) \\ \quad = Y (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} K (s -) d Y (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s -) d K (s) \\ \quad = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s -) K (s -) d X ^ {c} (s) + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} Y (s -) K (s -) \Delta X (s) \\ \quad = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} Y (s -) K (s -) d X (s) \\ \quad = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} Z ^ {X} (s -) d X (s). \end{array} \tag {11}\tag{11.5.22}
$$

This is ( 1 1 .5 . 1 6) . 

## 11.6 Change of Measure

Just as we can use Girsanov's Theorem to change the measure so that a Brownian motion with drift becomes a Brownian motion without drift, we can change the measure for Poisson processes and compound Poisson processes. For a Poisson process, the change of measure afects the intensity. For a compound Poisson process, the change of measure can afect both the intensity and the distribution of the jump sizes. We treat these two situations in the next two subsections, and in the third subsection we also include a Brownian motion component in the process under consideration. 

## 11.6. 1 Change of Measure for a Poisson Process

Let $N ( t )$ be a Poisson process on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mathbb { P } )$ relative to a filtration $\mathcal { F } ( t ) , t \geq 0 .$ We denote the intensity of $N ( t )$ by A, a positive constant $( \mathrm { i . e . , } \mathbb { E } N ( t ) = \lambda t )$ . The compensated Poisson process $M ( t ) = N ( t ) - \lambda t$ is a martingale under lP' (Theorem 1 1 .2.4) . Let $\tilde { \lambda }$ be a positive number. We define 

$$
Z (t) = e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) t} \left(\frac {\tilde {\lambda}}{\lambda}\right) ^ {N (t)}.\tag{11.6.1}
$$

We fix a time $\mathbf { \nabla } T > 0$ and will use $z ( T )$ to change to a new measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ under which $N ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ , has intensity $\tilde { \lambda }$ rather than A. It is clear that $Z ( T ) > 0$ almost surely. In order to use $z ( T )$ to change the measure, we also need to verify that $\mathbb { E } Z ( T ) = 1$ 

Lemma 1 1.6. 1. The process $ { \boldsymbol { Z } } ( t )$ of {1 1 . 6. 1} satisfies 

$$
d Z (t) = \frac {\tilde {\lambda} - \lambda}{\lambda} Z (t -) d M (t).\tag{11.6.2}
$$

In particular, $ { \boldsymbol { Z } } ( t )$ is a martingale under lP' and $\mathbb { E } Z ( t ) = 1$ for all t . 

PROOF: Define $\begin{array} { r } { X ( t ) = \frac { \tilde { \lambda } - \lambda } { \lambda } M ( t ) } \end{array}$ , which is a martingale with continuous part $X ^ { c } ( t ) = ( \lambda - \tilde { \lambda } ) t$ and pure jump part $\begin{array} { r } { J ( t ) = \frac { \tilde { \lambda } - \lambda } { \lambda } N ( t ) } \end{array}$ . Then $[ X ^ { c } , X ^ { c } ] ( t ) = 0$ 5 and if there is a jump at time $\mathbf { } ^ { t , \quad }$ then $\begin{array} { r } { \varDelta X ( t ) = \frac { \tilde { \lambda } - \lambda } { \lambda } } \end{array}$ , so 

$$
1 + \varDelta X (t) = \frac {\tilde {\lambda}}{\lambda}.
$$

Therefore, the process in ( 1 1 .6.1 ) may be written as 

$$
Z (t) = \exp \left\{X ^ {c} (t) - \frac {1}{2} [ X ^ {c}, X ^ {c} ] (t) \right\} \prod_ {0 <   s \leq t} \bigl (1 + \Delta X (s) \bigr).
$$

We see from this formula that $ { \boldsymbol { Z } } ( t )$ is the Doleans-Dade exponential $Z ^ { X } ( t )$ of Corollary 1 1 .5.6. In particular, 

$$
Z (t) = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} Z (s -) d X (s).
$$

Since $X$ is a martingale and $Z ( \pmb { \mathscr { s } } - \big )$ is left-continuous, $Z ( t )$ is a martingale. Because $Z ( t )$ is a martingale and $Z ( 0 ) = 1$ , we know that $\mathbb { E } Z ( t ) = 1$ for all $t \geq 0$ 0 

We may now fix a positive time $_ { T }$ and use $z ( T )$ to change the measure. We define 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {P}} (A) = \int_ {A} Z (T) d \mathbb {P} \quad \text { for   all } A \in \mathcal {F}.\tag{11.6.3}
$$

Theorem 1 1.6.2 (Change of Poisson intensity) . Under the probability measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } _ { : }$ , the process $N ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ , is Poisson with intensity $\tilde { \lambda } .$ 

KEY STEP IN PROOF: We compute the moment-generating function of $N ( t )$ under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ . For $0 \leq t \leq T .$ , we can change the $\widetilde { \mathbb { E } }$ expectation of $e ^ { u N ( t ) }$ to the lE expectation by using $ { \boldsymbol { Z } } ( t )$ as the Radon-Nikodym derivative rather than $z ( T )$ (see Lemma 5.2.1) . Using the formula for $Z ( t )$ and the moment-generating function formula ( 1 1 .3.4) , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathbb {E} \Big [ e ^ {u N (t)} Z (t) \Big ] = e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) t} \mathbb {E} \left[ e ^ {u N (t)} \Big (\frac {\tilde {\lambda}}{\lambda} \Big) ^ {N (t)} \right]} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) t} \mathbb {E} \left[ \exp \left\{\left(u + \log \frac {\tilde {\lambda}}{\lambda}\right) N (t) \right\} \right]} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) t} \exp \left\{\lambda t \left(e ^ {u + \log (\tilde {\lambda} / \lambda)} - 1\right) \right\}} \\ & {\qquad = \exp \left\{\tilde {\lambda} t (e ^ {u} - 1) \right\},} \end{array}
$$

which is the moment generating function for a Poisson process with intensity $\tilde { \lambda }$ (see again ( 1 1 .3.4) ) . 0 

Example 1 1 . 6. 3. Consider a stock modeled as a geometric Poisson process 

$$
S (t) = S (0) \exp \left\{\alpha t + N (t) \log (\sigma + 1) - \lambda \sigma t \right\} = S (0) e ^ {(\alpha - \lambda \sigma) t} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (t)},
$$

where $\sigma > - 1 , \sigma \neq 0 ,$ and $N ( t )$ is a Poisson process with intensity ). under the actual probability measure IP'. We saw in Example 1 1 .5.2 that $e ^ { - \alpha t } S ( t )$ is a martingale under $\mathbb { P } ,$ and hence $S ( t )$ has mean rate of return a. Indeed, in place of (1 1 .5.9) , we now have 

$$
d S (t) = \alpha S (t) d t + \sigma S (t -) d M (t),\tag{11.6.4}
$$

where $M ( t )$ is the compensated Poisson process $M ( t ) = N ( t ) - \lambda t$ . We would like to change to a probability measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ under which 

$$
d S (t) = r S (t) d t + \sigma S (t -) d \widetilde {M} (t),\tag{11.6.5}
$$

where $\pmb { r }$ is the interest rate, $N ( t )$ is a Poisson process with intensity $\tilde { \lambda }$ under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } ,$ , and $\widetilde { M } ( t ) = N ( t ) - \widetilde { \lambda } t$ is a compensated Poisson process under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ Then, under ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } ,$ the geometric Poisson process would have mean rate of return equal to the interest rate, and $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ would be the risk-neutral measure. 

To accomplish this, we note that the "dt" term in ( 1 1 .6.4) is 

$$
(\alpha - \lambda \sigma) S (t) d t\tag{11.6.6}
$$

(recall that $d M ( t ) = d N ( t ) - \lambda d t )$ and the $^ { \mathfrak { s } } d t ^ { \mathfrak { s } }$ term in ( 1 1 .6.5) is 

$$
(r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (t) d t.\tag{11.6.7}
$$

(Here again we are using the fact that $S ( t - )$ dt and $S ( t )$ dt have the same integrals, and we can thus use them interchangeably.) We set ( 1 1 .6.6) and ( 1 1 .6.7) equal and solve for 

$$
\tilde {\lambda} = \lambda - \frac {\alpha - r}{\sigma}.
$$

We then change to the risk-neutral measure by formula ( 1 1 .6.3) with $z ( T )$ defined by ( 1 1 .6.1) . 

To make the change of measure, we must have $\tilde { \lambda } > 0 ,$ , which is equivalent to 

$$
\lambda > \frac {\alpha - r}{\sigma}.\tag{11.6.8}
$$

If condition ( 1 1.6.8) does not hold, then there is no risk-neutral measure and hence there must be an arbitrage. Indeed, if $\sigma > 0$ and ( 1 1 .6.8) fails, then 

$$
S (t) \geq S (0) e ^ {r t} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (t)} \geq S (0) e ^ {r t},
$$

and borrowing at the interest rate r to invest in the stock is an arbitrage. If $- 1 < \sigma < 0$ , the inequalities are reversed and the arbitrage consists of shorting the stock to invest in the money market account. D 

## 11.6.2 Change of Measure for a Compound Poisson Process

Let $N ( t )$ be a Poisson process with intensity A, and let $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \dots$ . be a sequence of identically distributed random variables defined on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mathbb { P } )$ . We assume the random variables $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \ldots$ are independent of one another and also independent of the Poisson process $N ( t )$ . We define the compound Poisson process 

$$
Q (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} Y _ {i}.\tag{11.6.9}
$$

Note for future reference that if N jumps at time $\mathbf { } ^ { t , \mathrm { ~ ~ } }$ then $Q$ jumps at time t and 

$$
\Delta Q (t) = Y _ {N (t)}.\tag{11.6.10}
$$

Our goal is to change the measure so that the intensity of $N ( t )$ and the distribution of the jump sizes $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \dots$ both change. We first consider the case when the jump-size random variables have a discrete distribution (i.e. , each $Y _ { i }$ takes one of finitely many possible nonzero values $y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } , \dotsc , y _ { M } )$ . Let $p ( y _ { m } )$ denote the probability that a jump is of size ${ \boldsymbol { y } } _ { m }$ = 

$$
p (y _ {m}) = \mathbb {P} \{Y _ {i} = y _ {m} \}, m = 1, \dots , M.
$$

This does not depend on i since $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \dots$ are identicall distributed. We assume that $p ( y _ { m } ) > 0$ for every m and, of course, that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { m = 1 } ^ { M } p ( y _ { m } ) = 1 } \end{array}$ 

Let $N _ { m } ( t )$ denote the number of jumps in $Q ( t )$ o f size $y _ { m }$ up to and including time t, so that 

$$
N (t) = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} N _ {m} (t) \text { and } Q (t) = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} y _ {m} N _ {m} (t).
$$

According to Corollary 1 1 .3.4, $N _ { 1 } , \ldots , N _ { M }$ are independent Poisson processes and each $N _ { m }$ has intensity $\lambda _ { m } = \lambda p ( y _ { m } )$ 

Let $\tilde { \lambda } _ { 1 } , \dots , \tilde { \lambda } _ { M }$ be given positive numbers, and set 

$$
Z _ {m} (t) = e ^ {(\lambda_ {m} - \bar {\lambda} _ {m}) t} \left(\frac {\tilde {\lambda} _ {m}}{\lambda_ {m}}\right) ^ {N _ {m} (t)} \text {   and   } Z (t) = \prod_ {m = 1} ^ {M} Z _ {m} (t).\tag{11.6.11}
$$

Lemma 1 1.6.4. The process $ { \boldsymbol { Z } } ( t )$ of {1 1 . 6. 1 1} is a martingale. In particular, $\mathbb { E } Z ( t ) = 1$ for all t . 

PROOF: From Lemma 1 1.6. 1, we have 

$$
d Z _ {m} (t) = \frac {\tilde {\lambda} _ {m} - \lambda_ {m}}{\lambda_ {m}} Z _ {m} (t -) d M _ {m} (t),\tag{11.6.12}
$$

where 

$$
M _ {m} (t) = N _ {m} (t) - \lambda_ {m} d t.
$$

Because the integrand in ( 1 1 .6.12) is left-continuous and the compensated Poisson process is a martingale, the process $Z _ { m }$ is a martingale (Theorem 1 1 .4.5) . 

For $m \neq n$ , the Poisson processes $N _ { m }$ and $N _ { n }$ have no simultaneous jumps, and hence $[ Z _ { m } , Z _ { n } ] = 0 .$ Ito's product rule (Corollary 1 1 . 5.5) implies that 

$$
d \big (Z _ {1} (t) Z _ {2} (t) \big) = Z _ {2} (t -) d Z _ {1} (t) + Z _ {1} (t -) d Z _ {2} (t).\tag{11.6.13}
$$

Because both $Z _ { 1 }$ and $Z _ { 2 }$ are martingales and the integrands in ( 1 1 .6. 13) are left-continuous, the process $ { \boldsymbol { Z } } _ { 1 }  { \boldsymbol { Z } } _ { 2 }$ is a martingale. Because $\boldsymbol { Z } _ { 1 } \boldsymbol { Z } _ { 2 }$ has no jumps simultaneous with the jumps of $z _ { 3 }$ , Ito's product rule further implies 

$$
d \left(Z _ {1} (t) Z _ {2} (t) Z _ {3} (t)\right) = Z _ {3} (t -) d \left(Z _ {1} (t) Z _ {2} (t)\right) + \left(Z _ {1} (t -) Z _ {2} (t -)\right) d Z _ {3} (t).
$$

Once again, the integrators are martingales and the integrands are leftcontinuous. Therefore, $Z _ { 1 } Z _ { 2 } Z _ { 3 }$ is a martingale. Continuing this process, we eventually conclude that $Z ( t ) = Z _ { 1 } ( t ) Z _ { 2 } ( t ) \cdot \cdot \cdot Z _ { m } ( t )$ is a martingale. 0 

Fix ${ \boldsymbol { T } } > 0 .$ . Because $Z ( T ) > 0$ almost surely and $\mathbb { E } Z ( T ) = 1$ , we can use $z ( T )$ to change the measure, defining 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {P}} (A) = \int_ {A} Z (T) d P \mathrm{forall} Z \in \mathcal {F}.
$$

Theorem 11.6.5 (Change of compound Poisson intensity and jump distribution for finitely many jump sizes) . Under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } , Q ( t )$ is a compound Poisson process with intensity $\begin{array} { r } { \tilde { \lambda } = \sum _ { m = 1 } ^ { M } \tilde { \lambda } _ { m } } \end{array}$ , and $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \dots$ are independent, identically distributed random variables with 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {P}} \{Y _ {i} = y _ {m} \} = \tilde {p} (y _ {m}) = \frac {\tilde {\lambda} _ {m}}{\tilde {\lambda}}.\tag{11.6.14}
$$

KEY STEP IN PROOF: We use the independence of $N _ { 1 } , \ldots , N _ { M }$ under lP' to compute the moment-generating function of $Q ( t )$ under $\tilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ . For $0 \leq t \leq T$ Lemma 5.2. 1 and the moment-generating function formula ( 1 1.3.4) imply 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {u Q (t)} \right] = \mathbb {E} \left[ e ^ {u Q (t)} Z (t) \right]} \\ & {\qquad = \mathbb {E} \left[ \exp \left\{u \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} y _ {m} N _ {m} (t) \right\} \cdot \prod_ {m = 1} ^ {M} e ^ {(\lambda_ {m} - \tilde {\lambda} _ {m}) t} \left(\frac {\tilde {\lambda} _ {m}}{\lambda_ {m}}\right) ^ {N _ {m} (t)} \right]} \\ & {\qquad = \prod_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \exp \{(\lambda_ {m} - \tilde {\lambda} _ {m}) t \} \cdot \mathbb {E} \left[ \exp \left\{\left(u y _ {m} + \log \frac {\tilde {\lambda} _ {m}}{\lambda_ {m}}\right) N _ {m} (t) \right\} \right]} \\ & {\qquad = \prod_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \exp \{(\lambda_ {m} - \tilde {\lambda} _ {m}) t \} \exp \left\{\lambda_ {m} t \left(e ^ {u y _ {m} + \log (\tilde {\lambda} _ {m} / \lambda_ {m})} - 1\right) \right\}} \\ & {\qquad = \prod_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \exp \left\{(\lambda_ {m} - \tilde {\lambda} _ {m}) t + \tilde {\lambda} _ {m} t e ^ {u y _ {m}} - \lambda_ {m} t \right\}} \\ & {\qquad = \prod_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \exp \left\{\tilde {\lambda} _ {m} t (e ^ {u y _ {m}} - 1) \right\}} \\ & {\qquad = \prod_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \exp \left\{\tilde {\lambda} t \tilde {p} (y _ {m}) e ^ {u y _ {m}} - \tilde {\lambda} _ {m} t \right\}} \\ & {\qquad = \exp \left\{\tilde {\lambda} t \left(\sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \tilde {p} (y _ {m}) e ^ {u y _ {m}} - 1\right) \right\}.} \end{array}
$$

According to ( 1 1 .3.5) , this is the moment-generating function for a compound Poisson process with intensity $\tilde { \lambda }$ and jump-size distribution ( 1 1 .6. 14) . 0 

The Radon-Nikodym derivative process $ { \boldsymbol { Z } } ( t )$ of ( 1 1.6. 1 1 ) may be written as 

$$
Z (t) = \exp \left\{\sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} (\lambda_ {m} - \tilde {\lambda} _ {m}) t \right\} \cdot \prod_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \left(\frac {\tilde {\lambda} \tilde {p} (y _ {m})}{\lambda p (y _ {m})}\right) ^ {N _ {m} (t)} = e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) t} \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \tilde {p} (Y _ {i})}{\lambda p (Y _ {i})}.
$$

This suggests that if $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \dots$ are not discrete but instead have a common density $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { y } )$ , then we could change the measure so that $Q ( t )$ has intensity $\tilde { \lambda }$ and $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , . . .$ . have a diferent density $\widetilde { f } ( \boldsymbol { y } )$ by using the Radon-Nikodym derivative process 

$$
Z (t) = e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) t} \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (Y _ {i})}{\lambda f (Y _ {i})}.\tag{11.6.15}
$$

This is in fact the case, although the proof, given below, is harder than the one just given for the case of a discrete jump-size distribution. 

To avoid division by zero in ( 1 1 .6.15) , we assume that $\widetilde f ( y ) = 0$ whenever $\begin{array} { r } { f ( \pmb { y } ) = \mathbf { 0 } . } \end{array}$ This means that if a certain set of jump sizes has probability zero under $\mathbb { P } ,$ , then it will also have probability zero under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ considered in Theorem 1 1 .6.7 below. 

Lemma 1 1.6.6. The process $ { \boldsymbol { Z } } ( t )$ of {1 1 . 6. 1 5} is a martingale. In particular, $\mathbb { E } Z ( t ) = 1$ for all $t \geq 0$ 

PROOF: We define the pure jump process 

$$
J (t) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (Y _ {i})}{\lambda f (Y _ {i})}.\tag{11.6.16}
$$

At the jump times of $Q _ { i }$ which are also the jump times of N and $^ { J , }$ we have (recall ( 1 1 . 6 . 1 0) ) 

$$
J (t) = J (t -) \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} \left(Y _ {N (t)}\right)}{\lambda f \left(Y _ {N (t)}\right)} = J (t -) \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (\Delta Q (t))}{\lambda f (\Delta Q (t))},
$$

and hence 

$$
\Delta J (t) = J (t) - J (t -) = \left[ \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (\Delta Q (t))}{\lambda f (\Delta Q (t))} - 1 \right] J (t -)\tag{11.6.17}
$$

at the jump times of $Q$ . 

We define the compound Poisson process 

$$
H (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (Y _ {i})}{\lambda f (Y _ {i})}\tag{11.6.18}
$$

for which 

$$
\Delta H (t) = \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (\Delta Q (t))}{\lambda f (\Delta Q (t))}.\tag{11.6.19}
$$

Because 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left[ \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (Y _ {i})}{\lambda f (Y _ {i})} \right] = \frac {\tilde {\lambda}}{\lambda} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \frac {\widetilde {f} (y)}{f (y)} f (y) d y = \frac {\tilde {\lambda}}{\lambda} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \widetilde {f} (y) d y = \frac {\tilde {\lambda}}{\lambda},
$$

the compensated compound Poisson process $H ( t ) - \tilde { \lambda } t$ is a martingale (Theorem 1 1 .3. 1 with $\begin{array} { r } { \beta = \frac { \tilde { \lambda } } { \lambda } ) } \end{array}$ . We may rewrite ( 1 1 .6. 17) as 

$$
\Delta J (t) = J (t -) \Delta H (t) - J (t -) \Delta N (t),\tag{11.6.20}
$$

and because all these terms are zero if there is no jump at $\mathbf { } t ,$ this equation holds at all times $\mathbf { } ^ { t , }$ not just at the jump times of $Q .$ . Because J, H, and N are all pure jump processes, we may also write ( 1 1.6.20) as 

$$
d J (t) = J (t -) d H (t) - J (t -) d N (t).
$$

Because $\boldsymbol { J } ( t )$ is a pure jump process and $e ^ { ( \lambda - \tilde { \lambda } ) t }$ is continuous, the cross variation between these two processes is zero. Therefore, $\mathbf { I t } \hat { \mathbf { o } } \ ' \mathbf { s }$ product rule for jump processes (Corollary 1 1 .5.5) implies that $Z ( t ) = e ^ { ( \lambda - \tilde { \lambda } ) t } J ( t )$ may be written as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Z (t) = Z (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} J (s -) (\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) s} d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) s} d J (s) \\ = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) s} J (s -) (\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) s} J (s -) d H (s) \\ - \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) s} J (s -) d N (s) \\ = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) s} J (s -) d (H (s) - \tilde {\lambda} s) - \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {(\lambda - \tilde {\lambda}) s} J (s -) d (N (s) - \lambda s) \\ = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} Z (s -) d (H (s) - \tilde {\lambda} s) - \int_ {0} ^ {t} Z (s -) d (N (s) - \lambda s). \end{array} \tag {11.6.21}
$$

Theorem 1 1 .4.5 implies that $Z ( t )$ is a martingale. Since $Z ( t )$ is a martingale and $Z ( 0 ) = 1$ , we have $\mathbb { E } Z ( t ) = 1$ for all t. 0 

For future reference, we rewrite ( 1 1 .6.21) in the diferential form 

$$
d Z (t) = Z (t -) d \bigl (H (t) - \tilde {\lambda} t \bigr) - Z (t -) d \bigl (N (t) - \lambda t \bigr).
$$

This equation implies 

$$
\Delta Z (t) = Z (t -) \Delta H (t) - Z (t -) \Delta N (t).\tag{11.6.22}
$$

Fix a positive $_ { T }$ and define 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {P}} (A) = \int_ {A} Z (T) d \mathbb {P} \quad \text { for   all } A \in \mathcal {F}.\tag{11.6.23}
$$

Theorem 11 .6.7 (Change of compound Poisson intensity and jump distribution for a continuum of jump sizes) . Under the probability measure ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } ,$ the process $Q ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T _ { \ast }$ , of $( 1 1 . 6 . 9 )$ is a compound Poisson process with intensity $\tilde { \lambda } .$ Furthermore, the jumps in $Q ( t )$ are independent and identically distributed with density $\widetilde { f } ( \boldsymbol { y } )$ 

KEY STEP IN PROOF: We need to show that, under ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } ,$ , the process $Q ( t )$ has the moment-generating function corresponding to a compound Poisson process with intensity $\tilde { \lambda }$ and jump density $\widetilde { f } ( \boldsymbol { y } )$ . In other words, we must show that (see ( 1 1 .3.2)) 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} e ^ {u Q (t)} = \exp \left\{\tilde {\lambda} t \big (\widetilde {\varphi} _ {Y} (u) - 1 \big) \right\},\tag{11.6.24}
$$

where 

$$
\widetilde {\varphi} _ {Y} (u) = \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} e ^ {u y} \widetilde {f} (y) d y.\tag{11.6.25}
$$

$$
X (t) = \exp \left\{u Q (t) - \tilde {\lambda} t (\widetilde {\varphi} _ {Y} (u) - 1) \right\}
$$

and show that $X ( t ) Z ( t )$ is a martingale under IP'. At jump times of $Q ,$ , 

$$
X (t) = X (t -) e ^ {u \Delta Q (t)},
$$

and hence 

$$
\Delta X (t) = X (t) - X (t -) = X (t -) \left(e ^ {u \Delta Q (t)} - 1\right).\tag{11.6.26}
$$

We introduce the compound Poisson process 

$$
V (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} e ^ {u Y _ {i}} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (Y _ {i})}{\lambda f (Y _ {i})}.
$$

Because 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left[ e ^ {u Y _ {i}} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (Y _ {i})}{\lambda f (Y _ {i})} \right] = \frac {\tilde {\lambda}}{\lambda} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} e ^ {u y} \frac {\widetilde {f} (y)}{f (y)} f (y) d y = \frac {\tilde {\lambda}}{\lambda} \widetilde {\varphi} _ {Y} (u),
$$

the compensated compound Poisson process $V ( t ) - \tilde { \lambda } t \tilde { \varphi } _ { Y } ( u )$ is a martingale (see Theorem 1 1 .3.1 with $\begin{array} { r } { \beta = \frac { \tilde { \lambda } } { \lambda } \widetilde { \varphi } _ { Y } ( u ) ) } \end{array}$ At jump times of $Q .$ 

$$
\Delta V (t) = e ^ {u \Delta Q (t)} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} \widetilde {f} (\Delta Q (t))}{\lambda f (\Delta Q (t))} = e ^ {u \Delta Q (t)} \Delta H (t),\tag{11.6.27}

Because $X ( t )$ and $Z ( t )$ have no Ito integral components, ( 1 1 .6.26) , (1 1.6.22) , and (1 1 .6.27) imply

\begin{array}{l} [ X, Z ] (t) = \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} \Delta X (s) \Delta Z (s) \\ = \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} X (s -) Z (s -) \left(e ^ {u \Delta Q (s)} - 1\right) \Delta H (s) \\ - \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} X (s -) Z (s -) \left(e ^ {u \Delta Q (s)} - 1\right) \Delta N (s) \\ = \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} X (s -) Z (s -) \Delta V (s) - \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} X (s -) Z (s -) \Delta H (s) \\ - \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} X (s -) Z (s -) \left(e ^ {u \Delta Q (s)} - 1\right). \end{array} \tag {11}\tag{11.6.28}

We have omitted $\pmb { \varDelta N } ( s )$ in the last term because it is always either 1 or $0 ,$ and when it is zero, $e ^ { u \Delta Q ( s ) } - 1$ is also zero. In other words, 

$$
\left(e ^ {u \Delta Q (s)} - 1\right) \Delta N (s) = \left(e ^ {u \Delta Q (s)} - 1\right).
$$

We use Ito's product rule for jump processes to write 

$$
X (t) Z (t) = 1 + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X (s -) d Z (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} Z (s -) d X (s) + [ X, Z ] (t).

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\int_ {0} ^ {t} Z (s -) d X (s) + [ X, Z ] (t)} \\ & {= \int_ {0} ^ {t} Z (s -) d X ^ {c} (s) + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} Z (s -) \varDelta X (s) + [ X, Z ] (t)} \\ & {= - \tilde {\lambda} \big (\widetilde {\varphi} _ {Y} (u) - 1 \big) \int_ {0} ^ {t} X (s -) Z (s -) d s + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} X (s -) Z (s -) \big (e ^ {u \varDelta Q (s)} - 1 \big)} \\ & {\quad + \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} X (s -) Z (s -) \varDelta V (s) - \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} X (s -) Z (s -) \varDelta H (s)} \\ & {\quad - \sum_ {0 <   s \leq t} X (s -) Z (s -) \big (e ^ {u \varDelta Q (s)} - 1 \big)} \\ & {= \int_ {0} ^ {t} X (s -) Z (s -) d \big (V (s) - \tilde {\lambda} s \widetilde {\varphi} _ {Y} (u) d s \big) - \int_ {0} ^ {t} X (s -) Z (s -) d \big (H (s) - \tilde {\lambda} s \big).} \end{array}

This is a martingale because the processes $V ( t ) - \tilde { \lambda } t \widetilde { \varphi } _ { Y } ( u ) \mathrm { a n d } H ( t ) - \tilde { \lambda } t$ are martingales and the integrands are left-continuous 

We can now prove (1 1 .6.24) . Using Lemma 5.2 . 1 , we may write 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {u Q (t)} \big ] = \mathbb {E} \big [ e ^ {u Q (t)} Z (t) \big ].\tag{11.6.29}

But the martingale $X ( t ) Z ( t )$ has constant expectation 1, which implies 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {1 = \mathbb {E} \big [ X (t) Z (t) \big ]} \\ & {\quad = \exp \big \{- \tilde {\lambda} t \big (\widetilde {\varphi} _ {Y} (u) - 1 \big) \big \} \cdot \mathbb {E} \big [ e ^ {u Q (t)} Z (t) \big ].} \end{array}\tag{11.6.30}

Combining ( 1 1.6.29) and ( 1 1.6.30) , we obtain ( 1 1.6.24). 

11.6.3 Change of Measure for a Compound Poisson Process and a Brownian Motion 

Suppose now that we have a probability space $( \Omega , \mathcal { F } , \mathbb { P } )$ on which is defined a Brownian motion $W ( t )$ . Suppose that on this same probability space there is defined a compound Poisson process 

$$
Q (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} Y _ {i}
$$

as in ( 1 1.3. 1) with intensity A and jumps having density function $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { y } )$ . We assume there is a single filtration $\mathcal { F } ( t ) , t \geq 0$ , for both the Brownian motion and the compound Poisson process. In this case, the Brownian motion and compound Poisson process must be independent. (See Corollary 1 1 .4.9 for the case of a Brownian motion and a Poisson process. The case of a Brownian motion and a compound Poisson process is Exercise 1 1 .6.) 

Let $\tilde { \lambda }$ be a positive number, let $\widetilde { f } ( \boldsymbol { y } )$ be another density function with the property that $\widetilde f ( y ) = 0$ whenever $\pmb { f } ( \pmb { y } ) = \mathbf { 0 }$ , and let $\theta ( t )$ be an adapted process. We define 

$$
Z _ {1} (t) = \exp \left\{- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Theta (u) d W (u) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Theta^ {2} (u) d u \right\},\tag{11.6.31}
$$

$$

## 11.7 Pricing a European Call in a Jump Model

In this section, we consider the problem of pricing a European call when the underlying asset is a jump process. We work out the details for two cases: ( 1) the underlying asset is driven by a single Poisson process, and (2) the underlying asset is driven by a Brownian motion and a compound Poisson process. The market is complete in the first case and incomplete in the second. We discuss the nature of the incompleteness in the second case. 

## 1 1 . 7.1 Asset Driven by a Poisson Process

We return to Example 1 1 .6.3, in which the underlying asset price is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} S (t) & = S (0) \exp \left\{\alpha t + N (t) \log (\sigma + 1) - \lambda \sigma t \right\} \\ & = S (0) e ^ {(\alpha - \lambda \sigma) t} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (t)}, \end{array}\tag{11.7.1}
$$

for which the diferential is 

$$
d S (t) = \alpha S (t) d t + \sigma S (t -) d M (t).
$$

In this model, $N ( t )$ is a Poisson process with intensity $\lambda > 0$ on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mathbb { P } )$ , and $M ( t ) = N ( t ) - \lambda t$ is the compensated Poisson process. 

We fix a positive time T and wish to price a European call whose payof at time $_ { T }$ is 

$$
V (T) = \left(S (T) - K\right) ^ {+}.
$$

We saw in Example 1 1.6.3 that we must assume $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda > \frac { \alpha - r } { \sigma } } \end{array}$ in order to rule out arbitrage. Under this assumption, 

$$
\tilde {\lambda} = \lambda - \frac {\alpha - r}{\sigma}
$$

is positive, and there is a risk-neutral measure given by 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {P}} (A) = \int_ {A} Z (T) d \mathbb {P} \mathrm{forall} A \in \mathcal {F},
$$

where $Z ( t ) = e ^ { ( \lambda - \tilde { \lambda } ) t } \bigg ( \frac { \tilde { \lambda } } { \lambda } \bigg ) ^ { N ( t ) }$ . This risk-neutral measure is in fact unique; see Remark 1 1.7.2 below. 

Under the risk-neutral measure, the compensated Poisson process $\widetilde { M } ( t ) =$ $N ( t ) - \tilde { \lambda } t$ is a martingale, and 

$$
d S (t) = r S (t) d t + \sigma S (t -) d \widetilde {M} (t)\tag{11.7.2}
$$

or, equivalently, 

$$
d \big (e ^ {- r t} S (t) \big) = \sigma e ^ {- r t} S (t -) d \widetilde {M} (t).
$$

The discounted asset price is a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ . In terms of $\tilde { \lambda } ,$ we may rewrite the second line in ( 1 1 .7. 1) as 

$$
S (t) = S (0) e ^ {(r - \bar {\lambda} \sigma) t} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (t)}.
$$

For $0 \leq t \leq T ,$ , let V(t) denote the risk-neutral price of a European call paying $V ( T ) = \left( S ( T ) - K \right) ^ { + }$ at time T. The discounted call price is a martingale under the risk-neutral measure. In other words, the call price $V ( t )$ satisfies 

$$
e ^ {- r t} V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- r T} V (T) \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ] = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- r T} \big (S (T) - K \big) ^ {+} \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ].
$$

We have 

$$
\begin{array}{r} S (T) = S (0) e ^ {(r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) t} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (t)} \cdot e ^ {(r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) (T - t)} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (T) - N (t)} \\ = S (t) \cdot e ^ {(r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) (T - t)} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (T) - N (t)}. \end{array}
$$

It follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- r (T - t)} \big (S (T) - K \big) ^ {+} \big | \mathcal {F} (t) \big ] \\ & \qquad = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \Big [ e ^ {- r (T - t)} \Big (S (t) e ^ {(r - \bar {\lambda} \sigma) (T - t)} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (T) - N (t)} - K \Big) ^ {+} \Big | \mathcal {F} (t) \Big ]. \end{array}
$$

The random variable $S ( t )$ is $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ -measurable, whereas 

$$
e ^ {(r - \bar {\lambda} \sigma) (T - t)} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (T) - N (t)}
$$

is independent of $\mathcal { F } ( t )$ . According to the Independence Lemma, Lemma 2.3.4, 

$$
V (t) = c \big (t, S (t) \big),
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & c (t, x) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \Big [ e ^ {- r (T - t)} \Big (x e ^ {(r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) (T - t)} (\sigma + 1) ^ {N (T) - N (t)} - K \Big) ^ {+} \Big ] \\ & \qquad = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- r (T - t)} \Big (x e ^ {(r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) (T - t)} (\sigma + 1) ^ {j} - K \Big) ^ {+} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} ^ {j} (T - t) ^ {j}}{j !} e ^ {- \tilde {\lambda} (T - t)} \\ & \qquad = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \Big (x e ^ {- \tilde {\lambda} \sigma (T - t)} (\sigma + 1) ^ {j} - K e ^ {- r (T - t)} \Big) ^ {+} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} ^ {j} (T - t) ^ {j}}{j !} e ^ {- \tilde {\lambda} (T - t)}. \end{array}\tag{11.7.3}
$$

From this formula, the risk-neutral price of the call $c ( t , \pmb { x } )$ can be computed. The $j = 0$ term in ( 1 1 .7.3) is 

$$
\left(x e ^ {- \tilde {\lambda} \sigma (T - t)} - K e ^ {- r (T - t)}\right) ^ {+} e ^ {- \tilde {\lambda} (T - t)}.
$$

When $\mathbf { \nabla } t = T \mathbf { \nabla } \cdot$ , this term is $( { \pmb x } - K ) ^ { + }$ , and it is the only nonzero term in the sum in ( 1 1 .7.3) when $\mathbf { \nabla } t = T$ . Therefore, the function $^ { c }$ satisfies the terminal condition 

$$
c (T, x) = (x - K) ^ {+} \text {   for   all   } x \geq 0.\tag{11.7.4}
$$

We next derive the "partial diferential equation" that ${ \pmb c } ( t , { \pmb x } )$ must satisfy. The usual iterated conditioning argument shows that 

$$
e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) = e ^ {- r t} V (t) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \left[ e ^ {- r T} (S (T) - K) ^ {+} \mid \mathcal {F} (t) \right]
$$

is a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ . Therefore, we compute $d \big ( e ^ { - r t } c ( t , S ( t ) ) \big )$ and set the $" d t "$ term equal to zero. The stochastic diferential equation ( 1 1 . 7.2) may be rewritten as 

$$
d S (t) = (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (t) d t + \sigma S (t -) d N (t),\tag{11.7.5}
$$

which shows that the continuous part of the stock price satisfies 

$$
d S ^ {c} (t) = (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (t) d t.
$$

On the other hand, if the stock price jumps at time $t ,$ then 

$$
\Delta S (t) = S (t) - S (t -) = \sigma S (t -), \quad S (t) = (\sigma + 1) S (t -).
$$

The ItO-Doeblin formula implies 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \\ & \quad = c (0, S (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ - r c (u, S (u)) d u + c _ {t} (u, S (u)) d u \\ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + c _ {x} (u, S (u)) d S ^ {c} (u) \big ] \\ & \qquad + \sum_ {0 <   u \leq t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, S (u)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ] \\ & = c (0, S (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ - r c (u, S (u)) + c _ {t} (u, S (u)) \\ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (u) c _ {x} (u, S (u)) \big ] d u \\ & \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ] d N (u) \\ & = c (0, S (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ - r c (u, S (u)) + c _ {t} (u, S (u)) \\ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (u) c _ {x} (u, S (u)) \big ]. d u \\ & \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ] \tilde {\lambda} d u \\ & \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ]. d \widetilde {M} (u). \end{array}
$$

However, the integral 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ] \tilde {\lambda} d u
$$

is the same as the integral 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u)) - c (u, S (u)) \big ] \tilde {\lambda} d u.
$$

We have shown that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \\ = c (0, S (0)) \\ \quad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \left[ - r c (u, S (u)) + c _ {t} (u, S (u)) + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (u) c _ {x} (u, S (u)) \right. \\ \quad \left. + \tilde {\lambda} \big (c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u)) - c (u, S (u)) \big) \right] d u \\ \quad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \left[ c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \right] d \widetilde {M} (u). \end{array} \tag {11.7}\tag{11.7.6}
$$

The last integral is a martingale because the integrator $\widetilde { M } ( u )$ is a martingale and the integrand is left-continuous. Because left-hand side of ( 1 1 .7.6) , $\bar { e } ^ { - r t } c ( t , S ( t ) )$ , is also a martingale we can then solve for 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} c (0, S (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ - r c (u, S (u)) + c _ {t} (u, S (u)) + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (u) c _ {x} (u, S (u)) \\ & \quad + \tilde {\lambda} \big (c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u)) - c (u, S (u)) \big) \big ] d u \end{array}
$$

and see that it is the diference of two martingales and hence is itself a martingale. This can only happen if the integrand is zero: 

$$
\begin{array}{r} - r c (t, S (t)) + c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) \\ + \tilde {\lambda} \big (c (t, (\sigma + 1) S (t)) - c (t, S (t)) \big) = 0. \end{array}\tag{11.7.7}
$$

The way we have in the past argued for ( 1 1 .7.7) using ( 1 1 .7.6) (see the discussion preceding Theorem 6.4.3) is by first taking the diferential in ( 1 1 .7.6) to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \big (e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \big)} \\ & {\quad = e ^ {- r t} \big [ - r c (t, S (t)) + c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t))} \\ & {\qquad \quad + \tilde {\lambda} \big (c (t, (\sigma + 1) S (t)) - c (t, S (t)) \big) \big ] d t} \\ & {\qquad \quad + e ^ {- r t} \big [ c (t, (\sigma + 1) S (t -)) - c (t, S (t -)) \big ] d \widetilde {M} (t)} \end{array}
$$

and then setting the dt term equal to zero. This still works, provided we make sure the non-dt term has a martingale integrator, and if this integrator has jumps, then the integrand for this martingale is left-continuous. In particular, we also have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \big (e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \big) \\ = e ^ {- r t} \big [ - r c (t, S (t)) + c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) \big ] d t \\ \qquad + e ^ {- r t} \big [ c (t, (\sigma + 1) S (t -)) - c (t, S (t -)) \big ] d N (t), \end{array}\tag{11.7.8}
$$

but setting the $" d t "$ term 

$$
e ^ {- r t} \big [ - r c (t, S (t)) + c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) \big ] d t
$$

in this expression equal to zero gives an incorrect result because the non-dt term has integrator $d N ( t )$ and $N ( t )$ is not a martingale. 

We conclude by replacing the stock price process $S ( t )$ in ( 1 1 .7.7) by a dummy variable x. This gives the equation 

$$
- r c (t, x) + c _ {t} (t, x) + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) x c _ {x} (t, x) + \tilde {\lambda} \bigl (c (t, (\sigma + 1) x) - c (t, x) \bigr) = 0,\tag{11.7.9}
$$

which must hold for $0 \leq t < T$ and $\textbf { \em x } \geq \ \mathbf { 0 } .$ . This is sometimes called a diferential-diference equation because it involves c at two diferent values of the stock price, namely x and $( \sigma + 1 ) x$ . The function ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ defined by ( 1 1 .7.3) satisfies this equation because, by its construction, $e ^ { - r t } c ( t , S ( t ) )$ is a martingale under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } .$ 

Returning to ( 1 1 .7.6) and using equation ( 1 1 . 7.9) , we see that for $0 \leq t \leq$ $^ { T , }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \\ = c (0, S (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \left[ c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \right] d \widetilde {M} (u). \end{array}\tag{11.7.10}
$$

In particular, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} e ^ {- r T} \big (S (T) - K \big) ^ {+} \\ = e ^ {- r T} c (T, S (T)) \\ = c (0, S (0)) + \int_ {0} ^ {T} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ] d \widetilde {M} (u). \end{array}\tag{11.7.11}
$$

We use this observation t o construct the hedge for a short position i n the call. 

Suppose we sell the call at time zero in exchange for initial capital $X ( 0 ) =$ $c ( 0 , S ( 0 ) )$ . We want to invest in the stock and money market account so that $X ( t ) = c ( t , S ( t ) )$ for all t or, equivalently, 

$$
e ^ {- r t} X (t) = e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T ].
$$

To accomplish this, we match diferentials. From ( 1 1 .7. 10) , we see that the diferential of $e ^ { - r t } c ( t , S ( t ) )$ is 

$$
d \big (e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \big) = e ^ {- r t} \big [ c (t, (\sigma + 1) S (t -)) - c (t, S (t -)) \big ] d \widetilde {M} (t).\tag{11.7.12}
$$

The diferential of the value $X ( t )$ of a portfolio that at each time t holds $\boldsymbol { { \Gamma } } ( t )$ shares of stock (we use $\boldsymbol { { \Gamma } } ( t )$ rather than $\varDelta ( t )$ to denote the number of shares of stock held in the hedging portfolio to avoid confusion with the use of $\varDelta$ as the size of the j ump in a process) is 

$$
d X (t) = \Gamma (t -) d S (t) + r [ X (t) - \Gamma (t) S (t) ] d t.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \big (e ^ {- r t} X (t) \big) = e ^ {- r t} [ - r X (t) d t + d X (t) ]} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {- r t} [ \Gamma (t -) d S (t) - r \Gamma (t) S (t) d t ]} \\ & {\qquad = e ^ {- r t} \sigma \Gamma (t -) S (t -) d \widetilde {M} (t),} \end{array}\tag{11.7.13}
$$

where we have used ( 1 1 .7.2) in the last step. We are interested in determining the value of $\boldsymbol { { \cal T } } ( t { - } )$ , the position held just before any jump that may occur at time t. Comparing ( 1 1 .7.12) and ( 1 1 .7.13) , we conclude that we should take 

$$
\Gamma (t -) = \frac {c (t , (\sigma + 1) S (t -)) - c (t , S (t -))}{\sigma S (t -)}.\tag{11.7.14}
$$

This is the hedging position we should hold at all times, whether they are jump times or not. More specifically, if we define 

$$
\Gamma (t) = \frac {c (t , (\sigma + 1) S (t)) - c (t , S (t))}{\sigma S (t)} \text {   for   all   } t \in [ 0, T ],\tag{11.7.15}
$$

then ( 1 1 . 7. 14) will also hold and integration of ( 1 1 .7.13) yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} e ^ {- r t} X (t) \\ = X (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \left[ c (u, (\sigma + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \right] d \widetilde {M} (u). \end{array}\tag{11.7.16}
$$

Comparison of ( 1 1 .7. 10) with ( 1 1 .7. 16) shows that $X ( t ) = c ( t , S ( t ) )$ for all t . In particular, ( 1 1 . 7. 1 1 ) shows that $X ( T ) = \left( S ( T ) - K \right) ^ { + }$ ; the short position in the European call has been hedged. 

Remark 1 1 . 7. 1 {Sanity check). To convince ourselves that the hedge ( 1 1 .7. 15) really works, we consider separately the cases when the stock jumps at time t and when the stock does not jump at time t. In the event of a jump, the change in the option price is $c ( t , ( \sigma + 1 ) S ( t - ) ) - c ( t , S ( t - ) )$ . The change in the hedging portfolio value is 

$$
\Gamma (t -) \big (S (t) - S (t -) \big) = \Gamma (t -) \sigma S (t -) = c (t, (\sigma + 1) S (t -)) - c (t, S (t -)),
$$

which agrees with the change in the option price. 

On the other hand, if the stock price does not jump at time $t ,$ then the stock price follows equation ( 1 1 . 7.5) without the $d N ( t )$ term at time t: 

$$
d S (t) = (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (t) d t.
$$

At this time, ( 1 1 .7.8) shows that the discounted option price has the diferential 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \big (e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \big)} \\ & {= e ^ {- r t} \big [ - r c (t, S (t)) + c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + (r - \tilde {\lambda} \sigma) S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) \big ] d t} \\ & {= - e ^ {- r t} \tilde {\lambda} \big [ c (t, (\sigma + 1) S (t)) - c (t, S (t)) \big ] d t,} \end{array}
$$

where we have used the diferential-diference equation ( 1 1.7.9) to obtain the second equality. The diferential of the discounted portfolio value at this time is (from ( 1 1 .7. 13) without the $d N ( t )$ term implicit in $d \widetilde { M } ( t ) )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \big (e ^ {- r t} X (t) \big) = e ^ {- r t} \sigma \Gamma (t) S (t) (- \tilde {\lambda} d t)} \\ & {\qquad = - e ^ {- r t} \tilde {\lambda} \big [ c (t, (\sigma + 1) S (t)) - c (t, S (t)) \big ] d t.} \end{array}
$$

Once again, the discounted portfolio value tracks the discounted option price. 0 

Remark 1 1 . 7. 2 (Completeness). In this subsection, we have constructed the price and hedge for a European call on a stock driven by a single Poisson process. It is clear from the analysis that this same argument would work for an arbitrary European derivative security with payof $h ( S ( T ) )$ at time T written on a stock modeled this way. One could simply replace the call payof by the function h in equation (1 1 .7.3) . The diferential-diference equation ( 1 1 .7.9) would still apply, although now with terminal condition $c ( T , x ) = h ( x )$ replacing ( 1 1 .7.4) , and the hedging formula ( 1 1 . 7 . 1 5) would still be correct. 

The model is complete and the risk-neutral measure is unique if and only if every derivative security can be hedged (Second Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing, Theorem 5.4.9) . "Every" derivative security means also those derivative securities that are path-dependent. We have not considered pathdependent derivative securities in this subsection, but one can show that they also can be hedged, and thus the model is complete. 

## 11.7.2 Asset Driven by a Brownian Motion and a Compound Poisson Process

Let $( \Omega , \mathcal { F } , \mathbb { P } )$ be a probability space on which is defined a Brownian motion $W ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T .$ , and M independent Poisson processes ${ N } _ { 1 } ( t ) , \ldots , { N } _ { M } ( t )$ ， $0 \leq t \leq T$ . Let ${ \mathcal { F } } ( t ) , 0 \leq t \leq T$ , be the filtration generated by the Brownian motion and the M Poisson processes. 

Let $\lambda _ { m } > 0$ be the intensity of the mth Poisson process and let $- 1 < y _ { 1 } <$ $\cdots < y _ { M }$ be nonzero numbers. Set 

$$
N (t) = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} N _ {m} (t), \quad Q (t) = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} y _ {m} N _ {m} (t).
$$

Then N is a Poisson process with intensity $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda = \sum _ { m = 1 } ^ { M } \lambda _ { m } } \end{array}$ and $Q$ is a compound Poisson process. Let $Y _ { i }$ denote the size of the ith jump of $Q .$ Then the $Y _ { i }$ random variables take values in the set $\left\{ y _ { 1 } , \dots , y _ { M } \right\}$ , and $Q ( t )$ can be written as 

$$
Q (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} Y _ {i}.
$$

Define 

$$
p (y _ {m}) = \frac {\lambda_ {m}}{\lambda}.
$$

The random variables $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , . . .$ . are independent and identically distributed, with ${ \mathbb P } \{ Y _ { i } = y _ { m } \} = p ( y _ { m } )$ · These assertions all follow from Theorem 1 1 .3.3. 

Set 

$$
\beta = \mathbb {E} Y _ {i} = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} y _ {m} p (y _ {m}) = \frac {1}{\lambda} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \lambda_ {m} y _ {m}.\tag{11.7.17}
$$

According to Theorem 1 1 .3. 1 , 

$$
Q (t) - \beta \lambda t = Q (t) - t \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \lambda_ {m} y _ {m}
$$

is a martingale. 

In this subsection, the stock price will be modeled by the stochastic differential equation 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d S (t) = \alpha S (t) d t + \sigma S (t) d W (t) + S (t -) d \bigl (Q (t) - \beta \lambda t \bigr)} \\ & {\qquad = (\alpha - \beta \lambda) S (t) d t + \sigma S (t) d W (t) + S (t -) d Q (t).} \end{array}\tag{11.7.18}
$$

Under the original probability measure IP', the mean rate of return on the stock is a: The assumption that $y _ { i } > - 1$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , M$ guarantees that although the stock price can jump down, it cannot jump from a positive to a negative value or to zero. We begin with a positive initial stock price $S ( 0 )$ , and the stock price is positive at all subsequent times; see ( 1 1 .7. 19) below. If $S ( 0 ) = 0$ then $S ( t ) = 0$ for all t . 

Theorem 1 1 . 7.3. The solution to {1 1 . 7. 18} is 

$$
S (t) = S (0) \exp \left\{\sigma W (t) + \left(\alpha - \beta \lambda - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) t \right\} \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} (Y _ {i} + 1).\tag{11.7.19}
$$

PROOF: We show that $S ( t )$ defined by the right-hand side of ( 1 1 .7. 19) satisfies the stochastic diferential equation ( 1 1.7.18). Toward this end, define the continuous stochastic process 

$$
X (t) = S (0) \exp \left\{\sigma W (t) + \left(\alpha - \beta \lambda - \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2}\right) t \right\}
$$

and the pure jump process 

$$
J (t) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {N (t)} \left(Y _ {i} + 1\right).
$$

Then $S ( t ) = X ( t ) J ( t )$ . We show that $S ( t ) = X ( t ) J ( t )$ is a solution to the stochastic diferential equation ( 1 1 .7. 18) . 

The ltO-Doeblin formula for a continuous process says that 

$$
d X (t) = (\alpha - \beta \lambda) X (t) d t + \sigma X (t) d W (t).\tag{11.7.20}
$$

At the time of the ith jump, $J ( t ) = J ( t - ) ( Y _ { i } + 1 )$ and hence 

$$
\Delta J (t) = J (t) - J (t -) = J (t -) Y _ {i} = J (t -) \Delta Q (t).
$$

The equation $\Delta J ( t ) = J ( t - ) \Delta Q ( t )$ also holds at nonjump times, with both sides equal to zero. Therefore, 

$$
d J (t) = J (t -) d Q (t).\tag{11.7.21}
$$

Ito's product rule for jump processes implies that 

$$
S (t) = X (t) J (t) = S (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X (s -) d J (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} J (s) d X (s) + [ X, J ] (t).\tag{11.7.22}
$$

Since J is a pure jump process and X is continuous, $[ X , J ] ( t ) = 0 .$ Substituting ( 1 1 . 7.20) and ( 1 1 .7.21) into ( 1 1 . 7.22) , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S (t) = X (t) J (t) \\ \qquad = S (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} X (s -) J (s -) d Q (s) + (\alpha - \beta \lambda) \int_ {0} ^ {t} J (s) X (s) d s \\ \qquad + \sigma \int_ {0} ^ {t} J (s) X (s) d W (s), \end{array}
$$

which in diferential form is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d S (t) = d \big (X (t) J (t) \big)} \\ & {\qquad = X (t -) J (t -) d Q (t) + (\alpha - \beta \lambda) J (t) X (t) d t + \sigma J (t) X (t) d W (t)} \\ & {\qquad = S (t -) d Q (t) + (\alpha - \beta \lambda) S (t) d t + \sigma S (t) d W (t).} \end{array}
$$

This is ( 1 1 .7.18) .

The probability measure $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ is risk-neutral if and only if the mean E_ate of return of the stock under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ is the interest rate $^ { r , }$ In other words, $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } }$ is risk-neutral if and only if

Because there is one equation and $M + 1$ unknowns, $\theta , \lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { M }$ , there are multiple risk-neutral measures. 

Extra stocks would help determine a unique risk-neutral measure. We illustrate this point by taking $M = 2$ in the following example.

Suppose the jump sizes $Y _ { i }$ have a density $f ( y )$ rather than a probability mass function $p ( y _ { 1 } ) , \dots , p ( y _ { m } )$ 15 and this density is strictly positive on a set $B \subset ( - 1 , \infty )$ and zero elsewhere. Theorem 11 .7.7. The call price ${ \boldsymbol c } ( t , { \boldsymbol x } )$ of {1 1 . 7. 30} satisfies the equation

\begin{array}{l} - r c (t, x) + c _ {t} (t, x) + (r - \tilde {\beta} \tilde {\lambda}) x c _ {x} (t, x) + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} x ^ {2} c _ {x x} (t, x) \\ \qquad + \tilde {\lambda} \Big [ \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \tilde {p} (y _ {m}) c (t, (y _ {m} + 1) x) - c (t, x) \Big ] = 0, 0 \leq t <   T, x \geq 0, \end{array}\tag{11.7.33}

$$
\begin{array}{l} e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) - c (0, S (0)) \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \left[ - r c (u, S (u)) + c _ {t} (u, S (u)) + (r - \tilde {\beta} \tilde {\lambda}) S (u) c _ {x} (u, S (u)) \right. \\ \left. + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (u) c _ {x x} (u, S (u)) \right] d u + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \sigma S (u) c _ {x} (u, S (u)) d \widetilde {W} (u) \\ + \sum_ {0 <   u \leq t} e ^ {- r u} [ c (u, S (u)) - c (u, S (u -)) ]. \end{array} \tag {11.7.34}

We examine the last term in ( 1 1 . 7.34) . If u is a jump time of the mth Poisson process $N _ { m }$ , the stock price satisfies $S ( u ) = ( y _ { m } + 1 ) S ( u - \AA )$ . Therefore,

\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {0 <   u \leq t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, S (u)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ] \\ = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \sum_ {0 <   u \leq t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, (y _ {m} + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ] \varDelta N _ {m} (u) \\ = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, (y _ {m} + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ] d (N _ {m} (u) - \tilde {\lambda} _ {m} u) \\ \quad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \Big [ \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \frac {\tilde {\lambda} _ {m}}{\tilde {\lambda}} c (u, (y _ {m} + 1) S (u)) - c (u, S (u)) \Big ] \tilde {\lambda} d u \\ = \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- r u} \big [ c (u, (y _ {m} + 1) S (u -)) - c (u, S (u -)) \big ] d (N _ {m} (u) - \tilde {\lambda} _ {m} u) \\ \quad + \int_ {0}^{t} e ^ {- r u} \tilde {\lambda} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \big [ \tilde {p} (y _ {m}) c (u, (y _ {m} + 1) S (u)) - c (u, S (u)) \big ] \Big \} d u. \end{array}

Substituting this into ( 1 1 . 7.34) and taking diferentials, we obtain

\begin{array}{l} d \big (e ^ {- r t} c (t, S (t)) \big) \\ = e ^ {- r t} \Big \{- r c (t, S (t)) + c _ {t} (t, S (t)) + (r - \tilde {\beta} \tilde {\lambda}) S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t)) \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} S ^ {2} (t) c _ {x x} (t, S (t)) \\ \qquad + \tilde {\lambda} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \big [ \tilde {p} (y _ {m}) c (t, (y _ {m} + 1) S (t)) - c (t, S (t)) \big ] \Big \} d t \\ + e ^ {- r t} \sigma S (t) c _ {x} (t, S (t))   d \widetilde {W} (t) \\ + \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} e ^ {- r t} \big [ c (t, (y _ {m} + 1) S (t -)) - c (t, S (t -)) \big ]   d (N _ {m} (t) - \tilde {\lambda} _ {m} t). \end{array}\tag{11.7.35}
